An essay develops a larger argument: introduction (topic and central claim), body paragraphs (one related point each, with support) and conclusion (synthesis, not an unrelated new argument). Plan for audience and purpose; revise for organisation before proofreading individual sentences.

## Report writing
A report presents findings for a purpose and audience. Depending on instructions, include title, date, purpose, method or background, findings, conclusion and recommendations. Separate observed facts from interpretations; do not invent data. Example: a report on a campus workshop could state attendance from the verified register, summarise activities and recommend future improvements. Institutions may require different formats.

## Letters and email
Formal letter: sender/contact details if needed, date, recipient, subject where appropriate, salutation, concise body, courteous close and name. State the request clearly. Informal letter: adapt address, greeting and tone to a friend or family member; it still needs clear organisation. Email: use a specific subject line, appropriate greeting, short paragraphs, clear action or deadline and a name.

Sample formal email:
Subject: Request for a classroom projector on 12 August
Dear Sir or Madam,
Please arrange a projector for the English workshop on 12 August, from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. in Room 204. Kindly confirm whether it is available.
Thank you,
Anita Rao

## Notice, agenda and minutes
A notice informs a defined audience about an event or instruction. Include organisation, heading, date, what, when, where, who is concerned and contact or signature as required. An agenda lists topics to be considered before a meeting. Minutes record what happened after it: meeting details, attendance where required, decisions, assigned actions and deadlines. Minutes are not a verbatim transcript unless specifically required. Formats vary by institution and examination.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10 min: Correct three sentences. 10–20: Build a paragraph from a topic sentence and examples. 20–30: Compare a formal letter and an email. 30–40: Groups write a notice using who/what/when/where. 40–47: Turn a short meeting scenario into an agenda and one decision in the minutes. 47–50: Review clarity and audience.

## Practice with answers
1. Correct: “The students was ready.” → “The students were ready.”
2. Which comes before a meeting: agenda or minutes? Agenda; minutes record the meeting afterwards.
3. Improve the subject “Hello”: “Request for projector for English workshop.”
4. Write a report recommendation only after distinguishing evidence from opinion.

## Reading note
The linked Purdue guide compares professional writing genres and their purposes. Use the university’s exam instructions for any required layout.

course-2:4.title: Unit 5 · Personality Development
course-2:4.text:
# Unit 5: Personality Development
Communicative English · Semester 1

## Learning outcomes
Students should be able to explain personal and interpersonal skills, use self-assessment to set a realistic goal, describe emotional intelligence, practise inclusive teamwork and identify a professional ethics issue.

## Personality development and soft skills
In this course, personality development can be understood as reflection on habits and the development of communication, confidence and interpersonal skills. It does not mean that everyone must be outgoing or adopt the same personality. Soft skills are transferable interpersonal and self-management skills such as listening, teamwork, adaptability and problem-solving. They complement subject knowledge and technical skills.

## Self-assessment
Self-assessment involves identifying strengths, areas for development, evidence and a next step. A simple plan: “I can explain ideas in a small group, but rush during presentations. For two weeks I will practise a three-minute talk, record it and ask a peer for one suggestion.” Goals should be specific and manageable; feedback is useful when it describes an observable behaviour rather than labelling a person.

## Emotional intelligence or emotional quotient
Emotional intelligence commonly refers to recognising and managing one’s own emotions and responding thoughtfully to others’ emotions. “Emotional quotient” or EQ is sometimes used as a label or score, but there is no single universally accepted test or one number that fully captures a person’s emotional abilities. In practice: notice frustration, pause, ask for clarification and respond without an attack. Empathy involves trying to understand another’s perspective; it does not mean assuming that you know their feelings.

## Body language
Posture, gesture, facial expression, space and tone can contribute to a message. A relaxed posture may help a speaker appear approachable in some situations. Interpret cues with care: customs, neurodiversity, disability and individual comfort differ. Never treat eye contact, crossed arms or a facial expression as reliable proof of honesty, confidence or intent. Ask respectful questions if a message is unclear.

## Leadership qualities
Leadership can involve setting a shared purpose, listening, allocating tasks fairly, making decisions, supporting others and taking responsibility. A leader who invites ideas, explains deadlines and checks what support is needed may improve group coordination. Leadership is not identical to speaking most or controlling every decision. Rotate roles so different students can practise facilitating, recording and reporting.

## Time management
List tasks, identify deadlines, estimate realistic time and break large tasks into smaller steps. Prioritise important work, add breaks and buffer time, and revise the plan when circumstances change. Example: prepare a presentation by selecting sources on Monday, drafting on Tuesday and rehearsing on Wednesday. Time management is a practical skill, not a guarantee that every student has equal resources or free time.

## Professional ethics
Professional ethics concerns responsible conduct in a role. Relevant principles include honesty, fairness, respect, confidentiality when appropriate, accountability and acknowledging sources. Example: if you use another author’s ideas in a presentation, credit the source; if a classmate shares private information, do not circulate it without a valid reason or consent. Follow institutional rules and seek guidance where obligations conflict.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8 min: Students list a strength and a skill to practise privately. 8–18: Discuss soft skills and observable examples. 18–28: Role-play a misunderstanding; pause, clarify and respond respectfully. 28–38: A group plans a task with rotated roles. 38–45: Build a realistic weekly plan. 45–50: Exit ticket: identify an ethical issue and one responsible response.

## Practice with suggested answers
1. A teammate is late: instead of assuming laziness, ask privately what happened and agree on a plan.
2. You use a quotation in slides: acknowledge the source and check wording.
3. A presentation is due next week: divide preparation into research, draft and rehearsal, allowing time for revision.

## Questions
How can self-assessment lead to an actionable goal? What is the difference between empathy and assuming another person’s feelings? Why should body language be interpreted cautiously? Give two leadership practices and one ethical responsibility.

## Reading note
The linked open textbook discusses communication and perception; use the prescribed course references for additional material on leadership and professional ethics.

course-3:0.title: Unit 1 · Reading Comprehension
course-3:0.text:
# Unit 1: Reading Comprehension
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Objectives
Identify main ideas and details; infer meaning using evidence; assess tone, style and rhetorical choices; use skimming, scanning, intensive and extensive reading purposefully.

## Main idea and supporting detail
The topic is what a passage is about; the main idea is what it says about that topic. Supporting details give reasons, examples or evidence. For each paragraph, ask: What is its function? Does it introduce a claim, explain, qualify or conclude? A good title captures the whole passage rather than a single example.

## Inference and critical evaluation
An inference is a conclusion reasonably supported by stated evidence, not a free guess. Notice words such as “some”, “may” and “often”: replacing them with “all”, “must” or “always” may make an answer too strong. Critical reading asks who makes the claim, what evidence is supplied, what assumptions are necessary and whether alternative explanations exist. A claim and proof are different.

## Strategies
Skim for the general direction and structure. Scan for a particular name, figure or term. Read intensively when the exact logic or wording matters. Extensive reading means reading larger quantities, often for broad understanding and vocabulary development. In an exam, preview the questions, read for overall sense and return to the relevant lines; strategy can vary with the test.

## Tone, style and devices
Tone is the writer’s attitude, for example cautious, critical or enthusiastic; support the answer with language from the passage. Style concerns how the writer uses language. Rhetorical devices include contrast, repetition, analogy, rhetorical question and irony. An analogy explains one thing by comparing it with another; it can clarify an argument but does not by itself prove it. Irony depends on context: do not call every humorous sentence ironic.

## Worked exercise
Passage: “The town library extended its weekend hours. Attendance increased, but staff observed that many visitors still had difficulty reaching the building because buses were infrequent. The council is considering a later bus service.”
1. Main idea: the library’s longer hours increased use, while transport remained a problem.
2. Detail: buses were infrequent.
3. Inference: transport may affect some people’s ability to use the library. We cannot infer that all non-users lack transport.
4. Has the council introduced a later bus? No; it is considering one.
5. Tone: informative and measured; the text reports changes and qualifications without exaggerated language.

## 50-minute class
0–10 min: explain topic, main idea and detail. 10–20: skim and title the passage. 20–30: scan for facts and justify an inference. 30–40: evaluate a stronger but unsupported claim. 40–47: identify tone and one rhetorical device in a second passage. 47–50: exit ticket: explain how to test an inference.

## Practice and revision
1. A passage reports one successful trial. Can we conclude a method always works? No; one trial does not establish universal success.
2. Which strategy locates an examination date? Scanning, followed by checking context.
3. Explain how a contrast contributes to an argument using a passage of your choice.

## Reading note
Practise with passages from different genres, including academic prose, reports and opinion writing. Do not assume every exam uses the same pattern or marking scheme.

course-3:1.title: Unit 2 · Functional Grammar
course-3:1.text:
# Unit 2: Functional Grammar
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Parts of speech
A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands for a noun phrase; a verb expresses an action, state or relation; an adjective modifies a noun; an adverb often modifies a verb, adjective, clause or another adverb; a preposition links a noun phrase to another element; a conjunction connects words or clauses; an interjection expresses an immediate reaction. A word’s function depends on context: “book” is a noun in “a book” and a verb in “book a room.”

## Articles and prepositions
Use “a” before a consonant sound (“a university”) and “an” before a vowel sound (“an hour”); “the” usually identifies a specific or already understood referent. Some nouns in general statements take no article: “Books can help.” Prepositions express relationships, but usage is often conventional: “interested in”, “depend on”, “arrive at the station” and “arrive in Chennai.” Learn phrases in context, not as isolated lists.

## Subject–verb agreement
A singular subject generally takes a singular present-tense verb: “The student reads.” Plural: “The students read.” Find the actual subject, not just the nearest noun: “The list of books is on the table.” With “each”, agreement is normally singular: “Each student has a card.” Some collective nouns vary by dialect and meaning.

## Active and passive
Active: “The committee approved the plan.” Passive: “The plan was approved by the committee.” The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive; a form of “be” and a past participle are used. Retain tense when transforming. Passive is useful when the action or recipient matters more than the actor, but should not hide responsibility when the actor matters.

## Clauses, reported speech and phrasal verbs
A clause has a subject and predicate: “because it rained” is dependent; “the match stopped” can stand independently. “The match stopped because it rained” combines them. In reported speech, pronouns, time expressions and tense may change according to context: She said, “I am tired” → She said that she was tired. Backshift is common after a past reporting verb but is not automatic when a fact still holds. A phrasal verb combines a verb and particle: “look up a word”; “give up” means stop trying. Their meanings depend on context.

## Vocabulary relationships
An idiom is an expression whose meaning may not be predictable from its separate words; “once in a blue moon” means rarely. Synonyms are similar in a given context, not always interchangeable; antonyms express contrast. Use context to select the best answer.

## Practice with answers
1. “She is ___ honest person.” → an (initial vowel sound).
2. “The box of pencils ___ on the table.” → is (subject: box).
3. Change “They built the bridge in 2000” to passive. → “The bridge was built in 2000.”
4. “Because it rained” is a dependent clause; it needs an independent clause to complete that sentence.
5. Report “I am ready,” said Mira. → Mira said that she was ready, in an ordinary past-reporting context.
6. “Look up” in “look up the meaning” means search for information.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify parts of speech in context. 10–20: articles and agreement. 20–30: transform active/passive sentences. 30–40: clauses and reported speech. 40–47: contextual vocabulary. 47–50: one corrected sentence with explanation.

## Exam reminder
Read the complete sentence, identify its meaning and structure, and check agreement and tense after choosing an answer. Explanations above are introductory; context and accepted varieties matter.

course-3:2.title: Unit 3 · Written Communication
course-3:2.text:
# Unit 3: Written Communication
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Paragraphs and essays
A paragraph develops one central point with explanation and support. An essay typically introduces its topic and thesis, develops connected arguments in body paragraphs, and concludes by synthesising the response. For exam writing, interpret the instruction: “discuss” may require several perspectives, while “evaluate” requires reasoned judgement. Plan before writing.

## Description, narration and argument
Description presents features of a person, place or situation through selected details. Narration relates events in a meaningful sequence, using time markers where helpful. Argument makes a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence; acknowledge a relevant counterargument rather than misrepresenting it. Example: Claim: the college should extend library hours. Reason: students need access after class. Evidence should be a verified survey or usage record, not an invented statistic.

## Reports, letters and notes
A report’s headings depend on the question but may include purpose, method, findings and recommendations. A formal letter gives recipient and date as required, a clear purpose, supporting details and a courteous closing; an informal letter uses a tone appropriate to a personal relationship. Note-making selects main points and subpoints, using consistent abbreviations and a clear title or key when required.

## Summary, paraphrase and précis
A summary condenses the central ideas in fresh language. A paraphrase restates a selected passage in different words and structure while preserving its meaning and usually similar scope. A précis is a concise, coherent restatement of a longer passage’s essential argument; follow the exam’s word limit and format. In academic work, credit the original for summaries and paraphrases as well as quotations. Do not insert your own unsupported opinion into a neutral summary.

## Notice and poster
A notice conveys a specific announcement: organisation, heading, date, event or instruction, time, place, relevant audience and contact/signature as required. A poster combines brief text with visual hierarchy for an audience and purpose. Its format depends on the exam; include essential information rather than assuming decoration earns more marks than clarity.

## Worked example
Original: “The college opened a reading room in the evening. Students who worked during the day could use it after their shifts. The library plans to monitor attendance before deciding whether to continue.”
Possible summary: “The college is testing evening reading-room access to help working students and will review attendance before continuing.” This preserves the purpose and conditional future decision without claiming the service is permanent.

## 50-minute class
0–10: identify the purpose and audience of an essay. 10–20: draft a supported paragraph. 20–30: distinguish summary from paraphrase. 30–40: produce a notice with all key facts. 40–47: peer-review for omissions and invented details. 47–50: revise one sentence.

## Review
1. Difference between summary and paraphrase? A summary condenses central ideas; a paraphrase restates a selected passage with its meaning intact.
2. A notice must identify the event, time and place, among other required details.
3. Which claim is stronger: “The change is useful” or a claim with verifiable supporting evidence? The supported claim, assuming the evidence is relevant.

## Examination note
Follow the particular examination’s current word limits and marking instructions; the syllabus itself does not establish one universal format for all competitive exams.

course-3:3.title: Unit 4 · Listening and Speaking Skills
course-3:3.text:
# Unit 4: Listening and Speaking Skills
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Listening and hearing
Hearing is the perception of sound; listening includes attending, interpreting and responding. Listening helps candidates follow instructions, answer relevantly and understand other viewpoints. A useful routine is to focus, note key words, listen to the complete question, ask for clarification where permitted, and check the interpretation before responding.

## Effective speech
A clear speech suits the audience and purpose. Organise a central message, a few logically ordered points and a conclusion. Speak audibly at a comfortable pace, articulate key terms, and use examples accurately. Fluency does not require one accent or uninterrupted speech: effective communication is intelligible, appropriate and responsive. Avoid inventing facts or forcing unfamiliar vocabulary.

## Social exchanges and dialogue
Examples: greeting—“Good morning. How are you?”; request—“Could you please explain the next step?”; clarification—“Do you mean that the form is due on Monday?”; polite disagreement—“I see your point, but I think another factor matters.” Adapt formality to situation. A dialogue requires turn-taking as well as asking and answering questions.

## Persuasive arguments
A persuasive argument makes a specific claim and supplies reasons and appropriate support. Model: “The library should open later on two weekdays because many students have classes during the day. The college could pilot the change and review actual attendance.” Acknowledge limits: longer hours also need staffing and funding. A proposal does not become true merely because it is confidently delivered.

## Elocution
Elocution is the practice of clear and effective spoken delivery. In a short speech, mark pauses at meaningful boundaries, vary emphasis appropriately and rehearse for time. Interpret the speech’s purpose and audience. Volume, speed, stress and intonation can affect clarity; performance should not be judged by an arbitrary claim that only one accent is correct.

## Class practice
Pairs: one student gives three instructions for a campus event; the other paraphrases them before acting. Groups: give a one-minute persuasive proposal, followed by one question and a respectful answer. Elocution: read a short passage twice, first for meaning and then with deliberate pauses.

## Sample questions and responses
1. What is the difference between hearing and listening? Hearing is sound perception; listening actively attends to and interprets it.
2. Give an appropriate clarification. “Could you repeat the last date for submitting the form?”
3. Name two qualities of effective speech. Clear organisation and suitable pacing; other supported answers are possible.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: hearing and listening. 10–20: listening-and-paraphrase exercise. 20–30: social dialogue. 30–40: develop a claim and reason. 40–47: short delivery practice. 47–50: feedback on one specific behaviour.

## Exam reminder
Check the specific test’s interview or speaking instructions. Prepared scripts should not replace listening to the question actually asked.

course-3:4.title: Unit 5 · Study Skills
course-3:4.text:
# Unit 5: Study Skills
English for Competitive Exams · Semester 1

## Building vocabulary
Learn words in meaningful sentences. Record definition, part of speech, pronunciation, collocations and an example. Review across several sessions and use the word in your own writing. Check a dictionary when a meaning inferred from context is uncertain. Similar words may differ in register or collocation: accuracy matters more than using difficult words.

## Research and library tools
Begin with a focused question and useful keywords; add synonyms. A catalogue identifies items in a library’s collection. Books can offer sustained treatment; periodicals include journals and magazines, whose purposes vary. A bibliography lists works relevant to or used in a topic. An index helps locate a subject within a book or collection. Evaluate authorship, date, evidence and relevance before trusting a source. Search results are starting points, not automatic proof.

## Note-making and source use
Separate your own ideas from a source’s claims. Record author, title, publication details and page numbers as you read so you can return to the source. Use headings and concise points. Summarising condenses central ideas; paraphrasing restates a passage’s meaning in your own words and structure; quoting reproduces exact wording with quotation marks and an appropriate citation. All three require acknowledgement when using another person’s work. Follow the requested citation style rather than mixing systems.

## References list
A reference list gives readers enough information to locate cited material. Its exact order, punctuation and treatment of authors vary by style, such as MLA or APA. Check the edition of the relevant style guide and your teacher’s instructions. Do not fabricate missing publication information.

## Answering an exam question
1. Read the whole question and underline the task, topic and limits.
2. Allocate time in proportion to marks, while following the exam’s rules.
3. Draft a brief plan: direct answer, relevant points, examples and conclusion where needed.
4. Write legibly and stay within the requested scope; avoid memorised material that does not answer the question.
5. Reserve time to check meaning, omissions, calculations where relevant and grammar.
6. Evaluate your answer against the question and marking guidance, not merely its length.

## Worked example
Question: “Explain two barriers to listening and suggest a response to each.” A relevant plan has two barrier–response pairs: noise → move to a quieter space; unfamiliar terminology → ask for definitions and an example. A generic essay about communication that omits responses does not fully answer the task.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: vocabulary log. 10–20: catalogue, index and bibliography. 20–30: summary versus paraphrase and quote. 30–40: plan an answer to the example. 40–47: peer-check for both required responses. 47–50: self-assessment.

## Questions
Why do paraphrases need citation? What is the difference between a library catalogue and a book index? How can a student use a question’s command words when planning?

## Reading note
The Purdue research guide explains source use. Citation requirements depend on the assignment or exam.

course-4:0.title: Unit I · Working with Grammar
course-4:0.text:
# Unit I: Working with Grammar
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Sentence construction and types
A basic complete sentence has a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete thought: “The students are discussing the poem.” Sentences can make statements, ask questions, issue requests or commands, and express strong feeling. They may be simple (one independent clause), compound (independent clauses joined) or complex (an independent clause with a dependent clause). In conversation, shorter fragments can also be meaningful in context.

## Parts of speech and auxiliaries
Nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections perform different roles. Auxiliary verbs help form questions, negatives, tense, aspect or modality: “Do you read?”, “She is speaking”, “They have arrived”, “We can try.” Match the auxiliary to the intended meaning; “can” often expresses ability or possibility, while “must” can express strong obligation or inference depending on context.

## Number, agreement and determiners
Singular: “A student is ready.” Plural: “Students are ready.” The subject determines verb agreement: “The quality of the answers is important.” Determiners specify or quantify nouns: a/an, the, this, these, some, many and each. “A university” and “an hour” show that a/an depends on initial sound, not spelling. Context matters when choosing “some” or “any.”

## Active and passive; comparison
Active: “The teacher asked a question.” Passive: “A question was asked by the teacher.” Preserve tense and meaning when changing voice. Comparison: “clear, clearer, clearest”; “important, more important, most important.” Irregular forms include good, better, best. Avoid doubling the comparative: “more better” is not standard edited English.

## Punctuation and common usage
Written speech transcripts still need appropriate capitals, full stops, question marks and commas. Speech itself uses pauses and intonation, not visible punctuation. Compare “She speaks clearly” with “Does she speak clearly?” Common standard-form corrections: “He go” → “He goes”; “She is senior than me” → “She is senior to me.” Do not equate a regional accent with a grammatical error.

## Practice with answers
1. Form a question: “You are ready.” → “Are you ready?”
2. Agree: “Each student ___ a notebook.” → has.
3. Passive: “They completed the task.” → “The task was completed.”
4. Compare: “This road is ___ than that road.” → longer, or another suitable comparative adjective.
5. Identify the auxiliary in “She has finished.” → has.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: construct sentences from word cards. 10–20: auxiliaries and question formation. 20–30: agreement in a dialogue. 30–40: active and passive role-play. 40–47: comparison and corrections. 47–50: exit ticket with one explanation.

## Review
How does an auxiliary help form a question? Why does “list” rather than “books” control agreement in “the list of books is”? When is passive voice useful?

course-4:1.title: Unit II · Vocabulary Building and Pronunciation
course-4:1.text:
# Unit II: Vocabulary Building and Pronunciation
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Word formation
Prefixes attach before a base (un + clear → unclear); suffixes attach after it (teach + er → teacher). Some word classes change through suffixes: decide (verb), decision (noun), decisive (adjective). Form and meaning are not always predictable, so check a dictionary. A compound joins elements, as in “classroom”; spelling conventions differ.

## Word relationships and use
Synonyms are similar in context (begin/start); antonyms contrast (possible/impossible). Homonyms are words with the same spelling or sound but different meanings; terminology varies between dictionaries. For example “bank” can mean a financial institution or the side of a river. One-word substitutes condense a definition: a person who writes poems is a poet. For odd-one-out questions, identify a defensible shared feature: rose, jasmine, lotus, carrot → carrot is a vegetable while the others are commonly classified as flowers.

Idioms may have non-literal meanings: “break the ice” means ease an awkward beginning. Practise joining sentences with appropriate relationships: “It rained. We stayed indoors.” → “Because it rained, we stayed indoors.” Do not join clauses in a way that changes the original meaning.

## Vowels and consonants
Speech sounds are made by the vocal organs; spelling and sound do not correspond one-to-one in English. Vowels generally involve relatively open airflow, while consonants involve some obstruction or narrowing. A phoneme is a sound category that can distinguish meaning in a language or variety. Pronunciation varies legitimately across Englishes, so use a suitable model and seek intelligibility rather than erasing a speaker’s accent.

## Word stress, sentence stress and intonation
Word stress makes one syllable more prominent: in a common pronunciation, REcord is a noun and reCORD is a verb. Check the dictionary for the variety being taught. Sentence stress highlights information relevant to meaning: “I wanted the RED book” contrasts colour. Intonation is the movement of pitch across an utterance; a question may rise or fall depending on its form, meaning and context. Do not present one pitch pattern as universal for every question.

## Practice with answers
1. Change “happy” to a noun: happiness.
2. Antonym of “accept” in many contexts: reject.
3. Join: “She was tired. She completed the work.” → “Although she was tired, she completed the work.”
4. Explain “bank” in “river bank”: land alongside a river.
5. Say “I asked for the RED pen” and then “I asked for the red PEN”; discuss which contrast each emphasis suggests.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: form word families. 10–20: synonyms, antonyms and idioms in context. 20–30: listen and identify prominent syllables. 30–40: practise sentence emphasis and intonation in pairs. 40–47: join sentences with logical connectors. 47–50: record one new word and example.

## Review
Why does spelling not always predict pronunciation? How can sentence stress change the information highlighted? Why should students hear more than one intelligible variety of English?

course-4:2.title: Unit III · Conversational Skills
course-4:2.text:
# Unit III: Conversational Skills
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Beginning and sustaining conversation
A conversation involves listening, responding and taking turns. In a new setting, greet the person, introduce yourself and ask a relevant open or closed question. Example: “Good morning. I’m Meena from the English department. How did you find the workshop?” Follow up using what the person actually says. Respect the other person’s willingness to talk; a conversation is not a list of memorised questions.

## Asking and answering questions
Closed questions often invite a short answer: “Is the library open?” Open questions invite explanation: “What did you find useful about the session?” Use “Could you repeat that?” or “Do you mean…?” to clarify. Answer directly first, then add a relevant detail. Politeness depends on relationship and context, not a fixed formula alone.

## Description
For a person, choose relevant details such as role, interests or observed behaviour; avoid unnecessary assumptions about appearance or identity. For a place, orient the listener and select significant features. For an event, identify what happened, where, when and why it mattered. Example: “The seminar was held in the library on Tuesday. Students discussed how to evaluate online sources.”

## Extempore, persuasive and descriptive speaking
Extempore speaking uses limited preparation; take a moment to organise an opening, two points and a closing. A persuasive talk makes a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence. A descriptive talk helps the listener visualise a subject through purposeful detail. In all cases, adapt your voice, vocabulary and length to the audience; neither loudness nor an unfamiliar accent is a measure of the quality of ideas.

## Narration and character
A narrative usually establishes setting and characters, presents a sequence or problem and describes an outcome. Use time markers such as “first,” “later” and “finally” where useful. To describe a character, distinguish a stated fact from an interpretation: “She returns the lost book” is an action; “she is considerate” is an interpretation supported by that action. Explain situations without presenting an assumption as a fact.

## Model activity
Tell a one-minute account: “On Monday, our class planned a reading event. At first, the room was unavailable. We spoke to the librarian, found another space and held the event on Friday. The experience showed us the value of planning alternatives.” Listeners identify setting, problem, action and outcome; then ask one clarification question.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introductions in pairs. 10–20: open and closed questions. 20–30: describe a place without naming it; partner asks questions. 30–40: one-minute narration. 40–47: brief persuasive speech with one reason. 47–50: constructive peer feedback.

## Questions
What makes a follow-up question effective? How does a descriptive speech differ from a persuasive one? What evidence supports a claim about a fictional character?

course-4:3.title: Unit IV · Group Communication
course-4:3.text:
# Unit IV: Group Communication
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Group discussion
A group discussion is a structured exchange in which participants contribute to a shared purpose. It is not a competition to speak most. Begin by identifying the question and time available. Participants offer relevant points, listen, support claims with examples, respond to others and help the group summarise its position. If disagreement occurs, address the idea rather than attacking the person.

Useful expressions: “Could we define the problem first?” “I would like to add…” “What evidence supports that?” “We seem to agree on two points, but differ on the third.” A facilitator can invite a quieter member without forcing anyone to disclose personal information.

## Assigning tasks and leadership
Divide a task into manageable roles: facilitator, researcher, timekeeper, note-taker and presenter are possible examples. Explain each role, expected output and deadline. Rotate responsibilities so all students practise speaking and coordination. A leader checks progress, clarifies uncertainty and shares decisions; leadership need not mean doing all the work.

## Task completion and cohesion
Example task: plan a college reading event. Agree on audience, venue, budget assumptions, responsibilities and deadline. Each participant reports progress, identifies obstacles and asks for help where needed. Summarise decisions in writing. Group cohesion means a sense of shared purpose and respectful cooperation, not an obligation to agree on everything. Clear goals, fair participation and constructive conflict resolution can support it.

## Group presentations and slides
Organise the presentation with an introduction, coordinated sections and a conclusion. Rehearse transitions between speakers and keep to the allotted time. Slides should support, not replace, speech: use readable text, clear headings and relevant visuals, and credit sources. Do not overload slides or read every word aloud. Check accessibility, including contrast and descriptions of important visuals; provide materials in accessible formats when needed. Slide software is one possible tool, not a prerequisite for every presentation.

## 50-minute lesson
0–8: explain discussion purpose and roles. 8–15: assign roles for the reading-event task. 15–30: groups plan and record decisions. 30–42: each group presents for three minutes. 42–47: peers provide one strength and one improvement. 47–50: members reflect on whether everyone had an opportunity to contribute.

## Assessment checklist
Was the response relevant? Did the student listen and build on a point? Were reasons understandable? Was speaking time shared? Did the group report decisions accurately? Feedback should focus on observable actions, not assumptions about personality or accent.

## Questions
What is the difference between leadership and domination? How can roles improve accountability? What makes a slide useful? How can a group disagree respectfully?

course-4:4.title: Unit V · Listening Skills and Non-verbal Communication
course-4:4.text:
# Unit V: Listening Skills and Non-verbal Communication
Spoken English · Semester 1

## Why listening matters
Listening supports comprehension, cooperation and accurate responses. Hearing sound is not the same as understanding it. Active listening includes paying attention, recognising the speaker’s purpose, paraphrasing a key point and requesting clarification. It does not require agreement with everything said.

## Basics and barriers
Listen first for the situation and general message; then note important details, distinctions and the speaker’s purpose. Noise, a poor audio connection, unfamiliar vocabulary, fatigue, stress, prejudice and rehearsing a reply can interfere. Reduce distractions, request repetition or accessible formats, take selective notes and check interpretation. Treat listening as a learnable practice rather than a personality label.

## Listening for gist, style and tone
Gist is the overall point: “The speaker wants the meeting postponed.” Style refers to features of expression, such as formal or conversational wording. Tone is the attitude conveyed—perhaps concerned, enthusiastic or uncertain. Base tone judgements on words and delivery together, and recognise that accent, cultural differences or vocal disability can affect interpretation. If a message is ambiguous, ask rather than declaring what the speaker feels.

## Voice recording exercises
With participants’ permission, record a short speech or dialogue and listen back. First check whether the central point is clear; then review pace, audible volume, pauses and transitions. Identify one strength and one manageable next step. Recording must be optional or accommodated when necessary; do not share recordings without consent. The aim is intelligibility and confidence, not eliminating a regional accent.

## Non-verbal communication and etiquette
Gesture, posture, personal space, facial expression and eye behaviour can support or complicate spoken meaning. A listener may indicate attention by a verbal response, a nod, a question or another culturally and personally appropriate behaviour. Avoid diagnosing honesty or interest from a single gesture. Expectations differ by context, culture, neurodiversity and disability. Etiquette means respectful behaviour suited to the situation: wait for a turn, ask before recording, respect personal space and use a courteous form of address.

## Practice
A speaker says: “The event is moving to Friday because the hall is unavailable on Thursday.” Gist: the event has moved to Friday. Key reason: the hall is unavailable Thursday. A listener should not infer the event has been cancelled.
Pair activity: one student describes a route for thirty seconds; the other paraphrases and asks a clarification. Compare the original and paraphrase without penalising harmless differences in wording.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish hearing, gist and detail. 10–20: route-listening exercise. 20–30: identify barriers and solutions. 30–40: optional recording and self-review. 40–47: discuss different interpretations of a gesture. 47–50: exit ticket: give one respectful clarification question.

## Questions
What is listening for gist? Name two barriers and solutions. Why is one gesture not conclusive evidence of a person’s feelings? What makes feedback on a recording constructive?

course-8:0.title: William Blake · The Lamb
course-8:0.text:
# The Lamb
William Blake · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Context and overview
“The Lamb” appears in Songs of Innocence (1789). A child speaker addresses a lamb, asks who made it, and answers through Christian imagery. The poem’s apparently simple language carries ideas about creation, childhood and the relationship between the divine and the natural world. Innocence is a perspective represented in the poem, not evidence that suffering does not exist.

## Stanza-by-stanza explanation
Stanza 1: The speaker asks the lamb who gave it life, food by the stream and meadow, soft wool and a gentle voice. The repeated question creates a song-like rhythm. The lamb’s body and surroundings are presented as gifts, bringing attention to the ordinary life of a creature.
Stanza 2: The speaker offers the answer: the creator shares the name “Lamb,” is gentle, and became a child. This refers to Christ, called the Lamb of God in Christian tradition, and to the Incarnation. The speaker identifies as a child and connects child, lamb and Christ through shared names and qualities. The final blessing expresses affection and faith.

## Form and interpretation
Two ten-line stanzas create a question-and-answer structure. Repetition, simple vocabulary and rhyming sounds resemble a hymn or a child’s song. The lamb is both a literal young animal and a religious symbol. Compare the assured answer here with the more troubled question about creation in Blake’s “The Tyger”; the comparison is useful context, not a claim that “The Tyger” is prescribed in this unit.

## Classroom activity
Read the poem aloud. Students list the lamb’s physical gifts, then identify what religious meaning the second stanza gives them. Ask whether a child’s voice makes the answer seem more credible, more vulnerable, or both.

## Questions
1. How do question and answer organise the poem?
2. Why is the lamb a suitable image for the speaker’s account of Christ?
3. What effect does repetition create?
4. How can a literal animal also carry symbolic meaning?
5. What might a comparison with “The Tyger” add to the idea of creation?

## Reading note
Use the linked text or a reliable annotated edition; Blake’s illuminated editions and later print editions may differ in punctuation.

course-8:0.title: P. B. Shelley · Ode to the West Wind
course-8:0.text:
# Ode to the West Wind
Percy Bysshe Shelley · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Introduction
The speaker addresses the autumn wind as a powerful force that destroys and preserves. He first describes its effects on the natural world, then asks it to energise his own voice and carry his ideas to others. Written in 1819 and published in 1820, the poem can be read in relation to Romantic interest in nature, imagination and political renewal, without reducing it to a single political message.

## Section-by-section summary
I. Land: The wind drives dead leaves and carries seeds into the ground. The seeds lie dormant until spring. The wind appears destructive in autumn but also helps preserve the possibility of new life.
II. Sky: The wind moves clouds and gathers a storm. Images of rain, lightning and the closing year give the sky the force of a vast funeral song. The expected storm is both frightening and full of energy.
III. Sea: The wind disturbs the Mediterranean, imagined waking from summer calm and dreams of old palaces. It also divides Atlantic waters; marine growth responds to its force. The movement expands the poem’s scale from land to air to sea.
IV. Speaker: The speaker wishes he were a leaf, cloud or wave carried by the wind, and remembers a time when he felt freer. He describes himself as burdened by life and asks the wind to lift him. Description becomes a personal plea.
V. Poetry and renewal: He asks the wind to play him as an instrument, scatter his thoughts and words like leaves, ashes and sparks, and become a voice of prophecy. The final question connects winter with the possibility of spring: hope is voiced as a question rather than guaranteed as an immediate outcome.

## Form and themes
Five fourteen-line sections use interlocking rhymes related to terza rima, each ending with a couplet. Apostrophe addresses the wind directly; personification gives it agency. Destruction and renewal coexist, while the speaker’s wish to be the wind’s instrument complicates the idea of the poet as completely independent. Seeds are dormant, not biologically dead, even though the poem compares them to corpses.

## Teaching and questions
Map land, sky, sea, speaker and poem on the board. What makes the wind both destroyer and preserver? How does section IV change the poem’s perspective? What do lyre and trumpet suggest about poetic voice? Is the final question a promise or an expression of hope?

## Reading note
Read the full five sections in the linked Poetry Foundation text and check an annotated edition for classical and historical allusions.

course-8:0.title: Elizabeth Barrett Browning · How do I love thee?
course-8:0.text:
# Sonnets from the Portuguese 43: How do I love thee?
Elizabeth Barrett Browning · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Context and overview
This fourteen-line sonnet belongs to Sonnets from the Portuguese, published in 1850. The speaker answers an opening question by describing the breadth of her love, moving from spiritual dimensions to ordinary needs, ethical ideals, past suffering and a hope beyond death. The sequence is associated with Browning’s relationship with Robert Browning, but the speaker in a poem should not be treated as a complete, unmediated biography.

## Movement of the poem
Opening: The speaker asks how she loves and offers to count the ways. The response begins with spatial dimensions—depth, breadth and height—to suggest the reach of the soul towards existence and grace.
Everyday life: Love is also present in quiet daily needs, whether by sunlight or candlelight. The poem moves between the vast and the ordinary rather than treating them as opposites.
Moral freedom: The speaker describes love as freely and purely offered, using comparisons to the pursuit of right and a refusal of praise. Love is presented as an ethical commitment rather than a demand for public reward.
Memory and feeling: Passion once invested in grief and faith once associated with childhood are redirected into love. The reference to lost saints suggests a changing relationship to earlier devotion; its exact implications remain open to interpretation.
Conclusion: Love includes breath, smiles and tears across the speaker’s life. The final hope that love may continue after death is conditional on God’s will; do not present it as an unconditional prediction.

## Form and themes
The poem uses a Petrarchan or Italian sonnet framework, with an octave and sestet and an ABBA ABBA CDCDCD rhyme pattern in the standard text. Repetition of “I love thee” creates an accumulation that seems larger than a simple count. Themes include love and faith, everyday care, memory, agency and mortality.

## Teaching activity and questions
Ask students to group images into spiritual, daily, ethical and emotional categories. How does repetition change the force of the claim? Why combine ordinary needs with the soul’s reach? What does the conditional final line add? Compare its catalogue of love with Shakespeare’s definition in Sonnet 116.

## Reading note
Read the linked text in full and check punctuation and line references against the prescribed edition.

course-8:0.title: T. S. Eliot · The Waste Land, Parts I and II
course-8:0.text:
# The Waste Land: Parts I and II
T. S. Eliot · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Scope and approach
The syllabus specifies Part I, “The Burial of the Dead,” and Part II, “A Game of Chess.” Published in 1922, the poem uses changing voices, allusions, languages and abrupt transitions. It should not be forced into a single continuous plot or assigned one stable narrator throughout. The following overview covers the prescribed sections; later sections belong to the complete poem but are not substituted for them.

## Part I: The Burial of the Dead
1. Spring is presented as unsettling rather than simply joyful: it awakens memory and desire in a landscape associated with death. Winter, paradoxically, appears to offer a kind of protective forgetfulness.
2. A voice remembers a summer journey and childhood sledding, with references to European identity and the movement between places. The memory is fragmentary, not a complete biography.
3. Images of a dry, broken landscape and echoes of biblical prophecy introduce fear and a search for shelter or meaning. The poem then recalls an encounter with a “hyacinth girl,” ending in a moment of speechlessness and uncertain perception; interpretations of the moment differ.
4. Madame Sosostris, a fortune-teller with a cold, displays a set of cards and issues ominous warnings. The mixture of supernatural prediction and ordinary illness produces an ironic tone; the cards are not a straightforward, standard tarot reading.
5. In the “Unreal City,” a crowd crosses London Bridge in a deathlike routine. A speaker addresses Stetson and asks about a corpse planted in a garden. The disturbing image connects burial, possible growth and violence, ending with an address that implicates the reader.

## Part II: A Game of Chess
1. An elaborate interior of mirrors, perfume and luxurious objects suggests wealth but also confinement. Mythological and literary references include Philomela, whose story involves sexual violence and transformation; her voice persists despite violation.
2. An anxious exchange follows, with questions and disjointed responses or thoughts. The relationship between the voices is not fully explained. Their difficulty communicating creates tension within apparent intimacy.
3. The scene shifts to a pub conversation about Lil, her husband Albert, her appearance and the consequences of repeated childbearing and medication. The speaker pressures Lil to meet social expectations. Closing-time calls interrupt the conversation; farewells echo Ophelia in Hamlet. Read Lil’s situation with attention to reproductive pressure and class rather than mocking her.

## Techniques and interpretation
Fragmentation and montage place scenes without smooth explanation; allusion brings other texts into the present; shifting registers move between elevated description and colloquial talk. Motifs of dryness, death, memory and communication link the sections. The poem can be studied in relation to postwar modernism, but no single character should automatically be identified with Eliot or a person in his life.

## Questions
Why reverse the usual association of spring with hope? What connects the fortune-teller and the city crowd? How do the luxurious room and pub scene differ in class and setting? How do Philomela and Ophelia complicate the representation of women’s voices? What does fragmentation require readers to do?

## Reading note
Use a reliable edition and its explanatory notes. Quotations and allusions should be checked in the assigned text; the linked guide is secondary.

course-8:1.title: Philip Larkin · Church Going
course-8:1.text:
# Church Going
Philip Larkin · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Overview
A speaker enters an empty church, initially responding with awkward humour and apparent scepticism. He then considers why he keeps visiting such places and what churches may mean if traditional belief declines. The ending recognises their association with serious human experiences without simply declaring that the speaker has recovered religious faith.

## Movement through the poem
1. The speaker checks that no service is taking place and enters. He notices the familiar furnishings, flowers, organ and silence. Hatless, he removes his bicycle clips in an awkward gesture of respect.
2. He examines the building, reads briefly from the lectern, signs the visitors’ book and leaves a small donation. His casual expressions and comic gestures contrast with the solemn setting. He tells himself the visit was not worth it, yet admits he repeatedly stops at churches.
3. He wonders what will happen if churches cease to be used for worship: some might become museums while others fall into ruin. He imagines future superstitions and asks what remains when both belief and disbelief have faded.
4. He returns to the question of why the place draws him. Churches have gathered ceremonies and thoughts relating to birth, marriage and death. He comes to see the building as a place where people can confront serious questions and shared mortality, even when conventional belief is uncertain.

## Form and themes
Seven nine-line stanzas organise a conversational meditation. The title can suggest attending church and the possible disappearance of churches. Tone moves from comic deflation to reflective seriousness, without entirely abandoning doubt. Themes include secularisation, ritual, architecture, community and death.

## Questions and activity
Map the changes in tone: what is funny at the start, and what becomes serious? Why does the speaker keep visiting? What futures does he imagine for church buildings? Does the ending affirm a religious doctrine or the value of a space for reflection? Support different answers from the poem.

## Reading note
Use a licensed or library edition of the complete poem; the linked EBSCO overview supplies background and analysis.

course-8:1.title: Ted Hughes · Hawk Roosting
course-8:1.text:
# Hawk Roosting
Ted Hughes · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Overview
The poem gives a hawk a first-person voice. From its high perch, the bird describes its body, its view of the world, its power to kill and its desire to maintain control. The voice is imagined and personified; it is not a scientific account of what a hawk literally thinks.

## Stanza-by-stanza movement
1. The hawk sits at the top of the wood with closed eyes. Even in rest, the image of its hooked head and feet and its imagined perfect kills emphasises predatory form and instinct.
2. High trees, air and sunlight seem convenient to the bird. The earth is presented as if it exists for its inspection, showing how completely the speaker centres itself.
3. Its feet grip the bark. The hawk claims that creation was needed to produce each part of its body and then reverses the relation by claiming to hold creation in its foot.
4. Whether perched or flying, it asserts ownership and the power to kill. Its confident statements give no space to the perspective of prey.
5. The hawk describes death as something it allots and rejects elaborate justification. Violent images expose the physical reality of predation.
6. It asserts that nothing has changed and that its own eye has prevented change. The ending sounds absolute, although readers may question whether a single creature can actually control the world in this way.

## Form and interpretation
Six quatrains have no regular end-rhyme scheme. The direct first-person monologue, repeated claims of possession and short declarations create a forceful tone. The bird may be read as an image of natural predation, an imaginative voice of elemental power, or an analogy for authoritarian rule. Political readings are interpretations; they should not erase the animal or be asserted as the only intended meaning.

## Questions
How does height affect the hawk’s viewpoint? What happens to the relationship between creation and creature? Why is the voice unsettling? Does the poem criticise the hawk, admire its energy, or leave the response unresolved? Support an answer with details.

## Classroom activity
Divide the six stanzas among groups. Each group paraphrases the hawk’s claim and distinguishes what the bird asserts from what the reader must accept. Compare a natural and a political interpretation.

## Reading note
Read the complete poem in a licensed edition; the linked Guardian page includes the text, subject to availability.

course-8:1.title: Seamus Heaney · Seeing Things
course-8:1.text:
# Seeing Things
Seamus Heaney · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Scope and edition note
The syllabus names “Seeing Things” but does not specify sections. This note treats the three-part title poem in Heaney’s 1991 collection Seeing Things, not the entire collection. Confirm the prescribed edition and scope with the department.

## Overview
The poem explores how memory and imagination make familiar experiences visible in new ways. Its three parts consider a boat journey, an image carved in stone and a recollection of the speaker’s father after an accident. Physical things remain important even as they suggest what cannot easily be seen: risk, loss, memory and the nearness of death.

## The three parts
I. A remembered boat trip presents water so clear that it seems possible to see down through it. The boat’s weight and buoyancy make the journey physically vivid. The speaker then imagines a different viewpoint, as if looking down from another craft in the air. That imagined distance exposes the fragility of the people travelling together and the vulnerability that ordinary experience can conceal.
II. The speaker considers a carved image associated with baptism: solid stone represents water, movement and life. The skill of the sculptor makes something fluid seem present in a hard material. The poem’s attention to visibility invites readers to consider how art makes an invisible experience or meaning perceptible without making stone literally become water.
III. A childhood memory recalls the father returning, alive, after a mishap in or near a river. The child encounters him in a vulnerable, unfamiliar state. In the later act of remembering, the father’s eventual death colours the scene, so a moment of survival is also shadowed by mortality. The face-to-face encounter brings emotional closeness while leaving the relation between memory and loss open.

## Themes and form
The title can refer to perception, imagining what is not physically present and visions connected to the dead. Contrast weight and buoyancy, stone and water, seeing and the unseen. Classical journeys to the underworld and Christian imagery can enrich a reading, but specific allusions should be checked in an annotated edition rather than asserted as the only meaning.

## Teaching and questions
Ask students to identify one physical detail in each part and explain what it makes visible beyond itself. How does the imagined view in Part I alter a familiar journey? What can sculpture show that stone itself cannot do? Why does the father’s survival carry the shadow of later loss? How do memory and imagination work together?

## Reading note
The linked interpretive guide discusses the triptych. Consult a reliable edition of the poem, and verify the syllabus’s intended text before teaching.

course-9:0.title: Unit I · Introduction to Academic Writing
course-9:0.text:
# Unit I: Introduction to Academic Writing
Academic Writing Skills · Semester 2

## Learning goals
Explain the writing process, make purposeful choices about diction and mechanics, take accurate notes, and distinguish paraphrasing from summarising.

## The writing process
Writing usually involves understanding the task and audience, generating ideas, organising them, drafting, revising and proofreading. The process is recursive: a writer may return to research or planning after drafting. Pre-writing techniques include brainstorming, freewriting, listing and concept maps. For a question about online learning, list possible benefits, constraints and evidence before choosing a focused claim.

## Style, diction and mechanics
Style is the pattern of choices in language and structure; diction is word choice. Academic writing generally values precision and a tone appropriate to its audience, not unnecessary complexity. Compare “The results are bad” with “Attendance fell in the second week”; the latter identifies the observation. Mechanics include punctuation, spelling and layout. For example, a comma can separate introductory material: “After the lecture, students asked questions.” Use an appropriate style guide because conventions vary.

## Functional grammar and vocabulary
Grammar supports meaning: “The student writes” and “The students write” show subject–verb agreement. Check tense and reference so the reader knows what a pronoun refers to. Build vocabulary in context and verify collocations. An idiom such as “break the ice” may suit informal speech but may not fit a formal research argument; not every phrase is an idiom.

## Reading comprehension, note-taking and note-making
Identify a text’s central claim, supporting evidence, structure and assumptions. During reading or listening, note-taking captures useful points; note-making later organises and connects them. Mark direct quotations distinctly and record author, title and page or location. Separate your interpretation from the author’s argument.

## Paraphrase and summary
Paraphrasing restates a selected passage in new wording and structure without changing its meaning; summarising condenses the main point. Both require source acknowledgement when using another writer’s work. Example source: “The library extended evening hours for four weeks and will review attendance.” Paraphrase: “For a month, the library stayed open later and plans to assess usage.” Summary: “The library is testing longer hours.” Neither should imply the change is permanent.

## 50-minute class
0–10: interpret a prompt. 10–20: brainstorm and group ideas. 20–30: draft a paragraph. 30–40: paraphrase and summarise a short passage. 40–47: revise for clarity and acknowledgement. 47–50: name one improvement.

## Questions
Why is writing recursive? How does diction affect precision? How do notes distinguish a quotation from an interpretation? Why do paraphrases require citation?

## Reading note
The linked Purdue guide provides further practice; follow the department’s preferred style and edition.

course-9:1.title: Unit II · Writing in the Classroom
course-9:1.text:
# Unit II: Writing in the Classroom
Academic Writing Skills · Semester 2

## Effective sentences and cohesion
A sentence should express its intended relationship clearly. Avoid unnecessary wording, but do not sacrifice nuance for brevity. Cohesion connects ideas through logical organisation, appropriate transitions and clear reference. Example: “The library extended its hours. As a result, evening access improved.” This causal link is justified only if the evidence supports it. Avoid “this” with an unclear referent.

## Modes of writing
Description presents selected features; narration recounts events; exposition explains a concept; argument advances and supports a claim. Real assignments can combine modes. For example, an essay on a library may describe the building, explain its policy and argue for a change.

## Paragraph and essay organisation
A paragraph develops one main point with explanation and relevant evidence. Topic sentences often help readers, though not every paragraph must use the same formula. An essay introduction establishes the topic and a focused thesis. Body paragraphs develop the argument in a purposeful order; a conclusion brings the discussion together and explains its significance rather than merely repeating the introduction.

## Developing an argument and critical thinking
Move from claim to reason to evidence, then explain the connection. Consider a reasonable objection and respond fairly. “Longer library hours may help working students” is a claim; a properly conducted student survey could provide support. Ask whether the evidence is representative and whether staffing costs affect the proposal. Critical thinking means examining assumptions and alternatives, not simply criticising.

## Technical writing and reference skills
Technical writing explains specialised information for a specific audience and purpose, often using clear headings, definitions and procedures. Decide what the audience already knows. When collating material, group notes by idea, record source details and distinguish agreement from disagreement between sources. Attribute borrowed evidence and check the required citation style.

## Model paragraph
“Evening library access can support students who cannot visit during regular class hours. For example, a college could offer two later evenings as a trial and record attendance. The results would help staff decide whether the service meets a genuine need.” This is a proposal; it does not claim that a study has already proved the outcome.

## 50-minute class
0–10: compare wordy and clear sentences. 10–20: order paragraph sentences. 20–30: identify claim, reason and evidence. 30–40: groups address a counterargument. 40–47: draft an introduction and conclusion. 47–50: self-check one unclear reference.

## Questions
How do cohesion and coherence differ? What makes evidence relevant to a claim? Why should a conclusion avoid introducing an unsupported new argument? How can technical writing be adapted to a non-specialist audience?

course-9:2.title: Unit III · Professional Writing
course-9:2.text:
# Unit III: Professional Writing
Academic Writing Skills · Semester 2

## Purpose, audience and medium
Professional writing helps people request, inform, record and decide. Written messages can be reviewed and retained; spoken communication may allow immediate clarification, although both can be formal or informal. Choose tone and level of detail for the audience. Use plain, respectful language and state the action requested.

## Letters, cover letters and applications
A formal letter normally identifies the sender and recipient as required, date, purpose, supporting details and courteous close. A cover letter connects the applicant’s relevant experience to a particular role; it should not simply repeat a résumé. A job application must follow the employer’s actual instructions. Never invent qualifications, references or work experience.

Sample opening: “I am applying for the assistant professor position advertised on your website. My teaching experience in undergraduate literature has helped me design discussions and assess written work.” Replace this with truthful, relevant details.

## Emails and memoranda
Use a meaningful subject line, appropriate greeting, concise paragraphs, an explicit request or response and a suitable closing. Proofread names, attachments and dates. A memorandum is often used for internal communication; it typically identifies to, from, date, subject and a focused message, but organisations differ in format.

## Résumés
A chronological résumé typically presents work or education in reverse chronological order and can show progression clearly. A functional résumé groups experience by skill; it can help emphasise relevant abilities, though some employers prefer a dated work history. Whichever format is used, include accurate contact information, education and relevant evidence; tailor the document to the role and verify institutional requirements.

## Reports, newspaper reports and notices
A formal report may include purpose, method, findings, conclusions and recommendations; do not confuse observed data with interpretation. A short newspaper report prioritises verified facts and identifies what happened, who was involved, when and where. A notice communicates a specific event or instruction to an audience and includes essential details. Always follow the format specified by the organisation or examination.

## 50-minute class
0–10: identify audience and purpose. 10–20: rewrite an unclear email subject and request. 20–30: compare chronological and functional résumé structures. 30–40: draft an evidence-based report paragraph. 40–47: peer-check for accuracy and tone. 47–50: identify one ethical issue.

## Practice and answers
1. Weak subject “Hi” → “Request for meeting about course schedule.”
2. A student reports a result not yet measured. Correct response: label it as a proposal or omit the unsupported claim.
3. A cover letter should explain relevant fit, not copy the résumé verbatim.

## Questions
How do audience and purpose change tone? What is the difference between findings and recommendations? When might a functional résumé be useful?

course-9:3.title: Unit IV · Research Writing
course-9:3.text:
# Unit IV: Research Writing
Academic Writing Skills · Semester 2

## From topic to research problem
A broad topic such as “women in literature” needs a manageable question, defined corpus and rationale. Example: “How does the narrator represent women’s education in two selected chapters of a specified novel?” This is an illustrative question, not an assertion of an existing gap. Establish scope, access to texts and the value of the question before committing to it.

## Literature review and gap
A literature review identifies and synthesises relevant scholarship: compare approaches, evidence and disagreements rather than listing summaries one by one. A research gap is a specific area not adequately addressed in the literature you have reviewed. A researcher must search and read before claiming one; an absence from the first search is not proof of a gap.

## Types of research and methods
Descriptive research characterises a phenomenon; analytical research examines relationships or arguments. Quantitative approaches use numerical data and appropriate analysis; qualitative approaches explore meaning, experience or interpretation using suitable materials. Conceptual research develops or examines concepts; empirical research uses observations or collected evidence. Categories can overlap, and a literary close reading may be qualitative and analytical.

A method is a procedure (for example, close reading or interviews); methodology explains and justifies the overall approach and its assumptions. A working hypothesis is a provisional, testable or examinable proposition where appropriate. Not every interpretive humanities project needs a formal hypothesis; follow the discipline’s guidelines.

## Proposal, paper and abstract
A proposal may include title, problem, question, rationale, preliminary literature, method, scope, ethics and timeline. A paper presents a coherent argument with evidence and attribution; its precise sections depend on discipline. An abstract briefly states the problem, approach and main finding or contribution when known. Do not invent results in a proposal.

## Databases, citation and proofreading
Search academic databases using keywords, synonyms, filters and reference lists; assess relevance and credibility. MLA and APA have different rules for in-text citations and reference lists, and editions change. Use the required current guide. Footnotes or endnotes can provide citations or explanatory information depending on style. A bibliography or works-cited list must follow the chosen system and include genuine sources. Proofread argument, citations, quotations, names and formatting.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: narrow a broad topic. 10–20: formulate a research question. 20–30: identify suitable evidence and method. 30–40: outline a literature review without claiming an unverified gap. 40–47: draft an abstract for an imaginary completed paper only if findings are clearly labelled hypothetical. 47–50: check citations.

## Questions
How does a method differ from a methodology? What evidence is needed before claiming a research gap? How can quantitative and qualitative approaches overlap? What information should an abstract provide?

course-9:4.title: Unit V · Ethics in Writing
course-9:4.text:
# Unit V: Ethics in Writing
Academic Writing Skills · Semester 2

## Research and writing ethics
Ethical writing involves accurate representation, appropriate acknowledgement, responsible use of evidence and respect for people affected by the work. Research with human participants may require institutional review, informed consent, privacy safeguards and secure handling of data. Requirements vary by institution, discipline and study; consult the relevant ethics committee before collecting data.

## Plagiarism and acknowledgement
Plagiarism involves presenting another person’s words, ideas or work as one’s own. Copying without quotation and citation is an obvious case, but close rewriting without acknowledgement can also mislead. Cite borrowed ideas even when paraphrased; use quotation marks for exact wording and include the required location where applicable. Keep source details and distinguish your own notes from quotations. A similarity percentage by itself does not determine whether plagiarism has occurred; context and institutional rules matter.

## Publication ethics and conflicts of interest
Do not fabricate or falsify evidence, invent references, conceal relevant limitations or submit work in violation of publication rules. Authorship should reflect the publication’s criteria and genuine contributions. A conflict of interest is a financial, personal or other interest that could reasonably affect, or appear to affect, judgement; disclose it according to the relevant policy. Disclosure does not automatically prove misconduct.

## Inclusive language and political correctness
Use language that describes people accurately and respectfully, avoids unnecessary stereotypes and follows relevant self-identification and accessibility guidance. Discuss “political correctness” as a contested public term: classroom analysis should examine the effects and contexts of words rather than assume every disagreement has one simple answer. Respectful discussion permits reasoned critique without demeaning people.

## Copyright and intellectual property
Copyright protects many original expressions, while ideas, facts and legal protections have different rules. Citation acknowledges a source but does not by itself grant permission to reproduce a protected work. Whether an excerpt or educational use is lawful depends on jurisdiction, context, licences and applicable exceptions; consult institutional guidance and rights holders where necessary. Do not present a universal word-count rule as law.

## Open access and best practices
Open access generally means research can be read online without a paywall; reuse rights depend on the licence and are not identical for every item. Check journal credibility, author charges and licence terms. Good practice includes careful records, accurate citations, transparent correction of errors and following departmental policies, including any rules on AI assistance.

## 50-minute class
0–10: discuss acknowledgement. 10–20: distinguish quotation, paraphrase and unattributed copying. 20–30: evaluate a hypothetical conflict of interest. 30–40: compare access with reuse rights. 40–47: revise an exclusionary phrase in context. 47–50: exit ticket on one ethical decision.

## Practice and questions
1. Is adding a source to a bibliography enough when exact words are copied without quotation marks? No; represent exact wording properly and cite according to style.
2. Does free online access always permit unrestricted reuse? No; check the licence and applicable law.
3. What would you disclose if a company funding your study could benefit from its result? Follow institutional and publisher conflict-of-interest rules.

## Reading note
The linked Purdue guide addresses plagiarism. For binding requirements, consult your institution’s policies and current local law.

course-8:2.title: George Bernard Shaw · Arms and the Man
course-8:2.text:
# Arms and the Man
George Bernard Shaw · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 3

## Introduction
First performed in 1894, Shaw’s comedy is set during and shortly after the 1885 Serbo-Bulgarian War. It questions romantic ideas about war, love and social rank. The title echoes the opening of Virgil’s Aeneid, an epic of arms and a man; Shaw turns heroic expectations into comedy.

## The story, act by act
Act I: Raina Petkoff, a young Bulgarian woman, hears from her mother Catherine that her fiancé Sergius has led a successful cavalry charge. She imagines him as a splendid romantic hero. A fleeing soldier enters her bedroom and threatens her not to call out; she eventually hides him from the search party. He is Captain Bluntschli, a Swiss professional fighting for Serbia. Hungry and exhausted, he explains that experienced soldiers sometimes carry food rather than extra ammunition. Raina gives him chocolates and later calls him her “chocolate-cream soldier.” His account challenges the idea that Sergius’s charge succeeded purely through heroic skill: the enemy’s weapons could not be used effectively. With Catherine’s help, the fugitive leaves wearing an old coat belonging to Major Petkoff.

Act II: When the war is over, Major Petkoff and Sergius return. Sergius is disillusioned with his military prospects. In public, he and Raina exchange elevated professions of devotion, but in private he flirts with the servant Louka. Louka resists the limitations of her social position and is expected to marry the servant Nicola. Bluntschli unexpectedly arrives to return the coat and see Raina. Catherine fears that the family’s secret will be discovered. Instead, Petkoff and Sergius welcome Bluntschli and ask for help with practical troop movements, showing his competence.

Act III: Raina tells Bluntschli that she placed her photograph in the borrowed coat with an inscription for her “chocolate-cream soldier.” He has not found it, so its discovery threatens to reveal their earlier encounter. Louka tells Sergius about Raina’s attachment to Bluntschli. A challenge to a duel is defused rather than fought. Raina and Sergius abandon their engagement, exposing the contrast between their public pose and actual feelings. The photograph and story eventually reveal the truth. Nicola releases Louka from their arrangement, and Sergius commits himself to her.

Bluntschli receives news that his father has died and left him a prosperous hotel business. Raina’s parents become more receptive to the match when his resources are known. He has mistakenly thought Raina much younger; when her actual age is established, he proposes. Raina values the practical soldier rather than merely his wealth. Bluntschli completes the military arrangements and promises to return for the marriage. The play closes with admiration for his efficiency.

## Characters and themes
Raina learns to question the performance of ideal love; Bluntschli combines practical judgement with humanity. Sergius is more complicated than a simple coward or hero: his public image and private uncertainty conflict. Louka challenges class expectations, while Nicola shows a different strategy of working within them. Satire exposes romantic exaggeration, but the happy ending still depends partly on wealth and social approval.

## Class discussion
