What does the chocolate reveal about the difference between experience and heroic rhetoric? How do Raina and Sergius perform “higher love”? Does Louka gain independence, or another form of dependence? Why is Bluntschli’s inheritance important to the ending?

## Teaching plan
0–10 min: define romantic idealisation and satire. 10–25: compare the two soldiers’ accounts of the battle. 25–38: map the changing relationships. 38–45: discuss class and the inheritance. 45–50: exit ticket on one gap between appearance and reality.

## Reading note
Use the complete play in the prescribed edition. The linked synopsis is secondary; verify stage directions and exact dialogue in the text.

course-8:2.title: John Osborne · Look Back in Anger
course-8:2.text:
# Look Back in Anger
John Osborne · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 3

## Context and overview
First performed in 1956, the play is often associated with the “angry young men” and postwar British theatre. Jimmy Porter, an educated working-class man, lives with his wife Alison and their friend Cliff in a cramped Midlands flat. His anger at class hierarchy, disappointment and emotional restraint becomes entangled with his cruelty towards those closest to him.

## Story from beginning to end
Act I: On a Sunday in the attic flat, Jimmy reads newspapers and attacks the world around him in bitter speeches. Alison irons while Cliff tries to soften the conflict. Jimmy criticises Alison’s upper-middle-class family and accuses her of emotional passivity. Jimmy and Cliff play roughly; the ironing board is upset and Alison’s arm is burned. After Jimmy leaves, Alison tells Cliff that she is pregnant, but she has not told Jimmy. The couple’s private game of bear and squirrel reveals tenderness beneath the conflict. A call from Alison’s actress friend Helena announces her visit.

Act II: Helena stays at the flat and observes the painful marriage. Alison explains the family opposition they faced and Jimmy’s friendship with Hugh and Hugh’s mother. Helena encourages Alison to leave and contacts Alison’s father, Colonel Redfern. The Colonel arrives and shows sympathy, while also revealing his attachment to an older social order. When news comes that Hugh’s mother is seriously ill, Jimmy goes to her; Alison leaves with her father, leaving a letter. She has not told Jimmy directly about the pregnancy.

Jimmy returns to the letter. Helena tells him Alison is expecting a child. Their confrontation becomes physical: Helena slaps him, and they kiss. She stays and becomes Jimmy’s partner, despite her earlier condemnation of his treatment of Alison.

Act III: Some months later the household pattern resembles the earlier Sunday scene, now with Helena in Alison’s place. Cliff announces his intention to leave. Alison returns after suffering a miscarriage. Her loss confronts Helena with the consequences of what has happened; Helena decides she cannot continue the relationship with Jimmy and leaves. Alison and Jimmy face each other. Alison describes her suffering and the collapse of her former self-protection; Jimmy becomes gentler. They return to their bear-and-squirrel game and embrace.

## Interpretation and teaching cautions
The ending can suggest a renewed intimacy, but the play does not prove that the relationship’s harmful patterns have permanently changed. Jimmy’s class resentment deserves attention without excusing his verbal and emotional cruelty. Alison’s pregnancy loss should be discussed sensitively; it is not a lesson that suffering is necessary to deserve compassion. The small domestic setting, ironing and newspapers are features of kitchen-sink realism.

## Characters and questions
Jimmy mixes intelligence and vulnerability with aggression; Alison’s restraint can be read in more than one way; Cliff mediates but cannot solve the conflict; Helena both challenges and repeats aspects of the situation; Colonel Redfern represents another generation’s uncertainty.

Ask: How does class shape Jimmy’s anger? Why does Alison find it difficult to speak? What does the animal game make possible? How does the ending invite hope and doubt at once? Compare the flat’s domestic details with the characters’ larger social claims.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: postwar context and stage setting. 10–20: map relationships in Act I. 20–30: trace Alison’s departure and Helena’s arrival. 30–42: discuss the ending without assuming the conflict is solved. 42–50: evidence-based exit response.

## Reading note
The linked INFLIBNET discussion offers additional context. Check stage directions and exact words in the assigned script.

course-8:2.title: Tom Stoppard · Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
course-8:2.text:
# Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
Tom Stoppard · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 3

## Context and overview
Stoppard’s play, first performed in 1966, places two minor characters from Shakespeare’s Hamlet at the centre. Events from Hamlet interrupt their own conversations, but they rarely understand the larger plot. The work uses verbal games, theatrical self-awareness and absurdist comedy to explore uncertainty, identity, agency and death.

## Story, act by act
Act I: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern pass time by tossing coins; an extraordinarily long run of heads troubles Guildenstern, who tries to reason about chance. Neither can give a secure account of how their present situation began. A troupe of travelling actors, the Tragedians, arrives with their Player. Their offers of entertainment blur the boundary between performance and exploitation. The pair are then drawn into the Danish court of Hamlet: Claudius and Gertrude have summoned them to find out why Hamlet is behaving strangely. Even their names are confused. They practise questioning Hamlet but struggle to control the conversation when they meet him.

Act II: The two continue to wait, argue, play word games and discuss their situation. The Player explains the conventions of dramatic performance and the importance of an audience. The Tragedians stage a version of Hamlet’s play-within-the-play; their performance includes figures whose deaths resemble Rosencrantz and Guildenstern’s expected fate. After Hamlet kills Polonius, the pair are asked to find him and the body. They are repeatedly outmanoeuvred. Claudius sends them with Hamlet to England, carrying a sealed letter.

Act III: On the ship they discuss what will happen on arrival and examine the letter, discovering that it orders Hamlet’s death. While they sleep, Hamlet replaces it with a new letter ordering their own execution. The Tragedians, fleeing the court, appear aboard the ship. Pirates attack; after the confusion Hamlet has gone. When the pair examine the substituted letter, they discover the danger to themselves. Guildenstern challenges the Player’s representation of death and stabs him, only for the Player to reveal a theatrical trick. The two friends speak separately and disappear from the stage. In a scene recalling Hamlet’s conclusion, an ambassador announces that Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead. Their execution is not shown directly.

## Themes and dramatic methods
The impossible-seeming coin sequence makes chance and expectation unstable. The men’s confusion about names raises questions about identity, while their role in a plot already known from Hamlet raises questions about choice. The actors’ staged deaths contrast theatrical convention with the unknowability of death itself. The title tells the audience the outcome in advance; uncertainty concerns how the pair experience it, not merely what happens.

## Characters and questions
Rosencrantz often responds more directly to immediate events; Guildenstern more often searches for explanations, although they overlap. The Player understands performance conventions and challenges their assumptions. Ask: Who has control of the story? How does the play change our view of Hamlet? What does the coin game suggest about probability and expectation? Why is the staged stabbing significant? Is the pair’s fate shown or reported?

## Classroom plan
0–10: recall Rosencrantz and Guildenstern’s role in Hamlet. 10–20: discuss the coin game. 20–30: compare court scenes from the margins and centre. 30–42: examine the letter and staged death. 42–50: students defend one reading of choice or fate.

## Reading note
Read the assigned play and, where useful, the corresponding Hamlet scenes. The linked guide is a secondary synopsis; avoid treating every ambiguity as a factual answer.

course-8:3.title: Jane Austen · Pride and Prejudice
course-8:3.text:
# Pride and Prejudice
Jane Austen · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Introduction
Published in 1813, Austen’s novel follows Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy as they revise their judgements of each other. Courtship occurs within a society shaped by income, property, gender and reputation. The account below covers the principal plot and ending, not every chapter or minor episode.

## Detailed story
1. The Bennet family has five daughters: Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty and Lydia. Their home, Longbourn, is entailed away from the daughters to a male relative, Mr Collins, after Mr Bennet’s death. Mrs Bennet is therefore anxious to see her daughters securely married. The arrival of wealthy Charles Bingley at Netherfield creates excitement.
2. At a local assembly Bingley is sociable and quickly likes Jane. His friend Darcy appears aloof; Elizabeth overhears his dismissive comment about her and forms a poor opinion of him. At Netherfield, Jane becomes ill while visiting the Bingley sisters, and Elizabeth walks there to care for her. Darcy grows interested in Elizabeth despite his reservations about her family and connections.
3. Mr Collins visits Longbourn, planning to marry one of the Bennet daughters. He proposes to Elizabeth; she refuses despite her mother’s pressure. He later proposes to Elizabeth’s friend Charlotte Lucas, who accepts for practical security. The contrast between their decisions shows the limited choices available to women without independent wealth.
4. Elizabeth meets the militia officer George Wickham, who presents himself as unfairly treated by Darcy. His story supports her dislike of Darcy. Meanwhile Bingley’s party leaves Netherfield for London. Jane is disappointed, and Elizabeth suspects that Bingley’s sisters and Darcy have discouraged the match.
5. Elizabeth visits Charlotte at Hunsford and meets Mr Collins’s patron, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, Darcy’s aunt. Darcy, also visiting, unexpectedly proposes. He expresses love while referring to the obstacles posed by Elizabeth’s family and social situation. She refuses, accusing him of separating Jane and Bingley and of treating Wickham unjustly.
6. Darcy gives Elizabeth a letter explaining his actions. He says he believed Jane’s affection for Bingley was insufficiently clear. He also recounts that Wickham accepted money in place of a church living and later attempted to elope with Darcy’s young sister Georgiana. Elizabeth re-examines the evidence and recognises that her own pleasure in Wickham’s attention has helped her accept his story too readily.
7. Elizabeth later travels with her aunt and uncle, the Gardiners, and visits Pemberley, Darcy’s estate, believing him absent. They meet unexpectedly. Darcy behaves with consideration towards Elizabeth and her relatives and introduces her to Georgiana. Elizabeth begins to see him differently, although her new judgement is also shaped by circumstances and social impressions.
8. News arrives that Lydia has run away with Wickham. Because their marriage is not assured, the family fears serious social consequences. Elizabeth returns home; Mr Bennet and Mr Gardiner search. Lydia and Wickham eventually marry. The family initially believes Gardiner arranged the settlement, but Elizabeth learns that Darcy found the couple and contributed money to secure the marriage.
9. Bingley returns and proposes to Jane, who accepts. Lady Catherine visits Elizabeth and demands a promise that she will never marry Darcy; Elizabeth refuses to surrender her choice. Darcy proposes again, more respectfully, and Elizabeth accepts. The novel ends with the marriages of Jane and Bingley and Elizabeth and Darcy, while sketching continuing relationships among family members.

## Characters and themes
Elizabeth is witty and perceptive but capable of mistaken judgement; Darcy’s pride and social assumptions are challenged as he changes his conduct. Jane’s charity contrasts with Elizabeth’s sharper judgements. Wickham’s charm should be distinguished from reliability. Charlotte’s marriage makes economic survival visible, while Lydia’s actions reveal unequal consequences for women and men. Free indirect discourse brings readers close to a character’s thought while retaining the narrator’s ironic perspective.

## Questions
How do first impressions mislead Elizabeth and Darcy? What does the entail reveal about property and gender? Compare Charlotte’s and Elizabeth’s attitudes to marriage. How does Darcy’s letter change Elizabeth’s reasoning? Does the ending overcome class inequality or work within it?

## Teaching plan
0–10: draw the Bennet family and property situation. 10–25: trace Darcy, Wickham and Elizabeth’s early impressions. 25–35: examine the proposal and letter. 35–45: compare marriage choices. 45–50: exit ticket on a revised judgement.

## Reading note
Use the prescribed novel and its chapter divisions; the linked study guide is a secondary overview.

course-8:3.title: D. H. Lawrence · Sons and Lovers
course-8:3.text:
# Sons and Lovers
D. H. Lawrence · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Overview and content note
Published in 1913, the novel follows the Morel family in an English mining community, especially the intense bond between Gertrude Morel and her son Paul. It explores marriage, class, artistic ambition and divided attachment. It also includes domestic conflict, severe illness, an act intended to hasten death and suicidal despair; discuss these subjects sensitively.

## Detailed story
1. Gertrude Coppard marries Walter Morel, a coal miner, initially attracted by his warmth and physical energy. Their marriage deteriorates through differences in outlook, economic strain and Walter’s drinking and violence. Gertrude’s disappointment in the marriage increasingly directs her hopes and emotional energy towards her children.
2. Their eldest son William becomes a particular source of pride. He finds work and goes to London, pursuing advancement and a relationship that troubles his mother. William becomes ill and dies. Gertrude is devastated, and her attention gradually turns more intensely towards Paul, especially when Paul himself becomes seriously ill and recovers.
3. Paul grows up in the mining district, works as a clerk at Jordan’s in Nottingham and develops an interest in painting. He is close to his mother, who encourages his development. Their affection gives him support but also becomes a source of tension when he seeks intimacy elsewhere.
4. Paul meets Miriam Leivers, a thoughtful, religious young woman whose family lives on a farm. They share books, conversation and an appreciation of nature. Their relationship is emotionally intense but troubled by hesitation, conflicting expectations and Paul’s resentment as well as his mother’s dislike of Miriam. They become physically intimate, but Paul remains unable to commit to the relationship as Miriam hopes.
5. Through this circle Paul meets Clara Dawes, who is separated from her husband Baxter and associated with women’s political activism. Paul and Clara begin an affair. Their relationship brings physical passion but also uncertainty about independence, commitment and Clara’s own situation. Avoid reducing Clara and Miriam to simple opposites; both have concerns beyond Paul’s view of them.
6. Paul’s relationship with Baxter is initially hostile and includes a violent confrontation. Later, as circumstances change and Baxter is ill, Paul’s attitude becomes more sympathetic. Clara eventually returns to Baxter, though the process involves tensions that should be checked closely in the full text.
7. Gertrude develops a serious illness. Paul and his sister Annie care for her during a long decline. In a morally troubling episode, they give her an excessive dose of medicine in an attempt to ease or hasten the end of her suffering. The narrative does not make the ethical question simple. Her death leaves Paul grief-stricken; the family’s domestic life is permanently altered.
8. Paul feels disconnected from his work and relationships. After a later encounter, Miriam proposes marriage, but he does not accept. Drawn towards darkness and the wish to follow his mother, he finally turns towards the lights of the town. The ending suggests a fragile decision to continue living, not a complete resolution of his conflicts.

## Themes and form
The mother–son bond is loving and constraining; it should not be treated as the sole explanation of every difficulty. Work and the mining community shape the family’s possibilities. Miriam and Clara show different pressures around religion, sexuality and women’s autonomy. Psychological narration presents shifting feelings rather than a simple moral verdict. Some critics use psychoanalytic approaches; present them as interpretations, not diagnoses of fictional people.

## Questions
How does Gertrude’s marriage shape her hopes for her children? What does Paul gain and lose through his closeness to her? How are Miriam and Clara represented beyond Paul’s feelings? What does the final movement towards town suggest? How do work and class matter to the family?

## Teaching plan
0–10: family and mining context. 10–20: trace William’s death and Paul’s role. 20–35: compare the relationships without stereotypes. 35–45: discuss care and ethical complexity. 45–50: interpret the ending using evidence.

## Reading note
Consult the assigned edition for chapter sequence and wording. The linked synopsis covers the broader plot but should be checked against the novel.

course-8:3.title: Virginia Woolf · To the Lighthouse
course-8:3.text:
# To the Lighthouse
Virginia Woolf · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Overview
Published in 1927, Woolf’s novel has three sections: “The Window,” “Time Passes” and “The Lighthouse.” It moves through several characters’ perceptions rather than narrating events from one unchanging viewpoint. A long-delayed trip to a lighthouse and Lily Briscoe’s painting connect questions of family, time, loss and artistic form.

## Detailed story
Part I — The Window: Before the First World War, the Ramsay family and guests are at their summer house in the Hebrides. Young James wants to visit the lighthouse. Mrs Ramsay says the trip may be possible if the weather is suitable; Mr Ramsay predicts bad weather, frustrating James. The disagreement reveals different ways of speaking to a child as well as tensions within the family.

Mrs Ramsay cares for guests and children and tries to bring people together, but she also thinks about ageing, suffering and the fragility of happiness. Mr Ramsay, a philosopher, worries about his intellectual achievement and seeks reassurance. Among their guests are the painter Lily Briscoe, William Bankes and the student Charles Tansley. Lily struggles with her picture of Mrs Ramsay and James and with dismissive assumptions about women’s artistic abilities. Mrs Ramsay encourages a match between Paul Rayley and Minta Doyle; Lily is not persuaded that marriage is necessary for her own life.

A dinner party gathers the household. Its shifting conversations and Mrs Ramsay’s efforts produce a temporary feeling of unity, though the guests’ private thoughts do not disappear. The first section ends with the Ramsays together and the lighthouse journey still deferred.

Part II — Time Passes: Roughly a decade is compressed into a brief account of seasons, darkness, weather and the summer house’s neglect. The First World War occurs. Mrs Ramsay dies; Prue dies from an illness connected to childbirth; Andrew is killed in the war. Their deaths are reported in brief bracketed passages, a striking contrast to the slow attention given to a single day in Part I. The house decays until Mrs McNab and others work to restore it for the family’s return.

Part III — The Lighthouse: The surviving Ramsays return with Lily and others. Mr Ramsay sets out for the lighthouse with his children James and Cam. Both children feel anger and resistance towards him, but their thoughts change during the voyage. James, steering the boat, receives praise from his father, complicating his remembered hostility. The journey finally reaches its destination.

Back at the house, Lily resumes her painting and thinks about Mrs Ramsay, the family and the difficulty of seeing another person fully. She also struggles with Mr Ramsay’s demand for sympathy. As the boat reaches the lighthouse, Lily completes her picture with a final mark and experiences a sense of having achieved her vision. The novel does not guarantee that her work will last forever; the act of making meaning matters even in the face of loss.

## Themes and technique
Shifting interior perspectives and moments of consciousness make ordinary experiences psychologically rich. Time can feel slow in a remembered afternoon and rapid in the middle section. The lighthouse changes meaning according to distance and observer: it is not reducible to one fixed symbol. Gender expectations affect Mrs Ramsay’s care work and Lily’s art. The painting offers form without restoring the dead or solving every conflict.

## Questions and class activity
Why is the initial trip postponed? How do the three sections represent time differently? What does Lily’s painting reveal about the pressures on women artists? How do James and Cam’s responses to their father change? Compare the completed voyage and completed painting without claiming they have identical meanings.

## 50-minute plan
0–10: map the three sections. 10–20: examine the cancelled trip and perspectives. 20–30: discuss the bracketed deaths and the house. 30–42: compare the final voyage and painting. 42–50: write an evidence-based response on time or art.

## Reading note
Use the full novel in the assigned edition. The linked synopsis is a secondary guide; verify chronology and wording in the text.

course-8:4.title: H. G. Wells · The Empire of the Ants
course-8:4.text:
# The Empire of the Ants
H. G. Wells · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Introduction
First published in 1905, Wells’s short story imagines an organised species of ants threatening human settlement in the Amazon region. Its speculative premise questions the assumption that human dominance over nature is permanent. Do not confuse the story with later films that use its title but change the plot.

## Detailed story
1. Captain Gerilleau commands the Brazilian gunboat Benjamin Constant and has orders to travel upriver to help the settlement of Badama against an alarming outbreak of ants. The English engineer Holroyd accompanies the expedition. Gerilleau is initially inclined to think of ant incursions as natural troubles that eventually pass; reports suggest this outbreak is different.
2. The journey through the forest makes human settlements seem isolated within a vast environment. Holroyd reflects on the relative fragility of human occupation. Reports describe ants that remain in places they have occupied, attack effectively and appear organised. The crew’s apprehension grows as rumours and observation meet.
3. They encounter a vessel, a cuberta, apparently abandoned on the river. A boarding party investigates and finds the consequences of an attack. Lieutenant da Cunha is bitten or stung by the ants; he becomes seriously ill and dies, apparently from their poison. The scene transforms an alarming report into an immediate danger for the crew.
4. The crew destroys the abandoned craft and reaches Badama. The settlement is deserted and shows signs of the ants’ occupation. The crew is unwilling to land and face the threat directly. Gerilleau fires the gunboat’s large gun at the settlement, but the action offers no convincing solution. He withdraws downstream to seek further instructions.
5. The concluding frame presents Holroyd’s continuing concern that the ants may spread and challenge human control. It is a warning and speculation, not a completed account of ants conquering the whole world. The expedition ends without clearly defeating the threat.

## Themes and technique
The ants are a speculative rival whose apparent organisation and possible tool use disturb easy distinctions between human and animal intelligence. The story questions confidence in technology: a gunboat’s cannon cannot easily solve the problem. The Amazon setting is filtered through European and colonial perspectives; discuss how people and landscape are represented rather than accepting those assumptions uncritically. Narrative distance and an open future make the threat larger than the witnessed events.

## Characters and questions
Gerilleau confronts a threat for which familiar habits offer no clear plan; Holroyd becomes increasingly alert to the implications. Ask: How does the upriver journey alter the crew’s understanding? What does the abandoned boat establish? Why is the cannon inadequate? What does the unresolved ending suggest about human control?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss an assumption about human superiority. 10–25: map the expedition and its encounters. 25–35: compare Gerilleau’s and Holroyd’s responses. 35–45: analyse the ending as warning rather than completed conquest. 45–50: exit ticket on one piece of evidence.

## Reading note
The linked Standard Ebooks edition provides the complete story. Check the spelling of names and sequence against the course edition.

course-8:4.title: Graham Greene · The End of the Party
course-8:4.text:
# The End of the Party
Graham Greene · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Overview and content note
Greene’s psychological short story follows twins Peter and Francis Morton as they face a children’s party. Francis is intensely afraid of darkness, and the anticipated game of hide-and-seek becomes a source of mounting dread. The story ends with a child’s death; its treatment of fear deserves sensitivity.

## Detailed story
1. Francis wakes from a frightening dream and dreads the party to be held by Mrs Henne-Falcon. The twins are unusually close, and Peter understands that Francis’s fear is more serious than ordinary reluctance. Francis remembers the discomfort and humiliation of the previous party, especially the game played in the dark.
2. Francis tries to avoid attending, and Peter attempts to help him. The adults do not appreciate the full intensity of his fear and the boys are sent to the event. The approaching evening makes ordinary surroundings threatening from Francis’s perspective.
3. At the party the children play various games. The approaching hide-and-seek remains in Francis’s mind even while other activities continue. Peter tries to protect him and to prevent or change the game, but other children insist. The contrast between the party’s cheerful social purpose and Francis’s terror creates dramatic tension.
4. For hide-and-seek, the lights are extinguished. Francis hides alone, overwhelmed by the darkness. Peter seeks his brother and, because of their close connection, finds him. Peter reaches out and touches him in an attempt to offer comfort; in the darkness Francis cannot experience the gesture in the reassuring way Peter intends.
5. When the lights return, Francis is found dead. Peter remains beside his brother, struggling to understand a loss that is both emotional and bound up with their sense of being twins. The story presents an extreme fictional outcome; do not treat it as a general medical claim that fear routinely causes death, or claim a medically confirmed diagnosis not established by the text.

## Characters, form and themes
Francis’s perspective makes fear vivid and shows how an adult may underestimate a child’s experience. Peter’s protectiveness is sincere but cannot remove the danger. The twins’ resemblance and emotional closeness create a double or mirror motif. Darkness, dreams and foreshadowing give the story Gothic elements. The gap between intended comfort and experienced terror makes the ending especially painful.

## Classroom discussion
How does Greene build anticipation before the game begins? Why do the twins’ different responses matter? How do party games become frightening rather than harmless? What do adults and other children fail to notice? Why should the final touch be interpreted in context rather than as deliberate harm?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish a character’s fear from an outside observer’s judgement. 10–25: trace the sequence from dream to party. 25–35: examine darkness and foreshadowing. 35–45: discuss Peter’s intentions and the twins’ bond. 45–50: students write a brief evidence-based interpretation.

## Reading note
Read the complete story in a licensed course edition. The linked critical discussion is a secondary interpretation; check details and wording against the prescribed text.

course-8:4.title: Martin Amis · Heavy Water — preliminary outline
course-8:4.text:
# Heavy Water — preliminary outline, not yet a full story summary
Martin Amis · English Literature II · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Important limitation
This is an initial teaching outline only. The full sequence and ending have not yet been checked against the assigned edition, so they are deliberately not supplied. Read the story in the authorised collection before teaching or relying on a plot summary. The title story was revised for the later collection, so edition differences may matter.

## Verified starting point
The story concerns an ageing working-class mother and her adult son John on a cruise. The confined holiday setting brings their caring relationship into contact with other passengers and their reactions. A review of the revised story describes changes between versions, including the background of John’s father. Avoid transferring details from one version to another without checking.

## Questions to guide reading
1. How is the mother’s perspective represented, and what does it reveal and conceal about John’s own experience?
2. How do other passengers respond to the pair? What assumptions shape their reactions?
3. How do care, fatigue, social exclusion and control interact?
4. What does the cruise setting contribute to the story’s social criticism?
5. Which details and ending appear in the edition assigned by the department?

## Teaching caution
Use respectful, current language when discussing disability. Distinguish a character’s attitudes from the author’s narrative choices and do not assume that disability makes a person’s thoughts or agency inaccessible. The linked review supplies background, not a substitute for the story.

course-10:0.title: Communication: process, types and barriers
course-10:0.text:
# Basic communication skills
Professional Communication in English · Semester 2, Unit 1

## What communication does
Communication is the exchange and interpretation of meaning. In professional settings it coordinates work, shares decisions, builds relationships and helps people address problems. A message is not necessarily understood simply because it was sent.

## The process
A sender forms an intention, encodes a message in words or other signs and sends it through a channel. A receiver interprets it using their context and experience; feedback shows what was understood. Noise includes anything that interferes, from poor audio to ambiguous words. Communication is often interactive, not a one-way chain: participants take turns and adjust as they respond.

Example: A manager messages “Send it soon.” The colleague might not know whether “it” means the draft or final report, or whether “soon” means today. A useful revision names the document, deadline, format and contact for questions. Feedback confirms whether the instruction was understood.

## Types and frames of reference
Spoken communication allows immediate clarification; writing provides a record but needs careful wording. Non-verbal signals include expression, posture, distance and tone; their meaning varies across people and cultures, so do not assume that one gesture has a universal meaning. Formal communication follows an organisation’s designated channels; informal communication travels through personal networks. A frame of reference is the set of experiences, expectations and knowledge through which a person interprets a message.

## Barriers and solutions
Physical barriers include distance and noise; linguistic barriers include unfamiliar vocabulary and ambiguity; organisational barriers include unclear roles; psychological barriers include anxiety or assumptions. Ask what the listener already knows, use accessible language, choose a suitable channel, invite questions and check understanding without blaming the listener. Respect privacy and disability-related access needs.

## Practice and 50-minute lesson
0–10: students describe a communication misunderstanding. 10–20: label sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback. 20–30: compare written and spoken instructions. 30–42: rewrite three ambiguous workplace messages. 42–50: pairs explain how they would check understanding. Exit: give one barrier and one practical response.

## Check yourself
Why does feedback matter? How might two colleagues interpret the same instruction differently? Write a clear two-sentence request with a deadline.

course-10:1.title: Listening and note-taking
course-10:1.text:
# Listening and note-taking
Professional Communication in English · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Listening with a purpose
Hearing is perception of sound; listening involves attention and interpretation. Informational listening aims to understand, critical listening evaluates reasoning and evidence, empathetic listening seeks to understand another person’s experience, and appreciative listening attends to enjoyment or artistry. These purposes can overlap.

## Before, during and after
Before: identify the purpose and preview the topic; minimise distractions and check audio or access needs. During: listen for signposting, central claims, examples and transitions. Record keywords rather than attempting to write every sentence. Ask for clarification when appropriate. After: compare notes, check unfamiliar terms and summarise the speaker’s main point in your own words.

## Barriers
Interruptions, background noise, unfamiliar terminology, divided attention and pre-judgement can distort understanding. Accent is not a defect; both speaker and listener can improve access through clear pacing, captions, written materials and clarification. Avoid assuming silence means agreement.

## Notes and summary
Use a page with headings: topic, central claim, three supporting points, questions and action items. Mark uncertain details with a question mark. A summary gives the core idea and most important support in your own words; it does not add a conclusion the speaker did not make.

Example: From a talk arguing that meetings need agendas, note “agenda beforehand; clear decisions; actions with names and dates.” Summary: “The speaker argues that advance agendas and recorded actions make meetings more effective.”

## Lesson plan: 50 minutes
0–5: identify listening purpose. 5–15: teacher gives a short original talk twice. 15–25: individual notes; pairs compare missing details. 25–35: groups distinguish main claim from examples. 35–45: write a three-sentence summary. 45–50: exit ticket identifying one barrier and an adjustment.

## Check yourself
What is the difference between a detail and a central claim? How can you show empathy without pretending to agree? When should you ask a speaker to repeat or clarify?

course-10:2.title: Speaking: presentations, discussion and interviews
course-10:2.text:
# Speaking in professional settings
Professional Communication in English · Semester 2, Unit 3

## Public speaking and seminars
Begin with a clear objective: by the end, should the audience understand, decide or act? Analyse the audience’s knowledge and time. Collect ideas, choose a central message and select evidence. A short presentation can use an opening that introduces purpose, a body with two or three organised points and a conclusion that restates the takeaway and invites questions. A seminar often centres on a topic presented for informed discussion; prepare a few questions and concise notes rather than reading an entire script.

## Delivery and visual support
Rehearse aloud, time the presentation, speak at a steady pace and explain unfamiliar terms. Notes can contain keywords, transitions, examples and sources. Slides should support speech rather than reproduce every word. Provide readable contrast and accessible handouts. Respond to a question by listening fully, answering the actual question and acknowledging when you do not know.

## Group discussion
Discussions may explore a problem, evaluate a proposal or make a decision. Participants can introduce a point, offer evidence, invite a quieter voice, respectfully disagree and summarise. A useful sentence: “I see the benefit; could we also consider the cost?” Avoid interrupting, dominating or equating confidence with correctness. A group needs both ideas and fair participation.

## Interviews
Interviews can be structured, semi-structured or less formal. A typical sequence includes introduction, questions on relevant experience, the applicant’s questions and closing. Prepare by understanding the role and selecting honest examples. In a behavioural answer explain the situation, task, action and result; do not invent achievements. Seek clarification when a question is unclear.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: write an audience-centred objective. 10–20: plan a two-minute presentation. 20–30: deliver in pairs with feedback on structure and clarity. 30–40: group discussion with a rotating facilitator. 40–47: mock interview question. 47–50: exit ticket: one specific improvement.

## Check yourself
What is the difference between a topic and an objective? How can a participant disagree constructively? Which details make an interview example credible?

course-10:3.title: Reading: comprehension and evaluation
course-10:3.text:
# Professional reading and comprehension
Professional Communication in English · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Match strategy to purpose
Skimming gives a quick overview of topic and structure; scanning looks for a specific detail such as a date. Intensive reading analyses a shorter passage closely; extensive reading develops fluency and familiarity through a larger volume of reading. These are strategies, not rigid stages: return to close reading when an important detail needs checking.

## Understanding an argument
Find the main claim, reasons supporting it and evidence offered. A detail explains or illustrates the claim but is not automatically the claim itself. When a main idea is implied, infer it from repeated or related points and test whether it fits the whole passage. Separate what the author states from what you infer.

Example: A passage describes missed deadlines, unclear responsibilities and duplicated work, then proposes a shared task list. An implied central issue is lack of coordination. The proposed list is a solution, not evidence by itself that the solution works.

## Vocabulary and sources
Use context, word parts and a dictionary together: prefixes and roots offer clues but can mislead. Record the sentence and check which meaning fits. For reference and library work, identify author, title, date and publisher, use the library catalogue and databases, and record full source details as you go.

## Critical evaluation
Ask who wrote the text, for whom, for what purpose, and whether its evidence supports its claims. Check publication date, alternative explanations, potential conflicts of interest and whether references are reliable. Distinguish a source’s credibility from agreement with your own view.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: skim a short article and predict its focus. 10–18: scan for two named facts. 18–30: annotate claim and evidence. 30–40: infer an unstated main point and justify it. 40–47: evaluate source and date. 47–50: exit response distinguishing an inference from a stated fact.

## Practice
Explain how a prefix helps but does not guarantee a word’s meaning. Identify a claim and one supporting reason in an article you choose.

course-10:4.title: Writing: grammar and workplace genres
course-10:4.text:
# Professional writing
Professional Communication in English · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Clear sentences
Match the verb to its subject: “The report is ready”; “The reports are ready.” Maintain a consistent tense unless the time changes. Use punctuation to separate complete ideas and show relationships. Proofread spelling, names, dates and numbers. Grammar choices depend on audience and purpose; respect language variation while using appropriate conventions for a formal workplace.

## Paragraphs, description and narration
A coherent paragraph develops one controlling idea through explanations or examples and links sentences logically. Description selects relevant sensory or factual detail; narration orders events and makes their significance clear. An essay generally has an introduction, developed body and conclusion, but its structure should suit the assignment. Support claims rather than filling space with repetition.

## Workplace documents
A formal letter or business email includes a clear subject or purpose, relevant context, a specific request and a courteous closing. Example subject: “Request for leave on 12 March.” State dates and required action without excessive personal detail. A cover letter connects relevant experience to the role and does not simply repeat the résumé. A résumé uses accurate qualifications, dates and concise evidence; never invent employment or results.

A report identifies its purpose, method or information sources, findings and appropriate recommendations. Distinguish observation from recommendation. Note-making reduces a longer source to organised headings and key points; acknowledge the source. For all genres, edit for audience, accuracy, completeness and confidentiality.

## 50-minute class
0–10: correct ambiguous sentences. 10–20: arrange a paragraph. 20–30: write a professional email. 30–40: convert brief notes into an objective report. 40–47: peer check names, dates, tone and action. 47–50: exit ticket on one revision.

## Practice
Rewrite “Send the stuff soon” as a specific email request. Draft a résumé achievement only from a real example. Compare a factual finding with a recommendation.

course-11:0.text:
# The Lost Child and My Early Days

PRELIMINARY: Literature overview only. Detailed grammar notes for the assigned textbook units are not yet prepared; check the assigned edition.

Functional English I · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Mulk Raj Anand: The Lost Child — full story overview
A child travels with his parents to a spring fair. He lingers over toys and the sights of nature, while his parents call him to keep up. At the fair he wants sweets, a garland, balloons and other attractions, but often moves on knowing his parents may refuse. At a roundabout he asks for a ride and discovers that his parents are no longer beside him. Terrified, he runs through the crowd calling for them. Near a shrine a man lifts him out of danger and tries to comfort him by offering the attractions he had wanted. The child refuses everything and cries for his mother and father. The story does not show a reunion. Its changing view of the fair highlights security, attachment and the difference between desire and need.

## A. P. J. Abdul Kalam: My Early Days
In this autobiographical account Kalam recalls childhood in Rameswaram, the influence of his parents and the generosity, discipline and faith he associated with family life. Relatives and friends encourage his curiosity. Recollections of people from different religious communities make cooperation and prejudice important subjects for discussion. Compare details with the exact excerpt assigned in class: anthologies may select different passages.

## Grammar: assigned units 1–14
The syllabus names Raymond Murphy’s Essential English Grammar, but topic numbering can vary by edition. Use the assigned book’s contents page rather than assume which grammar item belongs to each unit. Practise identifying a subject and verb, forming a clear question and revising a sentence; map these exercises to the actual prescribed pages.

## Teaching plan (50 minutes)
0–10: recall a place that changed meaning when one felt afraid. 10–25: sequence the child’s changing desires and discuss the unresolved ending. 25–35: discuss the people and values in Kalam’s account. 35–45: grammar exercise from the prescribed units. 45–50: exit ticket contrasting a story detail and an interpretation.

## Questions
Why do the child’s earlier desires no longer comfort him? Is a reunion narrated? Which people shape Kalam’s childhood, and how?

course-11:1.title: The Affliction of Margaret, The Model Millionaire & grammar — outline, grammar incomplete
course-11:1.text:
# The Affliction of Margaret and The Model Millionaire

PRELIMINARY: Literature overview only. Detailed grammar notes for the assigned textbook units are not yet prepared; check the assigned edition.

Functional English I · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Wordsworth: The Affliction of Margaret — poem summary
Margaret addresses her absent son, from whom she has had no news for seven years. She remembers him lovingly and wonders whether he is alive, imprisoned, lost or dead. Earlier concerns about prosperity have lost importance; she wants him to return or send news in whatever condition he may be. Her shifting possibilities reveal the pain of uncertainty. The poem closes by stressing her loneliness. It does not establish what happened to the son. The direct address, questions and recurring hopes give the private voice urgency.

## Oscar Wilde: The Model Millionaire — story
Hughie Erskine loves Laura Merton, but her father requires him to have £10,000 before marriage. Hughie has little money. Visiting his painter friend Alan Trevor, he sees a model dressed as a beggar. Pitying the apparently poor man, Hughie secretly gives him a sovereign, although he can scarcely afford it. Later Trevor reveals that the model is Baron Hausberg, a very rich man posing as a beggar for a portrait. Embarrassed, Hughie fears he has made a fool of himself. Next morning a messenger brings a wedding gift from the Baron: a cheque for £10,000. Hughie and Laura marry, and Trevor’s final wordplay contrasts a millionaire posing as a model with a millionaire who behaves generously.

## Themes and technique
Both works examine care, but in different forms. Margaret’s address creates uncertainty and grief; Wilde uses mistaken appearance, reversal, dialogue and a pun. The story’s charitable ending can be appreciated while asking why the wealth gap gives the Baron so much power.

## Grammar and classroom plan
Murphy units 15–33 are assigned; confirm the edition and headings before matching exercises. 0–12 min: summarise Margaret’s conflicting hopes. 12–27: sequence Wilde’s story and identify the reversal. 27–38: compare two kinds of generosity. 38–47: exercise from the assigned grammar pages. 47–50: exit ticket on one image or irony.

## Questions
What does Margaret know and not know? Why does Hughie give the coin? How does the final title pun work?

course-11:2.title: Two Gentlemen of Verona, Punishment in Kindergarten & grammar — outline, grammar incomplete
course-11:2.text:
# Two Gentlemen of Verona and Punishment in Kindergarten

PRELIMINARY: Literature overview only. Detailed grammar notes for the assigned textbook units are not yet prepared; check the assigned edition.

Functional English I · Semester 2, Unit 3

## A. J. Cronin: Two Gentlemen of Verona — story overview
Near Verona a traveller encounters brothers Nicola and Jacopo selling fruit. He later sees them doing several other small jobs. Their seriousness, energy and economy make him curious. Jacopo asks the traveller for a Sunday lift to Poleta. There the brothers enter a villa that turns out to be a hospital. A nurse explains that war devastated their family: their father died, their home was destroyed, and the boys experienced hardship and joined the resistance. Their sister Lucia has tuberculosis of the spine; the brothers work to pay for her treatment and visit her. The narrator respects their privacy rather than confronting them with what he has learned. He sees their responsibility as a source of hope after war. The title calls them gentlemen for their conduct, not their social rank.

## Kamala Das: Punishment in Kindergarten — poem summary
An adult speaker recalls a school outing. As other children play, she sits apart; a teacher scolds her for being different and the children laugh. The bright surroundings contrast with humiliation and isolation. At the close the adult claims a greater measure of peace and suggests there is no need to remember, yet the vivid act of recollection leaves room to question how completely the hurt has faded. Treat this tension as interpretation, not a medical diagnosis of the speaker.

## Grammar and 50-minute plan
Units 34–48 of the specified Murphy book are assigned; check the edition’s table of contents. 0–10: discuss what the title “gentlemen” suggests. 10–22: map the brothers’ work and the hospital revelation. 22–35: track the poem’s changes between past and present. 35–45: grammar practice from the assigned pages. 45–50: exit ticket on one contrast in either text.

## Questions
Why does the narrator not disturb the visit? How does the poem contrast the child’s feeling with the other children’s response? How does the ending complicate the speaker’s claim to peace?

course-11:3.title: The Second Crucifixion, Mirror & grammar — outline, grammar incomplete
course-11:3.text:
# The Second Crucifixion and Mirror

PRELIMINARY: Literature overview only. Detailed grammar notes for the assigned textbook units are not yet prepared; check the assigned edition.

Functional English I · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Collins and Lapierre: The Second Crucifixion
The assigned historical narrative concerns Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination on 30 January 1948 and the response of leaders and mourners. Accounts describe the shock at Birla House, the need to prevent further communal violence, and the organisation of a public funeral. The title recalls a newspaper tribute comparing Gandhi’s killing to a crucifixion; it is a metaphor and interpretation, not a claim that the events were literally identical. Read the exact anthology extract and compare its framing with historical sources; reported conversations and details of the funeral should not be treated as independently proven simply because they appear in narrative form.

## Sylvia Plath: Mirror — poem summary
A mirror speaks in the first person, presenting itself as exact and without preferences. It describes the wall it usually reflects and interruptions by faces and darkness. In the second movement it imagines itself as a lake in which a woman searches for herself. She turns to gentler light, but returns and responds with distress. The final image represents youth as submerged and an older self rising, using a disturbing fish comparison. The poem concerns self-image, the passage of time and the tension between physical reflection and a complete sense of identity. The mirror’s claim to objectivity is itself open to analysis.

## Grammar and lesson plan
Units 49–63 of Murphy are prescribed; confirm edition-specific contents. 0–12 min: distinguish historical event from figurative title. 12–25: identify the poem’s two movements. 25–35: discuss personification and the lake image. 35–45: practise the assigned grammar topic. 45–50: write a short explanation supported by a detail.

## Questions
What does the title compare, and what are the limits of that comparison? Why does the mirror call itself truthful? Can an image of appearance provide the whole truth about a person?

course-11:4.title: Group discussion, listening and note-making
course-11:4.text:
# Group discussion, listening and note-making
Functional English I · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Discussion
A group discussion explores an issue or works towards a decision. Prepare a clear point and a reason, listen to other speakers and respond to their actual claims. Invite others in: “What do you think about this?” Disagree respectfully: “I understand that point, but the evidence may also suggest…” Summarise areas of agreement and unresolved questions. Clear communication matters more than speaking the most.

## Listening
Listen for the topic, speaker’s main point and supporting details. Attend without interrupting; use clarification questions where necessary. External noise, divided attention, unfamiliar terms and preconceptions can interfere. Written instructions, captions and a quieter room can make listening more accessible.

## Note-making
Record a topic heading, main points and supporting examples in a logical hierarchy. Abbreviate consistently but leave enough context to understand notes later. Distinguish a speaker’s words from your own response; mark uncertain facts for checking. Summarise the argument in your own words and record the source.

## Model activity
For a discussion on a library’s opening hours, one member proposes a later closing time, another identifies staffing costs and a third suggests a student survey. A note-taker records the proposal, concern, evidence required and next action; the group need not pretend it has reached a decision if it has not.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: model listening and clarification. 10–20: listen to a short original talk and note main ideas. 20–35: discussion in groups with rotating roles. 35–45: compare notes and write a short summary. 45–50: each student identifies one participation or listening improvement.

## Check yourself
How do notes differ from a transcript? What can you say when you do not understand a point? How can a group include someone who has not yet spoken?

course-12:0.title: Inspiration, creativity and reading
course-12:0.text:
# Introducing creative writing
Creative Writing in English · Semester 2, Unit 1

## Where writing begins
Creative writing makes deliberate choices of language, form and perspective to create an experience for readers. Inspiration can come from observation, memory, questions, conversations or imagined situations; it does not require waiting for a perfect idea. Keep a notebook of images and fragments. Be mindful of consent and privacy when using other people’s experiences.

## Reading as a writer
Read once for experience, then reread to notice craft: how does an opening establish expectations? What does the writer reveal or withhold? How do sound, sentence length and viewpoint shape feeling? Describe a technique before deciding whether it succeeds. Read across genres and languages rather than assuming one model of good writing.

## Exercises
1. Observe a familiar place for five minutes; record five concrete details without judging them.
2. Turn one detail into a question: “Who left the umbrella?” Write for five minutes without editing.
3. Change point of view and rewrite the opening. Compare the effect.
4. Choose a short passage from the class text. Note one craft decision and try the technique in an original scene without copying wording or plot.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: read an opening and identify its effect. 10–20: observation notebook. 20–30: freewrite from a question. 30–40: rewrite from another viewpoint. 40–47: volunteers share; listeners name one effective detail. 47–50: exit reflection on a choice made.

## Questions
How does observation differ from interpretation? What changes when a scene is told by a different person? How can a writer use influence without copying?

course-12:1.title: Voice, language and literary devices
course-12:1.text:
# Developing a distinctive craft
Creative Writing in English · Semester 2, Unit 2

## Voice and choices
Voice is the recognisable effect of choices in diction, rhythm, perspective and attitude. It is developed through practice, reading and revision rather than simply discovered once. A narrator’s voice is not automatically identical to the author’s. Audience, genre and context influence decisions about language variety and register.

## Devices in action
A simile makes an explicit comparison; a metaphor creates an implied identification. Personification gives nonhuman things human qualities. Image appeals to the senses, while repetition and rhythm can create emphasis. A device is useful when it contributes to effect: naming a metaphor is less helpful than explaining what it makes the reader notice.

## Syntax and language varieties
Compare “The rain stopped. She waited.” with “After the rain stopped, she waited.” The first can feel abrupt; the second makes the time relationship explicit. Experiment with sentence length and order while preserving clarity. Language varieties and dialects are not errors; render speech respectfully and avoid using stereotype as a substitute for character.

## Practice and lesson
0–10: identify an image and its effect. 10–20: rewrite a plain sentence in three rhythms. 20–30: describe a room from two narrators’ perspectives. 30–40: peer feedback focuses on a specific choice. 40–47: revise the strongest paragraph. 47–50: explain why the revision works.

## Questions
How does syntax affect pace? What assumptions does a narrator reveal through word choice? When does an image clarify and when does it distract?

course-12:2.title: Poetry, fiction and drama
course-12:2.text:
# Poetry, fiction and drama
Creative Writing in English · Semester 2, Unit 3

## Poetry
Poetic language can compress feeling and invite attention to sound, image and line breaks. Rhyme links words through sound; free verse does not follow a fixed traditional metrical pattern, though it may have rhythm and repetition. A dramatic monologue gives a particular speaker a voice addressed within a situation. For children, write with an awareness of age, rhythm and interest without assuming all children enjoy the same style.

Exercise: describe rain in four lines; change the line breaks and observe changes in emphasis. Write a short monologue from the viewpoint of a person waiting for a bus.

## Fiction
A short story generally builds a concentrated situation; a novel can sustain a wider or longer development. Both use viewpoint, character, setting, causality and selection. Popular and literary fiction are overlapping categories, not a quality ranking. A scene presents action and interaction; summary condenses time. Writing for young readers requires attention to experience and audience, not a single fixed vocabulary.

Exercise: a character wants to return a borrowed object but meets an obstacle. Write a scene using action and dialogue, then write a two-sentence summary of the same event.

## Drama and screenwriting
A play is made for performance: dialogue, action, stage space and silence all contribute. A screenplay communicates what can be seen and heard, with scene headings and action written for production. Character emerges through choices under pressure. When studying Indian playwrights, read the prescribed examples and consider language, performance traditions and context rather than treating Indian theatre as one style. Children’s theatre can make imaginative use of movement and participation while remaining age-appropriate.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare the three forms. 10–20: create a short poem. 20–30: build a fiction scene. 30–40: transform it into a dramatic exchange. 40–47: discuss what changes between page and performance. 47–50: exit reflection.

## Questions
How does a line break affect meaning? What does dialogue reveal without explanation? What can be shown on stage that a narrator might otherwise describe?

course-12:3.title: Writing for media
course-12:3.text:
# Writing for media
Creative Writing in English · Semester 2, Unit 4

## Audience, purpose and medium
The same idea changes when the audience reads it, hears it or sees it on a screen. Identify who the audience is, what they need and what the medium allows. Accuracy and transparency matter in all formats. Avoid presenting advertising as independent reporting.

## Print, broadcast and online
A print feature can develop context through headings, paragraphs and quotations. Broadcast writing is heard in time: use clear sentence structure, signal transitions and read the script aloud. Online writing benefits from informative headings, short meaningful sections, links and accessibility features such as descriptive link text. These are flexible principles, not rules forbidding longer sentences.

## Advertising
Advertising attempts to persuade. Identify the audience, offering, key benefit and call to action, but avoid unsupported claims and misleading omissions. Revise “guaranteed to transform everyone’s life” to a precise, supportable description of what the product or event actually offers. Respect privacy and relevant advertising rules.

## Adaptation exercise
Take the announcement “A college hosts a free poetry reading on Friday at 4 p.m. in the library.” Write a 70-word print notice, a 20-second spoken announcement and a concise online post. Keep time, place and cost consistent; do not invent a speaker or registration requirement. Compare how each version suits its medium.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify audience and medium. 10–25: draft two versions of one announcement. 25–35: read the broadcast version aloud. 35–45: peer-check factual consistency and accessibility. 45–50: exit ticket naming one adaptation choice.

## Questions
What makes a script easy to follow when heard once? What distinguishes persuasion from a misleading claim?

course-12:4.title: Revision, editing and publishing
course-12:4.text:
# Editing and publishing
Creative Writing in English · Semester 2, Unit 5

## Revision before proofreading
Revision rethinks purpose, structure, character, evidence or emphasis. Editing improves clarity, consistency and style. Proofreading is the later check for typographical, spelling and punctuation errors. These stages overlap but it is inefficient to polish every comma before deciding whether a scene belongs in the piece.

## Practical revision process
Put the draft aside, read it aloud and describe what each paragraph or scene contributes. Identify the intended reader and the most important effect. Move, expand, cut or rewrite material as needed. Seek specific feedback: “Where did the sequence become unclear?” rather than only “Did you like it?” Decide which feedback helps the work; the writer retains responsibility for the final draft.

## Proofreading checklist
Check names, dates, spelling, paragraph breaks, punctuation and consistent formatting. Verify factual claims and permissions. Check titles and submission instructions. Reading aloud or changing the display can reveal mistakes; neither replaces a careful final check.

## Preparing to publish
Research a suitable journal, publisher or platform; check eligibility, genre, word limits and submission dates. Follow its manuscript instructions and understand rights, licensing and whether simultaneous submissions are permitted. Keep a record of submissions; beware of unsolicited promises and unexplained fees. Rejection is not proof that a piece has no value.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare revision and proofreading. 10–25: mark structure and purpose in a draft. 25–35: exchange specific feedback. 35–45: revise a passage. 45–50: complete an exit checklist and identify one suitable publication venue to investigate.

## Questions
What changed between drafts, and why? What rights would you check before submitting? How does feedback differ from a command?

course-15:0.title: Medieval literature to the English Revolution
course-15:0.text:
# Medieval literature to the English Revolution
Semester 3 · Unit 1

## Periods and languages
The syllabus groups Anglo-Saxon, medieval and early modern literature. The “Anglo-Saxon 5th–14th century” label in the extract overlaps later medieval English: Old English literature is conventionally associated with the period before and around the Norman Conquest of 1066, while Middle English develops after that. These are useful categories, not sudden switches; Latin and French also mattered.

## Medieval traditions
Old English poetry includes heroic narrative and religious writing; Beowulf survives in a later manuscript and should not be assigned a precise composition date without evidence. Middle English works include romance, religious writing and Chaucer’s late-fourteenth-century Canterbury Tales. Chaucer’s pilgrims tell varied stories, linking social observation to a framing narrative. Manuscript culture shaped circulation before printing became established in England under William Caxton in the late fifteenth century.

## Renaissance and Reformation
Renaissance humanism encouraged renewed engagement with classical learning, rhetoric and education; the Reformation transformed religious institutions and debates. Neither was a uniform break with everything medieval. The syllabus lists Tudor and Elizabethan, Jacobean and Caroline periods, followed by the Commonwealth or Interregnum (1649–1660): remember that political dates do not divide literary styles neatly.

Elizabethan and Jacobean drama developed in professional playhouses alongside court and popular entertainments. Shakespeare, Marlowe and Jonson worked in different dramatic modes. Poetry includes sonnet sequences and varied religious and secular verse; Donne is associated with metaphysical poetry. Civil war and censorship affect the later period. Ask how religious change, patronage and performance shape writing without reducing works to their historical background.

## Review
Trace a broad change from manuscript to print; explain why Old English is not the same as Middle English; compare period names with forms that cross their boundaries.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10 min: recall the key terms. 10–25: work through the examples in pairs. 25–38: compare two forms or historical developments using a text from class. 38–45: groups share a claim and evidence. 45–50: write an exit response explaining one distinction.

course-15:1.title: Restoration, Augustan writing and Johnson’s age
course-15:1.text:
# Restoration, Augustan writing and Johnson’s age
Semester 3 · Unit 2

## Restoration and neoclassicism
The Restoration of Charles II in 1660 follows the Interregnum. The reopened commercial theatres produced comedy, tragedy and adaptations; women began appearing professionally on the English public stage. Restoration comedy often examines manners, marriage and reputation. Dryden’s work shows the importance of public controversy, satire and criticism.

Neoclassical writing values, in different ways, order, judgement, rhetoric and classical models; it is not a single set of rules followed identically by all writers. Augustan is a retrospective analogy to Roman literary culture, often applied to early eighteenth-century writers including Pope and Swift. Pope’s mock-epic treats a social dispute through elevated epic conventions; satire is not always equivalent to the author’s literal views.

## Print, prose and the novel
Periodicals, newspapers, coffee-house discussion and expanding print networks influenced prose forms and reading publics. Addison and Steele’s periodical essays address social behaviour and taste. Defoe, Richardson and Fielding are often discussed in histories of the English novel, but the novel has several histories and cannot be reduced to a single inventor.

## Johnson and the later century
Samuel Johnson contributed criticism, essays, biography and a major dictionary. Late eighteenth-century literature also contains forms of sensibility, early Gothic fiction and challenges to neat period boundaries. Questions about class, empire, slavery and women’s access to authorship complicate a story focused only on celebrated male writers.

## Review
How does a mock-epic use contrast? Why did expanding print matter? What is gained and lost by calling a period “Augustan”?

course-15:2.text:
# Romanticism: poetry, fiction and Gothic
Semester 3 · Unit 3

## Historical frame
The Romantic period is often dated approximately from the 1790s to the 1830s; dates vary by literary history. The French Revolution, industrialisation, political reform and imperial expansion form important contexts. Romantic writers respond differently to these developments and should not be treated as a single school.

## Poetry
Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lyrical Ballads (1798) is an important reference point for poetry, ordinary language and imagination. Other writers such as Blake, Byron, Shelley, Keats and women poets developed different forms and political positions. Nature in Romantic writing can be a landscape, a source of spiritual or imaginative reflection, and a site of social conflict; avoid assuming that it always provides comfort.

## Fiction and the Gothic
Austen’s fiction explores marriage, property and social judgement with irony and careful narration. The Gothic uses such resources as threatened spaces, secrecy, fear and unstable knowledge; it can also examine power and social boundaries. Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) combines Gothic and speculative elements to ask about creation, responsibility and exclusion. Its creature is not named Frankenstein: that is the creator’s surname.

## Reading questions
How does a speaker’s relationship to landscape affect a poem? Compare the handling of social constraint in a novel and a Gothic narrative. How can political history help interpretation without replacing close reading?

# Victorian literature and its contexts
Semester 3 · Unit 4

## Context
Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, while “Victorian” literature is often studied across a broader nineteenth-century context. The syllabus’s phrase “early 19th century (1832–1901)” spans much more than the early century; identify the dates explicitly instead of repeating the label uncritically. Industrialisation, urbanisation, the expansion of empire, religious debate, scientific developments and struggles over reform changed literary culture.

## Poetry and the novel
Tennyson and Browning use different poetic forms; the dramatic monologue can make a speaker reveal more than they intend. Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s poetry includes personal and public concerns. In fiction, Dickens depicts social institutions and inequality; the Brontës explore desire, constraint and narrative perspective; George Eliot examines moral choice and community. These are examples, not an exhaustive list.

Serial publication influenced how many novels reached readers. Education, journalism, class and women’s legal and economic position shape both authorship and subject matter. Imperial power and colonial resistance also matter, including in texts set in Britain.

## Questions
How can a dramatic speaker be distinct from the poet? What does serial publication change about reading? How do a novel’s characters encounter social institutions?

course-15:4.text:
# Hardy and modernism
Semester 3 · Unit 5

## Thomas Hardy
Hardy’s fiction and poetry bridge conventional period divisions. His novels use the imagined region of Wessex to examine rural change, social expectation, chance and the limits imposed on individuals. Tess of the d’Urbervilles and Jude the Obscure should be read in their specific social contexts rather than reduced to the claim that fate alone controls everything.

## Modernism
Modernism is a broad and varied set of formal experiments, not simply a synonym for “modern.” The world wars, urbanisation, technological change, empire and changing ideas of self and society are important contexts. Fragmentation, shifting perspectives, nonlinear time, allusion and experiments with consciousness appear in some works, but no feature applies to every modernist text.

Woolf’s To the Lighthouse changes pace and perspective across three sections; Eliot’s The Waste Land combines voices and allusions. Compare their methods rather than assuming fragmentation has one meaning. The syllabus highlights 1914–1945, but modernist writing begins before 1914 and continues beyond 1945.

## Questions
How does Hardy connect individual experience with social structures? What does a shifting viewpoint allow? Why should a literary period not be treated as a perfectly bounded box?

course-16:0.text:
# Tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy and satire
Semester 3 · Unit 1

## Tragedy
Tragedy often represents serious conflict, suffering and loss; the nature of the protagonist and ending vary across traditions. Aristotle’s discussion of tragedy is influential but is not a universal checklist for every play. Analyse what choices, institutions and circumstances contribute to the outcome.

## Comedy
Comedy can expose errors, misunderstandings and social pretensions. Some comedies end in reconciliation or marriage, but not all; laughter can be affectionate, critical or uncomfortable. Compare how Shaw uses comic contrast between idealised heroism and practical experience.

## Tragicomedy and satire
Tragicomedy combines or moves between serious danger and comic elements without necessarily producing a purely tragic ending. Satire criticises attitudes, institutions or conduct through irony, exaggeration, parody or ridicule. Its target must be argued from context: a satirical speaker’s claim is not automatically the writer’s own belief.

## Practice
Identify a scene’s emotional effect, the techniques producing it and the social assumptions under pressure. Can one scene be both funny and troubling?

# Drama, novel, short story and essay
Semester 3 · Unit 2

## Drama
Drama presents action for performance through dialogue, stage directions, movement, space and silence. A printed script and a particular production are related but not identical. Ask what audiences know and what characters know at each point.

## Novel and short story
A novel is an extended prose fiction capable of developing multiple events, characters and perspectives. A short story often concentrates on a smaller set of moments or relationships, though length alone does not determine its effect. Narrator, focalisation, sequence and selection influence both. A plot overview should not be mistaken for a full account of every chapter.

## Essay
An essay is prose organised around a subject or argument; essays may be personal, reflective, analytical or persuasive. Identify the central claim, structure, examples and implied audience. A literary essay may use voice and imagery as well as argument.

## Practice
Describe the same disagreement as a dialogue, a short narrative and a reflective essay. What can each form foreground?

course-16:2.text:
# One-act play, biography, autobiography and melodrama
Semester 3 · Unit 3

## One-act play
A one-act play has a single act, often concentrating action within a limited span, setting or conflict. It can still contain shifts of scene and complex characters. Observe how quickly the opening establishes stakes and how stage action leads to a conclusion.

## Biography and autobiography
Biography narrates a person’s life written by another; autobiography is a life account written by the subject, although collaborative writing can complicate simple categories. Both involve selection, narrative shaping and evidence. A remembered event is a perspective on the past, not automatically a complete record.

## Melodrama
Melodrama emphasises heightened emotion, conflict and theatrical effect; in particular historical forms music accompanied action. It may use recognisable moral oppositions, but individual works can complicate them. Calling something melodramatic should not replace analysis of its actual conventions and audience.

## Practice
Rewrite a remembered event as an autobiographical paragraph; then list evidence a biographer would need to check. Discuss how a one-act scene might show the same event through action.

course-16:3.title: Farce, ballad, masque and epic
course-16:3.text:
# Farce, ballad, masque and epic
Semester 3 · Unit 4

## Farce
Farce uses rapid complications, improbable situations, mistaken identities and physical or verbal comedy. Analyse timing and consequences rather than dismissing it as mere silliness.

## Ballad
A ballad is commonly a narrative song or poem associated with oral and written traditions. Repetition, dialogue and incremental variation appear in many examples, though not all ballads follow one fixed form. Compare versions before asserting a single authoritative text.

## Masque
A masque is a form of courtly entertainment associated with spectacle, music, dance, costume and allegory, especially prominent in early modern England. Its meaning depends partly on patronage and performance setting.

## Epic
Epic is a long narrative of significant action, often associated with heroic figures, communities and elevated style. Traditions vary greatly; oral and literary epics are not identical. A mock-epic applies epic conventions to an apparently minor subject for comic or critical effect.

## Practice
Compare the scale and purpose of an epic narrative with a ballad. What would be lost if a masque were studied without its spectacle?

course-16:4.text:
# Lyric, sonnet, elegy, prosody and ode
Semester 3 · Unit 5

## Lyric, elegy and ode
A lyric generally foregrounds a voice, feeling or moment rather than an extended plot. An elegy mourns or reflects on loss, often moving through remembrance and consolation, though not every elegy follows that sequence. An ode is a sustained lyric address or meditation, frequently developed through formal patterns; different odes have different structures.

## Sonnet
A sonnet traditionally has fourteen lines. The English or Shakespearean form often uses three quatrains and a couplet, frequently rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG; the Petrarchan form often has an octave and sestet with different patterns. A volta is a turn in thought or tone. These are conventions, not guarantees for every poem.

## Prosody
Prosody studies the sound and patterning of verse. A syllable is a unit of speech; stress gives relative prominence. An iamb is an unstressed–stressed pattern and pentameter has five metrical feet in a line. Real spoken lines can vary from a regular pattern. Rhyme concerns similar sounds, not merely spelling; rhythm also depends on syntax, pauses and performance.

## Practice
Read a short poem aloud. Mark a possible stress pattern and explain where performance permits more than one reading. Identify a turn and connect it to an argument.
