course-22:4.text:
# Herman Melville · Bartleby, the Scrivener
American Literature I · Semester 4

## Setting and narrator
An unnamed Wall Street lawyer tells the story of his employee Bartleby. The lawyer presents himself as a safe, comfortable man and introduces his copyists Turkey and Nippers and the office assistant Ginger Nut. Because the lawyer controls the account, his judgments and charitable self-image need examination.

## Story from beginning to end
The lawyer hires Bartleby to copy legal documents. At first he produces a great deal of work. When asked to help examine a document, however, he quietly replies that he would prefer not to. The phrase returns as the lawyer makes other requests. Bartleby’s calm refusal unsettles the office, and the narrator struggles to decide how to respond.

On a Sunday visit, the lawyer discovers evidence that Bartleby has been living in the office. He feels pity at the man’s isolation, but his sympathy is mixed with discomfort and concern about his own responsibilities. Bartleby declines to explain his history. Eventually he stops copying altogether. The lawyer dismisses him and offers money, but Bartleby does not leave.

Unable to resolve the situation and anxious about his business, the lawyer moves his office, leaving Bartleby behind. The new occupants complain when Bartleby remains in the building. The lawyer offers possible kinds of work and even invites him to stay at his own home, but Bartleby refuses. Other people have him removed to the prison known as the Tombs.

The lawyer visits and pays a prison attendant to provide food, but Bartleby declines to eat. On a later visit, the lawyer finds that he has died. Afterwards he reports a rumour that Bartleby once worked in a dead-letter office, handling undelivered correspondence, and had lost that post. The lawyer interprets the rumour as meaningful, but it remains unconfirmed; it does not definitively explain Bartleby’s motives.

## Interpretation
Walls, partitions and undelivered messages suggest limits on connection. Bartleby’s phrase is grammatically polite but resists the employer’s expectations. Readers differ on whether his refusal is a protest, a response to distress, an existential puzzle or something that cannot be reduced to one explanation. Avoid diagnosing him as a settled fact. Analyse the narrator’s compassion alongside the ways he seeks to escape responsibility.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: describe the office and its work. 10–22: trace how Bartleby’s refusals change. 22–32: examine the lawyer’s competing reactions. 32–42: discuss the prison and unverified rumour. 42–50: write an interpretation with a limitation.

## Questions
How does “prefer not to” differ from a direct order or explanation? Why does the lawyer move? What can and cannot be inferred from the dead-letter rumour?

Use the assigned text and edition alongside these teaching notes; check details and interpretations before teaching.

course-22:4.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman · The Yellow Wallpaper
course-22:4.text:
# Charlotte Perkins Gilman · The Yellow Wallpaper
American Literature I · Semester 4

## Context and care
Published in 1892, the story is a first-person account of a woman whose physician husband restricts her activity as treatment for a nervous condition. It invites criticism of a historical rest cure and unequal medical authority; it is not a guide to diagnosing or treating a real person. The narrator has recently had a baby, but the text does not establish a modern clinical diagnosis.

## Story from beginning to end
The narrator and her husband John rent a large house for the summer. John, a physician, dismisses her concerns and discourages work and writing. She believes activity and companionship would help her, but records her thoughts secretly. John chooses an upstairs room that she believes was once a nursery. Its barred windows, damaged floor and disturbing yellow wallpaper make her uneasy; her preferences about the room are overridden.

With little intellectual activity and much time alone, she studies the paper. Its colour and tangled design increasingly occupy her attention. She begins to discern a figure behind the outer pattern and eventually sees a woman shaking the apparent bars and creeping about. John and his sister Jennie, who helps with the household, do not share her account. The narrator hides the extent of her preoccupation and resists attempts to interfere with the paper.

As departure approaches, she becomes determined to release the woman she sees. She locks herself in the room, removes much of the wallpaper and creeps around the wall. John demands entry; she tells him where to find the key. When he enters and sees her, he faints. She declares that she has got out despite him and “Jane,” and continues creeping over his body. The identity of “Jane” is debated; the narrative does not securely explain the name.

## Interpretation
The wallpaper can be read as a figure for confinement, with the imagined woman reflecting the narrator’s experience. The ending combines a claim of escape with evident distress, so calling it simply a happy victory or simply a medical case misses its tension. Secret writing gives readers access to a perspective that other characters often discount. John’s concern for his wife does not remove the unequal authority he exercises.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish historical medical practice from present-day care. 10–22: map whose decisions govern the room. 22–32: trace the changing wallpaper descriptions. 32–42: debate escape and confinement at the ending. 42–50: write a claim that distinguishes evidence from inference.

## Questions
Why does the narrator write secretly? How does her perception of the wallpaper change? What remains uncertain about “Jane”?

Use the assigned text and edition alongside these teaching notes; check details and interpretations before teaching.

course-22:4.title: Kate Chopin · The Story of an Hour
course-22:4.text:
# Kate Chopin · The Story of an Hour
American Literature I · Semester 4

## Opening and false report
Louise Mallard has heart trouble. Her sister Josephine and her husband’s friend Richards try to tell her gently that her husband Brently has reportedly died in a railway disaster. Richards has checked the report with a second telegram. Louise immediately weeps with her sister, then goes alone to her room.

## At the window
Sitting before an open window, Louise notices signs of spring, sounds outside and patches of blue sky among clouds. She feels something approaching her awareness and at first tries to resist it. Gradually she recognises a sense of freedom and repeats the word to herself. She imagines future years belonging to her rather than being governed by another person’s will.

Her feelings are complex. She expects to grieve when she sees Brently’s body and remembers that he looked at her with love. She acknowledges that she loved him sometimes and sometimes did not. Her joy in anticipated independence need not mean that her initial grief was false or that Brently is portrayed as deliberately cruel.

## Reversal and ending
Josephine worries outside the locked door and asks Louise to come out. Louise eventually opens it and goes downstairs with her. At that moment Brently enters: he was far from the accident and did not know about it. Josephine cries out, and Richards attempts too late to screen him from Louise’s view. The narrative then reports that Louise has died; doctors attribute her death from heart disease to “the joy that kills.”

Readers often see dramatic irony in the doctors’ conclusion: they assume joy at her husband’s return, while the preceding scene has shown Louise’s joy in the prospect of autonomy. The exact emotional and medical mechanism of her death is not described in detail; the strength of the irony comes from the contrast between public interpretation and the private feelings readers have witnessed.

## Form and teaching
The story compresses a major change in expectation into a short span. The open window and spring images can suggest possibility without reducing them to a single fixed meaning. In 50 minutes: 0–10 predict how news might be received; 10–20 sequence the reported death and private response; 20–30 analyse the window; 30–40 compare the doctors’ conclusion with Louise’s thoughts; 40–50 write about the ending’s irony.

## Questions
Why are Louise’s grief and relief not necessarily incompatible? What does she imagine at the window? Why might readers question the doctors’ diagnosis?

Use the assigned text and edition alongside these teaching notes; check details and interpretations before teaching.

course-23:0.title: Background · Macaulay’s Minute on Indian Education (1835)
course-23:0.text:
# Background · Macaulay’s Minute on Indian Education (1835)
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Historical situation
In the early nineteenth century, officials of the East India Company debated how public educational funds should be spent. The controversy commonly called Orientalist–Anglicist concerned languages, institutions and kinds of knowledge, though individuals’ positions were more varied than two perfectly uniform camps. Thomas Babington Macaulay’s Minute, dated 2 February 1835, intervened in that debate; Governor-General William Bentinck’s resolution followed in March.

## Argument
Macaulay claims that English can open access to European science and literature and argues against continuing to privilege Sanskrit and Arabic learning with the disputed funds. He makes a sweeping, hostile comparison between European and Indian/Arabic literary traditions and proposes educating an intermediary class of Indians who can communicate between the colonial rulers and the population. He also anticipates that this group could develop Indian languages and transmit knowledge more widely.

## Critical reading
His ranking of knowledge is a colonial argument, not an objective fact. Ask what he knew directly, whose educational aspirations he selected, and whose learning he dismissed. The document concerns funding and policy under colonial government; it did not instantly make everyone speak English or erase all other educational institutions. English education’s later history includes unequal access, new careers and writing, reform and anticolonial critique. These outcomes cannot all be reduced to one person’s intention.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: distinguish a historical source from a neutral account. 10–20: identify the policy question. 20–30: map claims, assumptions and intended audience. 30–40: question whose knowledge is valued. 40–50: compare consequences with authorial intentions.

## Questions
What did Macaulay propose to fund? How does he justify hierarchy between traditions? Why should later outcomes not be equated with his intentions?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Sri Aurobindo · The Renaissance in India, Chapter 1
course-23:0.text:
# Sri Aurobindo · The Renaissance in India, Chapter 1
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Context and argument
The opening of Sri Aurobindo’s series on the Indian renaissance appeared in 1918. He considers what “renaissance” or rebirth might mean for India under the pressure of European influence. The chapter is an argument about culture and renewal, not a detached account on which every historian must agree.

## Following the essay
Aurobindo asks whether India is experiencing a genuine cultural awakening or merely adopting external forms. He compares the term with the European Renaissance but cautions against assuming that the two processes must be identical. In his account, renewal must involve the creative life of a people rather than only a fashionable change in institutions.

He argues that India’s cultural and spiritual inheritance has survived political subordination, while its outward intellectual, artistic and social forms have experienced stagnation. A true rebirth, he suggests, would reshape those forms rather than simply repeat the past or copy Europe. He resists the colonial stereotype that India is exclusively other-worldly and incapable of practical life, asserting that spiritual concerns can coexist with creative and active living.

## Critical questions
Distinguish Aurobindo’s claims about a shared Indian “spirit” from verifiable claims about every community. His broad generalisations about India and Europe invite scrutiny: whose voices are represented, and how might caste, gender, region and religion complicate a unified cultural account? He is not simply arguing that every outside influence is harmful; focus on what he says about creative response rather than mechanical imitation.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: define “renaissance” as a contested term. 10–20: map the contrast between imitation and renewal. 20–30: examine his response to a colonial stereotype. 30–40: test the idea of a single national spirit. 40–50: write a claim with a qualification.

## Questions
Why compare and distinguish Indian and European renaissances? What does he mean by new forms? What might a single cultural “soul” leave out?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: H. L. V. Derozio · The Harp of India
course-23:0.text:
# H. L. V. Derozio · The Harp of India
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

Unit coverage is incomplete: these selections do not yet cover all the prescribed texts. Check your assigned edition.

## Overview
Derozio’s fourteen-line poem addresses a neglected musical instrument as a figure for an artistic inheritance. It moves from lament over silence toward the speaker’s hope that he might make the instrument sound again. Read the symbolic “India” in the context of early nineteenth-century colonial rule without assuming the poem provides a complete history of every Indian literary tradition.

## Movement of the poem
The speaker asks why the harp hangs alone on a withered bough, unstrung and silent. Its music was once sweet, but now the breeze passes without drawing song from it. Silence seems to have bound it, and a simile compares its neglect to a ruined monument on a desert plain.

The speaker recalls earlier, worthier hands that played it and earned praise; their graves have flowers, suggesting that their achievements are remembered even after death. The closing lines imagine that a living person might awaken its music again. The speaker asks to strike the strain himself, turning grief into an aspiration to create.

## Techniques and debate
Direct address makes the instrument seem a listener; the extended metaphor connects musical performance with poetry and cultural memory. A sonnet-like form gives the argument a compact shape. The poem’s idea of silence is a representation made by the speaker, not evidence that Indian art had literally ceased. Ask which traditions and languages a claim about a single national harp might leave out.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss what an unused instrument might suggest. 10–20: paraphrase the questions. 20–30: examine the monument and graves. 30–40: analyse the hopeful closing turn. 40–50: write a claim that distinguishes metaphor from historical fact.

## Questions
Why address the harp directly? How does the ending change the opening mood? What are the limits of reading the harp as a single national voice?

course-23:0.title: H. L. V. Derozio · The Orphan Girl
course-23:0.text:
# H. L. V. Derozio · The Orphan Girl
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

Unit coverage is incomplete: these selections do not yet cover all the prescribed texts. Check your assigned edition.

## Summary
The speaker describes a young, beautiful girl as exposed to suffering in an unkind world. Her father has died in war; her mother, overwhelmed by grief after becoming a widow, has also died. The child is left without parents, home or a friend who will shelter her.

The poem then imagines the danger of a lonely life. It warns that, if she should stray from socially approved virtue, the world may respond with contempt rather than help. This is a conditional fear, not a narrated account of a particular offence. The speaker condemns cruelty toward a vulnerable person and praises whoever offers an orphan shelter from sorrow and shame. The poem does not show a specific rescuer arriving.

## Interpretation
Descriptions of beauty and fragile innocence invite pity, while the images of a cold world and a desert present social isolation as a harsh landscape. The father’s “glorious grave” can be discussed alongside the devastating cost of war for his family. The poem asks for compassion but also uses the language of female “virtue” and shame; readers can question how that language constrains the girl it seeks to defend. Avoid making a medical claim about the mother’s cause of death beyond the poem’s description of grief.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify whose voices are heard and absent. 10–20: trace the family’s losses. 20–30: distinguish events from the speaker’s warnings. 30–40: discuss compassion and the poem’s language of virtue. 40–50: write a response grounded in one image.

## Questions
How does war affect the family? What future does the speaker fear rather than narrate as fact? How does the poem criticise social judgment?

course-23:0.title: Toru Dutt · Our Casuarina Tree
course-23:0.text:
# Toru Dutt · Our Casuarina Tree
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

Unit coverage is incomplete: these selections do not yet cover all the prescribed texts. Check your assigned edition.

## Overview
The speaker describes a beloved tree and the life around it, then reveals its connection to lost companions and childhood. The poem moves across place and time, asking whether poetry and love can protect memory from forgetting. Biographical notes often connect the companions with Dutt’s deceased siblings Aru and Abju; the poem itself addresses them without naming them.

## Stanza-by-stanza
1. A creeper winds around the tree’s scarred trunk like a great python. The strong tree seems to wear it as a scarf; flowers, birds and bees gather around its branches, and a song fills the garden at night. The python comparison initially makes the embrace seem dangerous, while the scarf suggests ornament as well as endurance.
2. At dawn the speaker opens her window and sees the tree. A grey baboon watches the sunrise while young ones play; kokilas call, cows move toward pasture and water-lilies appear in the nearby tank. The tree supports a detailed living scene, not just an abstract symbol.
3. The speaker says the tree is dear above all because she played beneath it with loved companions. Their memory brings tears. The tree’s sound becomes a dirge-like murmur, imagined as a lament that might reach an unknown land.
4. In distant France or Italy, the sound of the sea recalls the tree. Physical distance does not erase the image: the speaker’s inner vision brings the remembered tree and native landscape near.
5. The speaker dedicates a song to the tree and the beloved people who now rest in death. She wishes the tree a place among enduring trees, alluding to Wordsworth’s Borrowdale yews, and asks love to defend it from oblivion. The wish is an act of remembrance, not proof that death can literally be reversed.

## Form and teaching
Five eleven-line stanzas combine visual imagery, sound, simile, personification and literary allusion. In 50 minutes: 0–10 sketch the living scene; 10–22 paraphrase each stanza; 22–32 trace the turn from description to grief; 32–42 discuss travel and memory; 42–50 explain how the final dedication resists forgetting.

## Questions
Why is the tree more than beautiful to the speaker? How does the sea evoke it abroad? What work does the Borrowdale allusion do?

course-23:0.title: Toru Dutt · Lakshman
course-23:0.text:
# Toru Dutt · Lakshman
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

Unit coverage is incomplete: these selections do not yet cover all the prescribed texts. Check your assigned edition.

## Context
The poem reimagines a moment associated with the Ramayana: Rama is away, Sita hears a cry she believes to be his, and Lakshman must decide whether to leave her. Retellings differ; distinguish the events Dutt stages from later events in broader versions of the story.

## Movement of the poem
Sita urgently asks Lakshman to go to Rama’s aid. She hears danger in the cry and is frightened by Lakshman’s apparent delay. Lakshman answers that Rama is powerful and that the voice is a deceptive trick by an enemy. He has a duty to protect Sita and tries to reassure her.

Their disagreement intensifies. Sita questions his courage and accuses him of a hidden desire to take her for himself if Rama dies. Her accusation wounds Lakshman; his conflicting duties—to follow Rama’s instruction to stay and to respond to Sita’s distress—become impossible to reconcile comfortably.

Lakshman finally decides to leave, acknowledging that this disregards his chief’s order. Before departing, he draws a protective magic circle with an arrow and urges Sita not to cross it. He asks her to think better of him and leaves with his weapons. A vulture’s harsh cry adds an ominous note. The poem ends with his departure; Ravana’s subsequent abduction of Sita belongs to the larger narrative, not an event depicted in this ending.

## Interpretation and teaching
Dramatic dialogue lets fear, loyalty and hurt emerge through clashing perspectives. Do not make Sita responsible for violence committed by another person: the poem’s emotional conflict can be analysed without blaming a victim. In 50 minutes: 0–10 establish the scene; 10–22 paraphrase each speaker’s reasons; 22–32 map Lakshman’s duties; 32–42 examine the circle and omen; 42–50 write a balanced account of the conflict.

## Questions
Why does Lakshman distrust the cry? What accusation makes his decision more painful? Where does Dutt’s poem end?

course-23:0.title: Michael Madhusudan Dutt · The Captive Ladie — preliminary outline
course-23:0.text:
# Michael Madhusudan Dutt · The Captive Ladie — preliminary outline
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Important limitation
This is an introductory outline, not the requested complete canto-by-canto explanation. The full prescribed text and edition have not yet been checked in sufficient detail. Do not infer unverified incidents or the exact wording of the ending from this outline.

## Context and broad narrative
Dutt published this English verse narrative in 1849. Its two cantos draw on traditions about Prithviraj, a princess of Kanauj and conflict culminating in his defeat by Muhammad Ghuri’s forces. Scholarship describes the princess’s confinement and her escape with the king among the narrative’s major elements. Names, historical interpretations and details may differ across sources and editions: distinguish a literary retelling of a legendary past from a direct historical record.

## Ways to read
Consider how the title foregrounds a captive woman while martial heroism, love and political conflict also shape the narrative. Ask how much agency the princess is given and how descriptions of opponents create a perspective on power. Dutt’s use of English narrative verse and South Asian material also invites discussion of literary influence without suggesting that either culture is uniform.

## Interim lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: explain that the outline is incomplete. 10–25: read the opening of the assigned canto and identify speaker and setting. 25–35: map characters and relationships using textual evidence. 35–45: examine one image of captivity or heroism. 45–50: list unanswered plot questions to investigate in the text.

## Questions
Whose perspective dominates the assigned passage? What is the difference between an epic retelling and historical evidence? What remains to be verified?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Rabindranath Tagore · Leave This Chanting
course-23:0.text:
# Rabindranath Tagore · Leave This Chanting
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary in sequence
The speaker addresses someone worshipping in a closed, dark temple and urges them to leave chanting and counting beads. Rather than imagining the divine as confined to the sanctuary, the speaker locates God with the tiller working hard ground and the pathmaker breaking stones, in sun and rain and covered with dust.

The worshipper is asked to put aside the outward mantle of holiness and join the workers. The poem questions deliverance conceived as escape from life: the divine has accepted the bonds of creation and remains connected with the world. Its conclusion invites the listener to meet God through work and participation, even if their clothes become dusty.

## Interpretation
Imperatives and rhetorical questions create an urgent challenge. The contrast between closed temple and open workplace gives spiritual value to labour and solidarity. This is a critique of a particular isolated form of devotion, not proof that every ritual or worshipper is insincere. Discuss how it might be read alongside the dignity and actual conditions of workers.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the addressee. 10–20: paraphrase temple and workplace images. 20–30: examine the question about deliverance. 30–40: discuss labour and devotion. 40–50: write a claim supported by an image.

## Questions
Where does the speaker locate God? What is questioned about deliverance? Why is dust important?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Rabindranath Tagore · Purity
course-23:0.text:
# Rabindranath Tagore · Purity
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Text identification
Some anthologies title the fourth English Gitanjali lyric “Purity”; its opening addresses the divine as the life of the speaker’s life. Check that this is the version assigned in class because titles can vary across editions.

## Summary
The speaker promises to keep the body pure because of a sense of divine presence in it. The next commitment concerns thought: the speaker will resist untruth, associating the divine with truth and the light of reason. The third concerns the heart: the speaker will strive to keep evil away and allow love to flower, imagining the heart as an inner shrine. Finally, the speaker intends to make the divine visible through actions, recognising a power that makes action possible.

## Interpretation
The movement joins body, thought, feeling and conduct rather than treating purity as outward appearance alone. Repetition of future intention makes the lyric a prayer and an ongoing ethical commitment; “try” and “endeavour” leave room for effort rather than claiming perfection. Body purity should be understood in the devotional language of the poem, not used to stigmatise illness, disability, menstruation or other bodily experiences.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the addressee and repeated promise. 10–22: map the four areas of life. 22–32: examine light, flower and shrine images. 32–42: compare inner conviction and action. 42–50: compose a paraphrase without copying the poem.

## Questions
How do the four commitments develop? Why does the speaker mention reason? How is love represented?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Sarojini Naidu · Summer Woods
course-23:0.text:
# Sarojini Naidu · Summer Woods
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary
The speaker is tired of decorated interiors, public conflict, festivities and fame. She longs instead for the colour and movement of summer woods, with gulmohars and flowering cassia. She calls her beloved to accompany her where koels sing, away from public toil and praise.

She imagines resting and dreaming beneath trees, wearing jasmine and playing flutes near banyan roots. The lovers would wander by the river and bathe in pools where panthers drink. At the end they are companions through dawn and night, compared with Krishna and Radhika. These are desires and imagined activities, not a factual travel report.

## Reading closely
Rich visual, musical and fragrant imagery makes the imagined forest an alternative to public life. The contrast does not require the claim that cities or all social activities are inherently bad. The allusion to Krishna and Radha gives the couple’s intimacy a cultural and devotional resonance; readers can ask how myth and sensual pleasure interact. The syllabic movement and repeated invitation produce a songlike tone.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: contrast the poem’s two settings. 10–22: collect images associated with the senses. 22–32: trace the speaker’s invitation. 32–42: discuss the mythological comparison. 42–50: write about one image without treating imagined details as events.

## Questions
What does the speaker wish to leave? How do sounds and scents shape the woods? What does the Krishna–Radhika allusion add?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Sarojini Naidu · The Palanquin Bearers
course-23:0.text:
# Sarojini Naidu · The Palanquin Bearers
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary
The speakers are palanquin bearers singing as they carry a woman. In the first stanza they describe her swaying like a flower, skimming like a bird and floating like laughter from a dream. Their repeated words suggest a gentle, rhythmic journey. They compare her to a pearl carried on a string.

In the second stanza the images shift to a star, a beam on water and a tear from a bride’s eyes. The tear introduces the possibility of sadness within the otherwise light song. The poem repeats the image of the pearl and the movement of carrying. Although wedding travel is a common context for interpretation, the comparison to a bride does not supply every detail of the passenger’s destination or feelings.

## Technique and discussion
Repetition and musical rhythm evoke coordinated movement; similes make the passenger seem delicate and precious. The bearers speak collectively, but the woman does not speak for herself. Ask how poetic beauty, the workers’ labour and the passenger’s absent perspective can be considered together without inventing a detailed story.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify who speaks. 10–20: read aloud and notice repeated sounds. 20–30: compare images of laughter and a tear. 30–40: discuss what the poem does and does not tell us. 40–50: explain the effect of one simile.

## Questions
How does repetition create motion? What mood might the tear introduce? Whose perspective is missing?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Nissim Ezekiel · Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T. S.
course-23:0.text:
# Nissim Ezekiel · Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T. S.
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary
A speaker addresses a farewell gathering for Miss Pushpa, who is soon going abroad to improve her prospects. The speaker praises her sweetness, both outward and inward, and says she smiles readily. He mentions her family and her father’s work as an advocate, but becomes uncertain about the place and digresses into a memory of visiting acquaintances and enjoying their hospitality.

Returning to Pushpa, he calls her popular and praises her willingness to help. She readily says yes to requests. The speaker wishes her a good journey, invites others to speak and says that Pushpa will sum up afterwards. We hear the occasion through his speech; Pushpa’s own speech is not included.

## Language and interpretation
The dramatic monologue’s repetitions, digression and conversational phrasing create humour and an individual voice. The poem stylises a variety of Indian English; Indian English is a legitimate, diverse variety, not a collection of errors to be corrected against British usage. Discuss whether the satire targets formulaic public praise, social aspiration or the speaker’s self-importance, and whether the humour also invites stereotypes. Different readings are possible.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify occasion and speaker. 10–22: follow the digression and return to Pushpa. 22–32: identify what we learn and do not learn about her. 32–42: discuss humour without mocking a community’s speech. 42–50: write a farewell opening that keeps the guest at its centre.

## Questions
What causes the speaker’s digression? How does the monologue create humour? Why does Pushpa’s missing voice matter?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Nissim Ezekiel · Night of the Scorpion
course-23:0.text:
# Nissim Ezekiel · Night of the Scorpion
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary
The adult speaker remembers a rainy night when a scorpion, driven indoors beneath a sack of rice, stung his mother and escaped. Neighbours arrive with candles and lanterns and search without finding it. They say that the creature’s movement will move the poison in her blood, and offer prayers and explanations involving past and future lives, suffering and purification.

While the neighbours gather, the mother twists and groans on a mat. The speaker’s father, described as a sceptic and rationalist, tries remedies and blessings; he even pours paraffin on the affected toe and lights it. A holy man performs a rite. After twenty hours the sting loses its force. The mother thanks God that she rather than her children was stung.

## Technique and interpretation
The repeated “they said” gives prominence to communal voices, while the crowd, light and rain surround the suffering woman. The father’s mixture of approaches complicates any simple division between “rational” and “traditional.” The mother speaks only at the end, shifting attention to her care for her children. This final remark is moving, but it should not be used to suggest that all mothers must silently accept pain.

## Safety note
The father’s burning of the toe is part of the poem, not medical advice. Scorpion stings can be dangerous, especially for children. Do not burn, cut or apply chemicals to a sting; seek urgent medical advice, particularly for severe symptoms.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: sequence the sting and gathering. 10–22: separate neighbours’ beliefs from observed events. 22–32: examine the father’s response. 32–42: analyse the delayed final voice. 42–50: explain how the poem changes focus.

## Questions
Why do neighbours search for the scorpion? What complicates the father’s rationalist label? How does the mother’s final statement alter the poem?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Kamala Das · An Introduction
course-23:0.text:
# Kamala Das · An Introduction
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Overview
The speaker introduces herself through nationality, colour, place, languages, gender and personal experience, then resists others’ attempts to define her. The poem uses a strongly personal voice, but a reader should distinguish the crafted speaker from an uncomplicated autobiography of Kamala Das.

## Movement of the poem
The opening refers to male political authority and then asserts the speaker’s identity as an Indian from Malabar who speaks, writes and dreams in different languages. She recalls being told not to write in English because it is not her mother tongue. She responds that the language she speaks becomes her own: its mixed and distinctive qualities carry her experience.

The poem turns to growing up and an early marriage, using painful bodily images to describe a loss of freedom and an unequal encounter with expectations of adulthood. The speaker also describes being instructed to fit feminine roles and names. She rejects attempts to confine her identity to those categories.

Toward the end, the pronoun “I” moves between the speaker and figures of male power or desire. Her insistence that she too can say “I” challenges the assumption that only certain people can claim a full, authoritative self. The shifting pronouns allow both overlap and conflict; follow the wording carefully rather than assigning every “I” to the same person automatically.

## Teaching and discussion
Free verse, direct address, repetition and abrupt shifts of subject give the poem a confrontational energy. The account includes intimate and potentially distressing experiences: offer students a respectful way to discuss imagery without disclosing personal experiences. In 50 minutes: 0–10 map opening identity claims; 10–22 discuss language ownership; 22–32 trace pressures on the body and roles; 32–42 examine shifting pronouns; 42–50 write a claim using a chosen passage.

## Questions
Why does the speaker claim English as hers? What roles do others prescribe? How does the meaning of “I” shift?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Kamala Das · Someone Else’s Song
course-23:0.text:
# Kamala Das · Someone Else’s Song
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary, stanza by stanza
The speaker declares herself to be countless people speaking together, comparing the clamour to women at village wells. A single “I” is already multiple rather than a stable solitary voice.

Next the speaker identifies with countless deaths. Images of disease and drying seeds suggest pain and also the possibility that something will be shed and grow as another person’s memory. In the third stanza, countless births appear in blood and an unsettling growing figure whose long-nailed hands mark the air. Birth is energetic but not simply gentle or reassuring.

The final stanza turns from voices to countless silences, imagined as crystal beads strung onto someone else’s song. The ending raises a question: does another’s song preserve those silences, use them without giving the speaker control, or both? The poem does not settle the answer.

## Technique and interpretation
The repeated opening phrase links the four stanzas while the images move through speech, death, birth and silence. The tension between “I” and “someone else” invites reflection on individuality, social roles and artistic ownership. A seed can imply continuity through memory, but the frightening birth-image complicates an easy reading of rebirth as triumph.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: list the four repeated identifications. 10–22: paraphrase the changing images. 22–32: contrast speech and silence. 32–42: debate the final song’s ownership. 42–50: support two possible interpretations with details.

## Questions
Why multiply the speaker into “a million” voices? How do death and birth connect? Who controls the final song?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Jayanta Mahapatra · Freedom
course-23:0.text:
# Jayanta Mahapatra · Freedom
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary in movement
The speaker imagines the country’s body floating somewhere down a river and likens his own isolation to a partly disembodied bamboo at the bank. Old widows and dying men pray; children desire the freedom to transform the world. The speaker fears drifting toward either position and speaks of being alone.

That solitude is not innocent. He imagines avoiding a woman and child in a remote village who have lacked enough rice, and avoiding the light on Parliament House. These juxtapositions bring hunger, national political institutions and the observer’s distance into the same field of vision. In a nearby temple the priest is said to know freedom while God hides like an outsider.

The speaker continues searching for light and the freedom of a body alone, then evokes shale, coal and streambeds. The poem closes with ashes the speaker tries to keep away. Its images resist a single, certain definition of freedom; solitude can feel like release, withdrawal or a failure to face others’ suffering.

## Interpretation
The floating body is a striking metaphor, not a documented account of the whole nation’s fate. Ask how the poem compares formal national freedom with material deprivation. The temple and Parliament images raise questions about institutions without proving that the poem rejects every religious or political practice. Its uncertainties are part of its force.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: collect different meanings of freedom. 10–22: follow the river and bamboo images. 22–32: analyse the hungry family and Parliament. 32–42: compare temple and solitude. 42–50: write a tentative interpretation with textual evidence.

## Questions
What kinds of freedom do different figures desire? Why is the speaker uneasy about solitude? How does hunger challenge a purely political definition of freedom?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:0.title: Jayanta Mahapatra · Twilight
course-23:0.text:
# Jayanta Mahapatra · Twilight
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit I

## Summary
An orange flare of late daylight illuminates the pale windows of a hospital; it is not yet dark. In a children’s ward, the speaker sees a mother’s face and the dead, described as always so young. The poem’s compressed phrasing does not offer a detailed history of the child or explain how death occurred.

The scene shifts toward water in a river whose startling sound is imagined as a cry. The speaker asks whether it is a plea to share a curse. Twilight will fall elsewhere too and hide the whiteness of jasmine about to bloom. Lights come on in houses across the street as the speaker looks at a wet August evening, which seems to hold the vast unknown in small, delicate hands.

## Interpretation
The movement from hospital to river, flowers and houses places personal grief beside an ordinary world continuing into evening. Light and darkness, youth and death, blooming and concealment remain in tension. The river’s “cry” and evening’s “hands” personify the landscape, but their precise meaning is uncertain: do not assume that nature is literally mourning or that the mother’s complete thoughts are known.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: describe the opening light. 10–22: paraphrase the hospital scene without adding facts. 22–32: trace shifts from river to jasmine to houses. 32–42: discuss the last image’s mixture of vastness and delicacy. 42–50: write a supported response to one unresolved question.

## Questions
How does the poem move between human and natural scenes? What does “not yet dark” contribute? Why leave the river’s cry as a question?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed text and edition before class.

course-23:1.title: Mulk Raj Anand · Two Leaves and a Bud
course-23:1.text:
# Mulk Raj Anand · Two Leaves and a Bud
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit II

## Context and reading care
Published in 1937, the novel exposes exploitation on a colonial-era Assam tea plantation. It includes coercion, racist abuse, violence and attempted sexual assault. Discuss these subjects without requiring students to recount personal experiences. The story’s derogatory terms for workers reflect a historical hierarchy and should be addressed critically.

## From Punjab to the plantation
Gangu, a poor Punjabi peasant, is persuaded by the recruiter Buta to go to Assam with his wife Sajani, daughter Leila and son Buddhu. Promises of wages and a better life attract the family, but the reality of the Macpherson tea estate is very different. Workers must perform exhausting labour, live in poor housing and face inadequate food, disease, debt and restrictions. The title names the tender tea leaves and bud workers are required to pluck, linking a familiar commodity with the people whose labour produces it.

## Work, illness and unequal power
The family discovers that low pay and debts keep workers dependent on the estate. Managers and officials possess substantial power over their lives, and women are vulnerable to sexual coercion. Different characters respond differently: the sympathetic doctor John de la Havre is disturbed by conditions, but individual sympathy does not dismantle the system. Conflict among workers and management brings punishment and further violence.

Sajani becomes ill and dies. Gangu’s grief is compounded by poverty: he struggles even to secure the resources needed for her funeral. His hope of providing a stable life for his family has become a deepening sequence of losses.

## Attack and trial
Assistant manager Reggie Hunt pursues Leila with the intention of sexually assaulting her. She runs for safety. Gangu intervenes to protect her, and Hunt shoots and kills him. The case goes to court, but the jury finds Hunt not guilty. The ending exposes the gap between formal legal process and justice in a system structured by colonial power. It does not turn Gangu’s death into a happy resolution.

## Interpretation
The novel connects landlessness, recruitment, work, illness, gendered violence and law rather than treating suffering as an individual accident. Read Leila as a person facing coercion, not merely as a symbol of her father’s honour. Compare the sympathetic doctor’s position with workers’ own experiences and collective action.

## Lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: establish a content-sensitive discussion. 10–22: map the recruiter’s promises against plantation conditions. 22–32: trace causes and consequences of debt and illness. 32–42: examine the attack and legal verdict. 42–50: write how the title connects commodity and labour.

## Questions
Why does the family leave home? How are economic and legal power connected? What does the verdict reveal about the limits of justice in the novel?

This is an extended story overview, not a complete chapter-by-chapter guide. Check the assigned novel and edition before teaching.

course-23:1.title: R. K. Narayan · The Guide
course-23:1.text:
# R. K. Narayan · The Guide
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit II

## Structure and context
The 1958 novel moves between Raju’s present after prison and accounts of his earlier life. His own storytelling, the narrator’s perspective and other people’s expectations shape what readers know. The relationship with Rosie and the novel’s ending invite more than one interpretation.

## Railway Raju and Rosie
Raju grows up near Malgudi’s railway station, helps with his father’s shop and becomes a confident tourist guide. Among his clients is a scholarly visitor whom he nicknames Marco, accompanied by his wife Rosie. Marco is absorbed in his research; Rosie longs to dance but faces her husband’s disapproval and social prejudice associated with her family background. Raju encourages her dancing, and they become involved. Their relationship becomes strained amid Marco’s discoveries and rejection.

Rosie comes to stay with Raju. His mother and uncle strongly disapprove, and his mother eventually leaves. Raju supports Rosie’s artistic work and manages her career as she becomes the successful dancer Nalini. Yet his management also becomes possessive: money, status and jealousy distort their relationship. Rosie’s ambition and artistic skill are her own, even though Raju likes to imagine himself as the source of her success.

## Forgery and prison
A document related to jewellery left with Marco becomes central to Raju’s downfall. Raju forges Rosie’s signature on a form, hoping to control the matter without her knowledge. The forgery is discovered and he is prosecuted and imprisoned. His account of these events can be read critically: self-justification and genuine regret may coexist.

## The holy man and the drought
After release, Raju stays near an abandoned riverside shrine. A villager, Velan, takes him for a holy man and seeks his advice. The role grows as villagers bring concerns and offerings. During drought and unrest, a misunderstanding helps turn Raju’s words into an expectation that he will fast to bring rain.

Raju confesses his past to Velan, but the confession does not simply end the villagers’ faith. He goes through with the fast as crowds and the media gather. His physical condition deteriorates. At the end he is supported at the river, says he senses rain in the hills, and sinks down. The text leaves both the rain’s arrival and his ultimate fate open; do not substitute the film’s ending as a confirmed account of the novel.

## Interpretation and lesson
Discuss whether Raju’s final action is deception, sincere transformation, social pressure or a mixture; the text permits debate. In 50 minutes: 0–10 organise the two time strands; 10–20 discuss Rosie’s goals; 20–30 trace the forgery; 30–40 examine the fast; 40–50 defend an interpretation of the ending without resolving its ambiguity.

## Questions
How does Raju become a guide in different senses? How does support for Rosie become control? What is and is not certain at the ending?

This is an extended story overview, not a complete chapter-by-chapter guide. Check the assigned novel and edition before teaching.

course-23:1.title: Raja Rao · Kanthapura
course-23:1.text:
# Raja Rao · Kanthapura
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4, Unit II

## Narrative voice and setting
Raja Rao’s 1938 novel tells the story of a south Indian village and the effects of Gandhian nationalism through Achakka, an older village woman. Its storytelling draws on local legend and oral rhythms, often called a sthala purana, or story of a place. The village is not socially uniform: caste, gender and wealth organise its life.

## The movement reaches the village
Achakka introduces Kanthapura, its goddess Kenchamma, social quarters and local figures. Moorthy, a young Brahmin influenced by Gandhi, encourages spinning, the use of khadi and resistance to colonial rule. He also works across caste boundaries, challenging untouchability. Orthodox authorities and the local moneylender Bhatta oppose him. His excommunication deeply affects his mother Narasamma, who dies.

At the nearby Skeffington coffee estate, plantation workers live under harsh control. Moorthy tries to bring the message of reform and nationalism to them. Conflict with the policeman Bade Khan produces violence despite the movement’s commitment to nonviolence. Moorthy feels responsible and undertakes a fast. The local Congress organisation grows, but the risks to supporters increase.

## Arrest and women’s organising
Moorthy is arrested and imprisoned. Rangamma, an educated widow, and other women organise volunteers, share political knowledge and prepare for demonstrations. Ratna, another widow, becomes an energetic participant. Their work complicates any account of the freedom movement as the achievement of male leaders alone; it also operates within continuing caste and gender hierarchies.

## Escalation and aftermath
Protests against colonial controls and liquor sales are met by police force, arrests and serious violence. As repression intensifies, the village is burned and its inhabitants are scattered. Survivors seek refuge elsewhere, including Kashipura; the community described at the beginning cannot simply return unchanged. News of national political developments and Moorthy’s later changing sympathies enters the closing account. The novel was published before Indian independence, and the ending should not be presented as an eyewitness account of independence in 1947.

## Interpretation and lesson
Achakka adapts national politics into familiar stories, religious imagery and local speech. Discuss both the power of a collective village voice and the limits of a narrator situated within a caste system. In 50 minutes: 0–10 draw the village’s social map; 10–22 trace Moorthy’s activities; 22–32 examine women’s organising; 32–42 discuss nonviolence and repression; 42–50 explain what displacement does to the local legend.

## Questions
How does Achakka make national events local? Why is Moorthy’s crossing of caste boundaries controversial? How do women sustain the movement?

This is an extended story overview, not a complete chapter-by-chapter guide. Check the assigned novel and edition before teaching.

course-23:2.title: Shashi Deshpande · The Intrusion
course-23:2.text:
# Shashi Deshpande · The Intrusion
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Content note and approach
The story concerns sexual violence within marriage. Offer students a choice about how they engage with sensitive passages, and do not ask anyone to share personal experience. Marriage is not consent; the narrator’s reluctance and resistance matter.

## Story in sequence
A newly married couple travel through a fishing village to a secluded place overlooking the sea. The unnamed woman narrates. She and her husband barely know each other, and she is uneasy about being alone with him. He welcomes the privacy of their honeymoon, while she wants time, conversation and familiarity.

His embraces make her uncomfortable. She tries to create distance, moves toward the veranda and wishes they might become friends. When she resists his attempt to kiss her, he reacts with anger. She says they do not know each other, hoping to explain her desire to talk, but finds it difficult to continue. He turns away, and she experiences both guilt and temporary relief.

Later she wakes from a dreamlike perception of the sea to find him forcing himself on her. Frightened and unable to push him away, she experiences the act as an intrusion into her bodily and personal privacy. Afterwards he sleeps while she is left with the humiliation and loss of control. The contrast between the sea’s imagined force and her husband’s actions makes the difference between being physically hurt and being violated by another person painfully clear.

## Interpretation
First-person narration brings the reader close to the woman’s shifting sensations and limited opportunities to speak. The secluded room is “private” for the husband but does not protect her autonomy. Analyse her silence and attempts to resist without implying that a victim must say or do a particular thing for a violation to count.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: set content-sensitive discussion boundaries. 10–22: map the couple’s different expectations. 22–32: identify moments of resistance and interruption. 32–42: discuss the sea and the meaning of privacy. 42–50: write an evidence-based response without graphic detail.

## Questions
Why does the narrator seek conversation? How does “privacy” mean different things to the two characters? How does the sea image change by the end?

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:2.title: Khushwant Singh · The Agnostic
course-23:2.text:
# Khushwant Singh · The Agnostic
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Story overview
A family’s visitor declares his scepticism about God in conversation with his hostess. She believes in God and is distressed at the thought that his arguments might influence her children. Their exchange becomes spirited: the adults appeal to contrasting beliefs and literary or religious language, while the children find the dispute entertaining. The visitor questions received faith, and the hostess defends it.

The next day, during an outing, a child’s ball becomes stuck in a tree. The visitor offers a test: if God brings the ball down and he catches it, he will believe. A breeze dislodges it and the ball comes down to him. His apparent change of position delights the hostess, bringing the dispute to a comic close.

## Interpretation and uncertainty
The event has an ordinary physical explanation as well as the meaning the participants may attach to it. A reader can ask whether the visitor’s response is sincere, playful, a concession or a comment on how people interpret coincidence. The ending need not prove that the story establishes or disproves God’s existence. Agnosticism concerns uncertainty about what can be known; it should not automatically be equated with certainty that no deity exists.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish belief, disbelief and uncertainty. 10–20: identify the speakers’ positions. 20–30: trace the ball incident. 30–40: debate the effect of a comic coincidence. 40–50: write a response acknowledging more than one reading.

## Questions
Why is the hostess worried? What test does the visitor suggest? Why can the same event support different interpretations?

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:2.title: Rita Nath Keshari · The Transplanted Wife — unverified selection
course-23:2.text:
# Rita Nath Keshari · The Transplanted Wife — unverified selection
