course-23:2.title: Temsula Ao · Laburnum for My Head
course-23:2.text:
# Temsula Ao · Laburnum for My Head
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Story in sequence
Lentina loves the yellow blossoms of the laburnum and repeatedly tries to grow one in her garden, but her efforts do not succeed. Her attachment becomes a persistent, private desire rather than a passing taste. After her husband’s death, a visit to the cemetery gives her an idea: she wants a laburnum to grow at her own grave instead of an imposing headstone.

With the help of her trusted driver Babu, Lentina explores how to secure a burial place and eventually arranges land for a new cemetery. The arrangements favour flowering trees rather than conventional headstones, linking her personal wish with a space others can use. Babu helps care for the tree. In time it blossoms; Lentina sees her wish realised before her death. Thereafter the golden tree flowers above her burial place.

## Interpretation
The recurring flowers connect individual desire, death and continuing life without requiring a single fixed symbolism. Lentina’s planning lets her express a preference about how she will be remembered. Ask how resources and social connections make her plan possible, and how Babu’s labour contributes to it. The title story is part of a collection with the same title; the course edition should be checked to confirm whether other stories are also assigned.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish a story from a collection. 10–22: trace garden, cemetery and tree. 22–32: examine Lentina’s decisions and Babu’s role. 32–42: discuss flowers and memorials. 42–50: write how the ending changes the opening desire.

## Questions
Why does Lentina want a tree by her grave? Who helps make it possible? How can the blossoms function as a memorial?

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:3.title: Anita Desai · The Village by the Sea
course-23:3.text:
# Anita Desai · The Village by the Sea
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Setting and beginning
In the coastal village of Thul, Lila and her brother Hari help hold their family together. Their mother is seriously ill, their father drinks heavily, and their younger sisters Bela and Kamal need care. Lila takes on domestic work while Hari seeks ways to earn money. News of possible industrial development raises hopes of employment as well as questions about changes to the village.

## Two parallel journeys
The wealthy De Silva family visits its nearby holiday home. The children earn some money by helping them. Hoping to find work, Hari travels to Bombay, where the unfamiliar city is frightening and overwhelming. The De Silvas are not available when he first seeks them out, but a watchman helps him find Jagu, proprietor of the Sri Krishna Eating House. Hari works there under difficult conditions, gradually forming connections.

Nearby watch repairer Mr Panwallah teaches Hari about watches and the need to adapt to changing circumstances. Hari learns a practical skill and begins to imagine a way to earn a living at home. In Thul, meanwhile, Lila cares for her sisters and mother and receives help from the De Silvas, who assist in getting her mother hospital treatment. Hari’s father is shaken by his wife’s illness and begins to stop drinking and care for her.

## Return and ending
Hari eventually returns to Thul, bringing savings, skills and ideas, including watch repair and raising poultry. His family’s circumstances have improved, though change remains ahead. A visiting birdwatcher, Mr Ali, talks about adaptation. At a village celebration, Hari sees his recovering mother among women at the sea and calls Lila’s attention to her. The hopeful reunion is not a claim that poverty or environmental uncertainty have disappeared.

## Interpretation and lesson
The novel balances unequal access to wealth with acts of assistance and children’s resourcefulness. Discuss how Lila’s labour differs from Hari’s visible journey, and how industrialisation can create both work and disruption. In 50 minutes: 0–10 map family responsibilities; 10–22 compare Thul and Bombay; 22–32 trace Lila’s care and Hari’s learning; 32–42 examine adaptation; 42–50 write a qualified account of the ending.

## Questions
Why does Hari leave? What work does Lila do in his absence? How does the idea of adaptation connect the watchmaker and the birdwatcher?

This is a story overview, not a full chapter-by-chapter guide.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:3.title: Nayantara Sahgal · Rich Like Us
course-23:3.text:
# Nayantara Sahgal · Rich Like Us
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Context and structure
The 1985 novel moves between the Emergency in India (1975–77) and earlier family and political histories. It centres on Sonali, an Indian civil servant, and Rose, an Englishwoman married into an Indian business family. Their different experiences allow the novel to connect public power with private relationships. Its accounts of political violence and coerced sterilisation should be situated historically and checked against independent sources.

## Narrative overview
Sonali has built a career in the civil service and is committed to professional judgment. As the Emergency changes the political climate, she faces pressure connected with commercial interests and is removed from her senior position. Her colleague Ravi Kachru adapts more successfully to the new order. Sonali reflects on what career, principle and loyalty mean in a system where proximity to power can determine outcomes.

Rose’s story reaches back to her life in England and her marriage to Ram, an Indian businessman already married to Mona. Rose must negotiate an unconventional household, cultural difference and an insecure legal and social position. Her relationship with Mona cannot be reduced to a simple rivalry; affection and tension coexist. When Ram becomes incapacitated, his son Dev’s pursuit of money and influence leaves Rose particularly vulnerable.

As the narrative returns to the Emergency, Dev becomes associated with opportunism and intimidation. Rose resists his behaviour and is eventually killed; the circumstances are made to resemble a different account. Sonali tries to understand Rose’s fate and the networks of power around it. Family documents and memories concerning the historical practice of sati also enter Sonali’s reflections, connecting violence against women across different periods without making those situations identical.

## Interpretation and lesson
The title invites scrutiny of wealth and privilege: who is protected by prosperity and who bears its costs? Compare official language about order with the experiences of those subjected to coercion. In 50 minutes: 0–10 establish the Emergency timeline; 10–22 map Rose’s household; 22–32 trace Sonali’s career; 32–42 compare public and domestic power; 42–50 write a claim about the title.

## Questions
Why is Rose’s household position precarious? How do Sonali and Ravi respond differently to political power? Why does the novel move between present and past?

This is an overview rather than a chapter-by-chapter account.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:3.title: Easterine Kire · A Terrible Matriarchy
course-23:3.text:
# Easterine Kire · A Terrible Matriarchy
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Context and narrative focus
This 2007 coming-of-age novel follows Dielieno, often called Lieno, in an Angami Naga family. It explores gender, generations, kinship and education. Its portrayal of one family must not be treated as a complete account of all Naga communities or all traditions.

## Story overview
As a young child, Lieno notices that her grandmother Vibano gives boys preferred treatment, including better portions of food. The seemingly ordinary meal reveals an unequal hierarchy of value. Vibano takes Lieno into her household, intending to train her in the duties she believes a girl and future wife should perform. The child misses the relative warmth of her parents and brothers and struggles with her grandmother’s strict expectations.

Growing up, Lieno sees how women’s domestic labour and access to schooling are judged differently from boys’. She questions the rules while also depending on family members for support. Her mother and other relatives offer perspectives that complicate the idea that every older person or every woman holds the same view. Education becomes one important way Lieno imagines a life beyond the restrictions imposed on her.

Family conflicts, illness and losses continue as Lieno matures. The grandmother’s history helps explain the insecurity and property relations behind her preference for sons, but it does not erase the harm she does. Lieno’s later choices show care for relatives as well as resistance to unequal expectations. The family’s relationships remain complex rather than dividing neatly into wholly good and wholly bad characters.

## Interpretation and lesson
The title is ironic: an older woman has authority in the household while enforcing values that favour men. Ask how the distribution of food makes hierarchy visible and how a child narrator’s understanding changes over time. In 50 minutes: 0–10 compare what characters receive at meals; 10–22 map the household; 22–32 discuss schooling; 32–42 distinguish explanation from excuse; 42–50 write about the title’s irony.

## Questions
Why does the opening food division matter? How can a matriarch reinforce a patriarchal system? How does Lieno’s view change as she grows?

This is an introductory overview; detailed chapter and ending explanations still need preparation.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:3.title: Amitav Ghosh · Countdown
course-23:3.text:
# Amitav Ghosh · Countdown
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Context
Published in 1999, Countdown is nonfiction responding to the nuclear tests conducted by India and Pakistan in 1998. Ghosh combines travel, observation, interviews and political reflection. Its accounts are situated in that historical moment; contemporary nuclear policy and figures must be checked separately.

## Main concerns
Ghosh speaks with people holding different positions on the tests and travels through places connected with security and its consequences. Rather than presenting nuclear weapons only as technical objects, he examines the stories nations tell about prestige, security and power. Interviews and encounters place official arguments beside anxieties about conflict and the lives of ordinary people.

The work asks how nuclear competition is understood in a region shaped by colonial history, Partition and recurrent hostility. It also questions the distance between abstract claims about national strength and the human consequences of possible nuclear war. Different interviewees’ opinions should be attributed to them; they are not automatically all Ghosh’s own conclusions or verified facts.

## Critical reading
The travel-and-interview form makes political debate concrete, but selection and arrangement still shape a reader’s response. Compare claims about deterrence and security with Ghosh’s concerns about escalation, human vulnerability and the distribution of public resources. Avoid treating either position as a substitute for independent evidence.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: place the tests on a 1998 timeline. 10–22: identify argument and reported voices in an assigned passage. 22–32: map prestige, deterrence and risk. 32–42: assess how travel writing shapes political argument. 42–50: formulate a question requiring independent evidence.

## Questions
Why use interviews rather than a single policy statement? How can an account distinguish security claims from observed consequences? What does the 1998 context contribute?

This is an introductory guide; verify the prescribed selection and the full sequence of encounters.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:3.title: Arundhati Roy · The Greater Common Good
course-23:3.text:
# Arundhati Roy · The Greater Common Good
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Context and purpose
Roy’s 1999 essay is an advocacy intervention in debates about large dams, especially the Sardar Sarovar project in the Narmada valley. It combines personal observation, argument, reported testimony and claims about policy. It is a source for Roy’s position at that time, not a neutral or automatically current account of every project outcome.

## Main argument
Roy asks who pays for projects justified as serving a “greater common good” and who receives their benefits. She draws attention to people facing displacement, including Adivasi and other marginalised communities, and argues that loss of land, livelihood, social ties and place cannot be measured only by a compensation figure. She questions whether resettlement can provide adequate land and sustain communities.

She also disputes official estimates and promises about costs, irrigation and development. Her essay relates the issue to the Narmada Bachao Andolan and to decision-making by governments, courts and funding institutions. Her forceful comparisons and rhetorical questions are part of an attempt to make readers confront unequal power and the people hidden by aggregate benefits.

## Critical reading
Attribute numbers and allegations to their sources and dates; estimates and later project outcomes are contested and require independent verification. Supporters emphasise water, irrigation and electricity, while opponents dispute the distribution and costs of those benefits. A strong discussion can compare evidence for both without treating displacement as an abstract arithmetic problem or assuming that one passage resolves every technical question.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify a development decision and its stakeholders. 10–22: map Roy’s claims about displacement and benefits. 22–32: distinguish a reported figure from its source. 32–42: compare competing arguments and missing evidence. 42–50: write a qualified response to the title.

## Questions
Who does Roy argue bears the costs? Why is resettlement more than cash compensation? How does the essay use rhetoric alongside evidence?

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:4.title: Manjula Padmanabhan · Harvest
course-23:4.text:
# Manjula Padmanabhan · Harvest
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Setting and content
This dystopian play imagines a future in which wealthy recipients acquire body parts from poorer people through a company. It includes coercive medical procedures, reproductive coercion and a character’s threat of self-harm; discuss these elements sensitively. The fictional system should not be confused with ethical, voluntary organ donation in real life.

## Action in sequence
Om, unemployed and living with his wife Jaya and mother Ma in a cramped Mumbai room, enters a contract with InterPlanta to supply organs. The company brings material comforts but also invasive rules, sanitation measures and surveillance. A screen-like contact module presents Ginni, the apparent recipient, who monitors the household and dictates how its members should live. Jaya is alarmed by the loss of autonomy; Om and Ma respond differently to the promised security.

Om’s brother Jeetu, who has a complicated relationship with Jaya and the household, returns. The guards take Jeetu rather than Om and remove his eyes. He comes back distressed and dependent on a technological device. What appears to be a mistaken substitution raises the question of how much control the family ever had. Jeetu is later taken again, and Om leaves the household in pursuit of the donor relationship. Ma increasingly retreats into a technologically mediated world of entertainment.

At the end, Jaya is alone and encounters Virgil through the contact system. He reveals that Ginni was an image and claims a relationship to Jeetu’s body; the play’s mediated presentation makes the nature of that transformation open to interpretation. Virgil wants Jaya to bear his child through a procedure arranged by the company. She refuses to surrender control on those terms, insists that he come to her in person, and threatens to take her own life if the guards force the issue. Her statement is a desperate tactic within the fictional coercive situation, not an instruction or model for real life. The confrontation ends without an assured solution to the system’s power.

## Interpretation and staging
Food, housing and entertainment arrive as inducements alongside control. The screen and the absent receiver make distance and surveillance visible onstage. Jaya’s resistance matters, yet its costs complicate any simple celebration of victory. Examine economic inequality and gender together; neither poverty nor identity alone makes exploitation inevitable.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish fictional coercion from ethical donation. 10–22: map the contract’s benefits and costs. 22–32: trace changing control of the room. 32–42: analyse screen presence and Jaya’s final demand. 42–50: write a claim about the unresolved ending.

## Questions
How do gifts become instruments of surveillance? Why is Jeetu’s treatment significant? What does Jaya demand at the end?

This is an action overview, not a complete scene-by-scene guide.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-23:4.title: Girish Karnad · The Dreams of Tipu Sultan
course-23:4.text:
# Girish Karnad · The Dreams of Tipu Sultan
Indian Writing in English I · Semester 4

## Context and form
Karnad’s historical play uses Tipu Sultan’s recorded dreams and the politics of writing history to revisit the ruler of Mysore’s final years and death in 1799. The play was first produced in 1997; check the publication and language of the assigned edition rather than treating all dates as equivalent. A play based on historical documents can imaginatively reshape events and should not be used as the sole authority for historical claims.

## Dramatic framework and action
After Tipu’s defeat and death at Seringapatam, the court historian Kirmani and British scholar-officer Colin Mackenzie discuss an account of his life. Their positions differ: one has personal ties and memories, while the other is connected with the victorious colonial power and its interest in recording its opponent. Their conversation frames scenes that move back into Tipu’s political and military world.

The play interweaves conflict, diplomacy and court life with dreams attributed to Tipu. These dreams make ambitions, anxieties and images of power dramatically visible. They are not simply predictions that the audience must accept as factual prophecy. The historical conflict with the East India Company and other regional powers leads toward the fall of Seringapatam and Tipu’s death; the frame returns attention to those who will record and interpret his defeat.

## Interpretation
Ask who controls the archive, what a conqueror may want from a history of an enemy and how a remembered person differs from a figure in official accounts. The dreams add another kind of evidence, but staging, selection and interpretation remain the playwright’s choices. Tipu’s historical legacy is disputed; evaluate differing historical claims against evidence rather than turning the play into a complete verdict.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish history from historical drama. 10–22: map the frame and shifts in time. 22–32: compare Kirmani’s and Mackenzie’s positions. 32–42: analyse one assigned dream as a theatrical device. 42–50: write what an archive can reveal and what it cannot settle.

## Questions
Why frame Tipu’s story through historians after his death? How do dreams affect the audience’s understanding? Why should a dramatic portrayal be compared with other historical sources?

This is an introductory overview, not a full scene-by-scene explanation.

Teaching draft: compare the assigned text and edition before class.

course-24:0.title: Ecocriticism · Reading people, places and power
course-24:0.text:
# Ecocriticism · Reading people, places and power
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Core idea
Ecocriticism studies relationships between literature and the material environment. It asks how texts represent landscapes, animals, resources, pollution and the power to define or change a place. It can combine close reading with history, ecology and environmental justice. A literary image is evidence about the text; it is not by itself a scientific measurement of an ecosystem.

## Four useful concepts
Pastoral often imagines rural life as simpler or more harmonious than urban life. Ask whose labour sustains this view. Wilderness describes places perceived as outside human settlement, but the label can erase Indigenous inhabitants and histories of management. Dwelling focuses on lived attachment, work and responsibility in a place rather than treating it as scenery. Apocalypse imagines catastrophic endings; its urgency can also make gradual harm or possible collective action less visible.

## Reading method
First identify who speaks and the represented place. Then look closely at images, genre and narrative choices. Ask whose perspective is missing, who benefits and who bears risk. Finally use reliable contextual evidence rather than assuming a novel is a factual report.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: collect images of “nature”. 10–20: distinguish scenery from a lived place. 20–30: compare pastoral and wilderness. 30–40: apply dwelling or apocalypse to a passage. 40–50: write a claim and one limitation.

## Questions
How can wilderness erase people? What can apocalyptic stories reveal or obscure?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:0.title: Ecological positions · Conservation, politics and justice
course-24:0.text:
# Ecological positions · Conservation, politics and justice
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Main approaches
Scientific conservation uses ecological evidence to protect species, habitats and resources. Ask who defines conservation goals and whether communities are consulted. Green politics connects environmental priorities with public institutions, democratic action and policy. Social ecology examines relationships between ecological degradation and unequal social structures; it does not reduce every environmental problem to one individual choice.

Environmental justice asks how environmental benefits, burdens and decision-making power are distributed across class, caste, race, gender and other differences. It also asks whether affected people can participate meaningfully. A factory may create employment and also expose neighbouring residents to pollution: fair analysis investigates both and identifies who experiences each.

Spiritual ecology examines relationships between ecological life and religious or spiritual meanings. Traditions vary; avoid claiming that all communities with spiritual attachments relate to land in the same way. Evidence about a sacred river and evidence about water quality answer related but different questions.

## Practice
Choose a local water issue without requiring students to disclose private experiences. Draw a stakeholder map: water users, workers, decision makers and nonhuman life. Separate verified facts from questions needing investigation.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: distinguish conservation from justice. 10–22: map stakeholders. 22–32: compare ecological and social evidence. 32–42: discuss participation. 42–50: propose a question for further research.

## Questions
What is the difference between equal and fair distribution? Whose knowledge counts in a decision?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:0.title: Ecofeminism, deep ecology and bioregionalism
course-24:0.text:
# Ecofeminism, deep ecology and bioregionalism
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Three lenses
Ecofeminism explores connections between the domination of women and the exploitation of nature. Some versions analyse systems of power, labour and resource control; not all claim that women are naturally closer to nature. Treat that claim critically because it can reinforce stereotypes and ignore differences among women.

Deep ecology challenges a purely human-centred valuation of the nonhuman world, emphasising the intrinsic value of living beings and ecological interdependence. Critics ask whether some formulations insufficiently address inequality and the rights and knowledge of people who live in protected landscapes.

Bioregionalism encourages attention to a place’s ecological features—such as watersheds, climates and species—alongside ways people inhabit it. Ecological boundaries and political boundaries rarely match neatly, and communities within one region may have conflicting interests.

## Comparison
For a river threatened by industrial waste, an ecofeminist might ask who performs water collection and care; a deep-ecological reading might ask what happens to fish beyond human usefulness; a bioregional reading might follow the watershed beyond administrative borders. These are questions, not mutually exclusive solutions.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: define human-centred thinking. 10–25: compare the three approaches. 25–35: apply each to a river case. 35–45: identify risks of stereotyping. 45–50: write a balanced comparison.

## Questions
Why is “women are naturally closer to nature” too simple? What does a watershed reveal?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:0.title: Tinai, environmental movements and place-based reading
course-24:0.text:
# Tinai, environmental movements and place-based reading
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Tinai
In classical Tamil akam poetics, tinai connects landscapes, social situations, characteristic plants and animals, time and emotional situations. The five commonly taught landscapes include kurinji (mountain), mullai (pastoral), marutam (cultivated), neytal (coastal) and palai (arid). Their conventional associations are interpretive patterns, not a claim that every poem follows one rigid formula. Tinai is an ancient literary framework; using it for modern ecocriticism is a contemporary interpretation, not proof that ancient poets used today’s environmental science.

## Movements and justice
Environmental movements bring people together around particular lands, waters or harms. India’s Chipko movement is often associated with resisting commercial tree-felling in the Himalayan region; the Narmada Bachao Andolan contests large-dam displacement and development policy. Each has a specific history, multiple participants and contested outcomes. Avoid describing any community as speaking with one voice.

## Method
Read a poem’s landscape in relation to its speaker and emotional situation. For a movement, identify the issue, groups involved, demands and evidence. Compare without assuming classical poems and modern activism have identical aims.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: locate the five tinai. 10–22: connect landscape and situation in a poem. 22–35: map a movement’s stakeholders. 35–45: compare the two ways of reading place. 45–50: write one important difference.

## Questions
How does tinai connect place and feeling? Why must a movement be studied in its particular historical setting?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:1.title: Rachel Carson · Silent Spring
course-24:1.text:
# Rachel Carson · Silent Spring
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Argument and structure
Carson’s 1962 environmental nonfiction begins with “A Fable for Tomorrow”: an imagined, composite community loses birdsong and other signs of life. The fable is not a report that every event happened in one real town. It draws readers into the book’s investigation of pesticide use and ecological interdependence.

Carson assembles scientific studies, reported incidents and explanations of chemical pathways to argue that indiscriminate use of persistent pesticides can damage organisms beyond their intended targets. Chemicals can travel through soil and water and accumulate in food chains. She challenges assurances of safety, questions who decides acceptable risk, and advocates more carefully studied alternatives, including biological controls. Her argument is not simply that all pest control must stop.

## Environmental reading
The vanished birdsong makes gradual and distributed harm perceptible. Notice the shift from fable to evidence: literary force and scientific argument work together but are not interchangeable. Check pesticide-specific hazards and current regulations with current scientific authorities; Carson’s 1962 book is historically situated.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: describe the fable’s change in sound. 10–20: distinguish composite story and evidence. 20–32: map a chemical pathway. 32–42: assess a claim and source. 42–50: write how genre supports the argument.

## Questions
Why begin nonfiction with a fable? What does “interdependence” add to a pesticide debate?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:1.title: Terry Tempest Williams · Refuge
course-24:1.text:
# Terry Tempest Williams · Refuge
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Overview
Refuge: An Unnatural History of Family and Place interweaves Williams’s mother Diane’s cancer and death with the rising Great Salt Lake in the 1980s and the flooding of the Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge in Utah. Bird observations, family memories, grief and spiritual reflection move together. The book is memoir and environmental writing, not a conventional fictional disaster story.

Its changing lake levels and bird-centred sections make ecological change a structural part of the narrative. The word refuge can mean a protected bird habitat, the family’s search for shelter in illness, or an inner resource that cannot simply restore what has been lost.

In the epilogue, “The Clan of One-Breasted Women,” Williams connects her family’s cancers and communities downwind of nuclear testing to histories of radioactive fallout and political silence. Exposure to ionising radiation can increase cancer risk, but a literary account cannot establish the precise cause of an individual person’s cancer. Distinguish her testimony and argument from an independently assessed medical conclusion.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the two narrative strands. 10–22: map connections between family and place. 22–32: read a bird image. 32–42: discuss testimony and evidence. 42–50: explain the title’s multiple meanings.

## Questions
What does the bird refuge mean to the narrator? How can memoir make a public issue personal without proving individual causation?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:1.title: Barbara Kingsolver · Animal Dreams — overview
course-24:1.text:
# Barbara Kingsolver · Animal Dreams — overview
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Story overview; assigned excerpts must be checked
Codi Noline returns to Grace, Arizona, to teach biology and be near her father, Doc Homer, whose memory is failing. She feels she does not belong. Her sister Hallie leaves for Nicaragua to help with agriculture during violent political conflict; the sisters exchange letters. Codi reconnects with her friend Emelina and with Loyd Peregrina, whom she knew in school.

Codi and her students find that the river is gravely polluted by mining waste, threatening the orchards and the town’s future. A proposed dam would cut off water to Grace. Local women organise, make and sell peacock piñatas, and publicise the threat. They work toward historic protection for the town and its water. In this process Codi learns that her family has deeper roots in Grace than she had believed.

Hallie is kidnapped and killed by the US-backed Contras. Codi grieves and initially plans to leave Grace, but her flight turns back after mechanical trouble, and she returns. The novel later shows her with Loyd, pregnant, after her father’s death. Environmental organising does not undo the family’s loss.

## Reading
Compare personal memory, family secrecy and a community’s relationship to water. Do not assume every event is in the syllabus’s unspecified excerpts; confirm the actual selection. This is a whole-novel overview rather than chapter-by-chapter coverage.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: map family and setting. 10–22: sequence the river conflict. 22–32: identify collective action. 32–42: compare loss and belonging. 42–50: link a claim to a passage in the assigned excerpt.

## Questions
Why is the river vital to Grace? How does Codi’s understanding of belonging change?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:1.title: Arif Anwar · The Storm — introduction
course-24:1.text:
# Arif Anwar · The Storm — introduction
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Interwoven narratives
The novel moves across decades and places, combining stories linked to the 1970 Bhola cyclone, Partition, the Second World War and migration. In a fishing village by the Bay of Bengal, Honufa and her family face a devastating storm. Decades later Shahryar, a Bangladeshi scholar in the United States, faces visa uncertainty and possible separation from his young daughter Anna.

Other strands include a Japanese pilot, a British doctor and a couple moving from Calcutta to East Pakistan after Partition. The story’s structure gradually reveals connections among lives that at first seem separate. The historical cyclone is not simply a backdrop: the novel invites attention to warning, shelter, geography, class and the continuing consequences of loss.

## Reading disaster critically
A cyclone is a physical event; the extent of harm also depends on access to shelter, infrastructure, information and political power. Avoid implying that all storms have one cause or that a fictional character’s experience represents every survivor. Compare the novel with carefully sourced historical accounts.

This is an introductory overview; relationships, later revelations and the ending need further checking against the assigned edition.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: locate the Bay of Bengal and establish a timeline. 10–22: map the narrative strands. 22–32: identify conditions of vulnerability. 32–42: discuss shifts in time. 42–50: write one claim and a question requiring historical evidence.

## Questions
How does the novel connect family history and disaster? Why are vulnerability and the physical storm not the same thing?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:2.title: Dipesh Chakrabarty · The Climate of History: Four Theses
course-24:2.text:
# Dipesh Chakrabarty · The Climate of History: Four Theses
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## The argument
In this 2009 essay Chakrabarty argues that anthropogenic climate change challenges the old separation of natural history from human history. Humans collectively have become a geological force: actions associated with industrial civilisation affect planetary processes over very long timescales. This does not mean that all people contribute equally to emissions or experience equal harm.

## Four linked propositions, in accessible language
1. Human and natural histories can no longer be treated as fully separate when human activity changes the conditions of life at planetary scale.
2. The idea of an Anthropocene complicates accounts of freedom centred on industrial civilisation and fossil-fuel energy.
3. Analyses of capitalism and inequality remain necessary but need to be read together with a history of humans as a species and a geological agent.
4. Species history raises questions about shared planetary risk but is difficult to experience as a single collective human story; it also challenges historical understanding.

## Critical questions
“Species” is an analytical scale, not a licence to erase the unequal roles of colonialism, wealth or fossil-fuel industries. The Anthropocene is widely used as an interdisciplinary concept; its formal status as a geological epoch is contested and a proposal for a formal epoch was rejected in 2024. Identify Chakrabarty’s argument before offering a critique.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: compare human and geological timescales. 10–25: restate the four theses in pairs. 25–35: map fossil energy and freedom. 35–45: debate species and unequal responsibility. 45–50: write a qualified argument.

## Questions
Why connect geological time and human history? Can species-level analysis coexist with unequal responsibility?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:2.title: Rob Nixon · Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor
course-24:2.text:
# Rob Nixon · Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Key concept
Nixon’s “slow violence” names harm that is gradual, dispersed across time and space, and often difficult to see as a single dramatic event. Toxic contamination, erosion or the delayed effects of radiation can be examples when evidence supports their effects. Slowness is not the same as harmlessness.

The phrase “environmentalism of the poor” draws attention to struggles by communities whose livelihoods and health depend on land, forests and water and who may bear disproportionate environmental costs. Such movements may be described in terms of survival or rights rather than the label “environmentalism”. Poverty does not make a community politically uniform or voiceless.

## Narrative challenge
News and entertainment often favour sudden, spectacular events. Writers, activists and artists must find forms that make long-term, uneven damage visible without inventing evidence or using people merely as symbols. Link a close reading to carefully dated scientific and community sources.

The syllabus specifies an excerpt but does not identify its pages. This is an introduction to the book’s framework, not a summary of that particular passage.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: compare a sudden disaster with gradual contamination. 10–22: construct a timeline. 22–32: identify affected groups and uncertainty. 32–42: discuss narrative visibility. 42–50: write a claim grounded in an assigned passage.

## Questions
Why can slow harm be hard to narrate? How do class and power affect visibility?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:2.title: Amitav Ghosh · Gun Island — overview
course-24:2.text:
# Amitav Ghosh · Gun Island — overview
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Story in sequence
Dinanath Datta, or Deen, is a rare-book dealer interested in an old Bengali legend of the Gun Merchant and the snake goddess Manasa Devi. In the Sundarbans he visits a shrine with young Tipu and meets Rafi, who knows local stories. A dangerous snake encounter brings the visit to an abrupt crisis. The coast is also a place of storms, livelihood pressures and movement; no individual migration has only one cause.

Deen’s search takes him through conversations with marine biologist Piya and historian Cinta, and across places including Los Angeles and Venice. Cinta’s historical and linguistic knowledge helps him reconsider the merchant’s journey and the possible meaning of the legendary “Gun Island”. The old story increasingly resonates with contemporary journeys, unexpected animals and environmental disturbance.

Rafi and Tipu undertake a dangerous migration route and are separated. In Venice, Deen encounters Rafi; news of a crowded migrant vessel leads friends to try to help those on board, including Tipu. The culminating rescue unfolds amid extraordinary weather and encounters with nonhuman creatures. Cinta dies near the end. The novel invites more than one reading of its connections between legend and events: supernatural certainty is not required for a thoughtful interpretation.

## Reading
Compare routes taken by people, animals and stories. Ask how borders and unequal resources shape mobility. Myth does not replace climate science; it changes how characters imagine connection and responsibility. This is an overview, not a chapter-by-chapter explanation.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: map places and travellers. 10–22: retell the shrine episode. 22–32: compare legend and present journeys. 32–42: discuss environmental change and unequal mobility. 42–50: explain one connection without reducing the novel to a message.

## Questions
How does Deen’s understanding of the legend change? Why must migration be explained through more than climate alone?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:3.title: Jeff Orlowski · Chasing Ice
course-24:3.text:
# Jeff Orlowski · Chasing Ice
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Documentary sequence
The 2012 documentary follows photographer James Balog and the Extreme Ice Survey as they establish time-lapse cameras at glaciers in places including Greenland, Iceland, Alaska and Montana. Equipment fails in difficult weather, requiring the team to adapt. Repeated photographs over months and years show substantial changes at selected sites.

A major sequence records a dramatic glacier-calving event: ice breaks away into the water. Calving is a natural process; an individual calving event alone does not prove the cause of global climate change. The larger documented trends need scientific context, measurements and comparison with broader research.

## Film techniques
Time-lapse compresses long change into moments visible on screen. Camera placement, editing, music and the focus on an individual photographer shape emotion and authority. Ask what images show directly, what explanations the film supplies and what cannot be determined from images alone.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: distinguish observation from explanation. 10–22: trace the survey’s method and challenges. 22–32: analyse a time-lapse sequence. 32–42: discuss evidence and limitations. 42–50: draft a caption separating observation from inference.

## Questions
What does time-lapse make visible? Why does a single calving event require context?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:3.title: Sekhar Kammula · Godavari
course-24:3.text:
# Sekhar Kammula · Godavari
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Film overview
In the 2006 Telugu film, Sita, an independent fashion designer whose business and marriage prospects face setbacks, takes a boat journey on the Godavari. Ram, an idealistic young man disappointed in love, is travelling to a family wedding at Bhadrachalam. Their first meeting is awkward: when Ram carries Sita onto the boat without asking, she objects and he apologises. Their exchanges gradually develop into friendship and affection.

Other passengers, including the child Chinna and a dog, create subplots. Ram’s complicated relationship with Raji produces misunderstanding, and Sita leaves feeling hurt. Ram later reads the diary she has left and visits her. He explains his actions and proposes; Sita accepts. The story is a romance and ensemble journey, not a documentary about river pollution.

## Eco-cinema reading
Ask how shots of the river, boat, riverbanks and changing light structure movement, mood and encounters. Consider whether the river appears as a living environment, a livelihood, a route or a picturesque backdrop, and what the film leaves outside the frame. Interpret specific shots from the assigned version rather than attributing an environmental campaign to the film without evidence.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: map the river journey. 10–22: sequence Sita and Ram’s relationship. 22–32: describe a shot of the river. 32–42: discuss landscape versus backdrop. 42–50: write an argument supported by a scene.

## Questions
How does the journey bring the characters together? What does a river setting contribute beyond location?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:3.title: Bong Joon-ho · Snowpiercer
course-24:3.text:
# Bong Joon-ho · Snowpiercer
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Content and premise
This 2013 dystopian film contains intense violence, including violence against children and references to cannibalism. In its fictional future, an attempted technological response to global warming causes catastrophic freezing. Survivors occupy a perpetually moving train arranged by class: wealthy passengers live near the front, while those in the tail face deprivation and control. The scenario is speculative fiction, not a forecast of a particular climate technology.

## Action and ending
Curtis leads a rebellion from the tail towards the engine. He and the others enlist security specialist Namgoong Minsoo and his daughter Yona to open doors. Different carriages reveal radically unequal living conditions. The journey is violent and many rebels die.

At the engine, Wilford claims that rebellions have served population control and offers Curtis his position. Yona discovers that children taken from the tail are being used to keep parts of the engine working. Curtis saves Timmy at great personal cost. Namgoong detonates explosives to open a way out; the blast triggers an avalanche and derailment. Yona and Timmy emerge and see a polar bear. It shows that at least one animal survives outside, not that the children’s survival is guaranteed.

## Interpretation
The train functions as a tightly controlled, unequal social system. Analyse how changing spaces, lighting and violence expose class division, and question Wilford’s claim that oppression is necessary for ecological balance.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: set viewing boundaries. 10–22: map the train by class. 22–32: trace the rebellion. 32–42: debate Wilford’s ecological justification. 42–50: write a qualified interpretation of the bear.

## Questions
How does the train organise inequality? What does the ending show, and what does it leave unresolved?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:3.title: Jaydeep Sarkar · Water Wives
course-24:3.text:
# Jaydeep Sarkar · Water Wives
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Context and focus
The ActionAid short film, written by Swati Bhattacharya and directed by Jaydeep Sarkar, draws attention to “water wives”: women in water-scarce settings whose labour collecting water is connected with men marrying more than one wife. Its advocacy focus is the unequal burden of unpaid domestic and care work. Reports describe particular communities in Maharashtra; do not generalise the practice to all villages or assume all women’s experiences are the same.

## Environmental justice reading
Water scarcity interacts with gender, income, infrastructure and household power. Ask whose journey and work are visible, who makes decisions, and how a short film selects and frames testimony. An account of a particular household does not automatically establish distances travelled or causes of scarcity across a whole region.

## Viewing practice
Describe a specific shot, sound or spoken statement from the assigned film, then explain how it shapes the viewer’s understanding. Compare the film’s advocacy with independent reporting and ask what affected women say about their own choices and circumstances.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: define unpaid care work. 10–22: watch or describe a selected sequence. 22–32: map water, work and power. 32–42: check the evidence and whose voice is heard. 42–50: suggest a question for community-led research.

## Questions
How can a water problem also be a gender-justice issue? What must be checked before generalising?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: William Wordsworth · Composed Upon Westminster Bridge
course-24:4.text:
# William Wordsworth · Composed Upon Westminster Bridge
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
The speaker sees London from Westminster Bridge in the morning and calls the sight extraordinarily beautiful. Buildings, ships and public spaces appear still and open to fields and sky. The early light and clear air bring city and landscape into one scene. The speaker compares the sight with sunlit valleys and hills, notices the river’s apparently free movement and imagines the houses asleep. The final image makes the whole city a mighty heart temporarily at rest.

## Form and meaning
This fourteen-line sonnet uses personification, exclamation and a garment simile to make a built environment seem alive. The calm is a particular moment, not proof that the city is always peaceful or free of pollution. An ecocritical reading can question a simple opposition between city and nature: sunlight, air and river shape the urban scene.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: imagine the view. 10–22: follow the movement from city to sunlight and river. 22–32: identify personification. 32–42: discuss nature and city. 42–50: write an evidence-based response.

## Questions
How does the city appear alive? Why is the morning setting important?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Gary Snyder · Mother Earth: Her Whales
course-24:4.text:
# Gary Snyder · Mother Earth: Her Whales
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
The poem moves from close attention to an owl, lizard, sparrow and growing grasses toward a critique of political and economic decisions that harm living worlds. It invokes destruction of forests and Indigenous people, whaling and pollution, and the loss of animals and habitats across regions. Images of whales diving and rising repeatedly interrupt the language of governments and resource exploitation.

The speaker calls for solidarity among humans and nonhuman beings—trees, birds, sea creatures and land animals—and questions whether distant political representatives can speak for soil and leaves. The poem returns to the owl, lizard and whales, ending with living movement rather than a technical policy solution.

## Reading
Changes of scale—from small creatures to nations to whales—make ecological interdependence felt. The confrontational tone and repeated “people” challenge a narrow human definition of community. References to countries and political systems are the poem’s historically situated rhetoric, not complete descriptions of their peoples.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: list nonhuman beings. 10–22: trace the poem’s shifts of scale. 22–32: compare political language with whale imagery. 32–42: examine the call for solidarity. 42–50: write an argument about the final return.

## Questions
Why does the poem return to its opening creatures? Who gets included in the idea of “people”?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Mary Oliver · Wild Geese
course-24:4.text:
# Mary Oliver · Wild Geese
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
The speaker addresses someone burdened by guilt or loneliness and rejects the need for punishing self-reproach. She invites the listener to acknowledge bodily life and offers to share despair. Meanwhile, the world continues: sun and rain move over landscapes, and wild geese travel home through the air. Their calls become an invitation to imagine belonging within a larger community of living things.

## Reading
Direct address makes the poem intimate; repeated transitions widen the perspective from one person’s pain to a whole landscape. The “family of things” is a metaphor for connection, not a promise that loneliness or environmental harm will disappear. The poem’s consolation does not require the reader to ignore personal suffering.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the listener’s possible feelings. 10–22: trace the shift from body to landscape. 22–32: examine repeated transitions. 32–42: discuss the call of geese. 42–50: explain belonging with one detail.

## Questions
How does the poem move from despair to belonging? What work does direct address do?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Joy Harjo · Speaking Tree
course-24:4.text:
# Joy Harjo · Speaking Tree
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
The poem begins with experiences of loss and violence that seem difficult to speak. The speaker challenges people who cannot imagine trees as sentient or hear their responses to wind, water and injury. She longs to be a tree, grounded in earth, while carrying human heartache. Conversely, the imagined tree longs to move to water and drink. The closing imagined voices of trees evoke dancing together and a thirst that reaches beyond literal drinking.

## Reading
This exchange of desires unsettles a strict division between human and tree. The tree is not just a decorative symbol for a human emotion: the poem asks readers to imagine its own voice and vulnerability. Harjo is a citizen of the Muscogee Nation, but the poem should not be presented as a statement on behalf of every Indigenous person or culture.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the opening mood. 10–22: trace the woman’s and tree’s contrasting desires. 22–32: examine sound and voice. 32–42: discuss human and nonhuman perspective. 42–50: write an interpretation of the final image.

## Questions
Why does the tree want to move? How does imagined speech alter the reader’s relationship to a tree?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Mamang Dai · Small Towns and the River
course-24:4.text:
# Mamang Dai · Small Towns and the River
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
The speaker associates small towns with death and recalls a recent death, the mourners and funeral flowers. The repeated cycle of life and death contrasts with the persistence of ritual. Attention then moves to a river imagined as having a soul: it travels through the land, carrying a sense of grief and a longer perspective than a single human life.

The poem brings memories of childhood and anxiety about the future into conversation with beliefs about death and the soul’s journey towards the rising sun. Its closing desire to walk with gods suggests a spiritual connection among place, life and loss. These are the poem’s images and beliefs, not a universal account of every community in Arunachal Pradesh.

## Reading
Personification makes the river more than scenery. Notice that “water is immortal” is the poem’s spiritual and imaginative language, not a scientific guarantee that a particular river cannot be damaged. The river’s presence can comfort without removing grief.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify the opening association. 10–22: follow the movement from mourning to river. 22–32: discuss personification. 32–42: examine ritual and memory. 42–50: explain the contrast between human life and water.

## Questions
How does the river relate to grief? Why distinguish a poetic image of immortality from a scientific claim?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Ammuvanar · Ainkurunuru 113
course-24:4.text:
# Ammuvanar · Ainkurunuru 113
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
In this short neytal poem, a woman addresses her friend. People in the town have spoken about her relationship with a man from the coast, where high waves break against white sand. Her mother hears the talk and asks her about it. The woman recounts her quiet reply. A traditional contextual note imagines the man listening nearby; this is an interpretive setting supplied with the poem, not a separately narrated event.

## Tinai and interpretation
The shore and breaking waves locate the poem in neytal, the coastal landscape associated in akam conventions with longing and relationships. The public talk and the mother’s question bring social pressure into the intimate situation. The final wording has variant readings in Tamil commentaries, so compare the assigned translation instead of assuming that every version presents the reply in the same way. Do not add a plot beyond the short poem.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify speaker and listener. 10–22: sequence gossip, question and reply. 22–32: examine the waves and sand. 32–42: compare a translation with the contextual note. 42–50: explain how landscape and social situation interact.

## Questions
Why does the mother question the speaker? How might the breaking waves relate to the social situation?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-24:4.title: Tevakulattar · Kuruntokai 3
course-24:4.text:
# Tevakulattar · Kuruntokai 3
Literature and Environment · Semester 4

## Poem summary
In a translation associated with A. K. Ramanujan, a woman describes her love for a man of the mountain slopes as greater than the earth, higher than the sky and deeper than the waters. The man’s mountain country is associated with bees making honey from kurinji flowers. The enormous comparisons present love as beyond ordinary measurement; the compact landscape image gives that feeling a particular place.

## Tinai and translation
Kurinji is the mountain landscape in classical Tamil akam poetics, conventionally associated with lovers’ union. Do not infer a full story or a later event from this brief poem. Translations differ in wording and lineation; compare the assigned edition and the Tamil where available. The flower and bees are literary details as well as part of a convention connecting place and feeling.

## Classroom lesson · 50 minutes
0–10: identify speaker and comparison. 10–22: trace earth, sky and water images. 22–32: examine bees, honey and kurinji. 32–42: compare translation choices. 42–50: explain how scale and place express feeling.

## Questions
Why use three vast comparisons? How does the mountain detail connect love and place?

Teaching draft: consult the assigned edition or film and check claims before teaching.

course-27:0.title: Aristotle · Poetics
course-27:0.text:
# Aristotle · Poetics
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Context and central question
Aristotle’s surviving Poetics examines poetic making and representation, with extended attention to tragedy. It is an ancient critical text, not an absolute rulebook for every kind of drama. Translation affects terms such as mimesis and catharsis.

## Key ideas
Mimesis is representation or imitation: art represents action, but it need not merely copy a particular event. Poetry can present what is possible or probable; Aristotle distinguishes this from the historian’s account of particular events. Tragedy represents a serious, complete action in dramatic performance and, through pity and fear, brings about catharsis. Scholars debate whether catharsis is best understood as purgation, purification, clarification or another effect; Aristotle does not settle every detail in the surviving text.

Aristotle lists six parts: plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Plot is the arrangement of incidents and is especially important because tragedy represents action. A whole action has beginning, middle and end linked intelligibly, not simply a sequence of events.

A complex plot may involve peripeteia, a reversal, and anagnorisis, a movement from ignorance to knowledge. Hamartia can mean an error or mistake; translating it automatically as a fixed moral “tragic flaw” oversimplifies debate. In Oedipus the investigation and discoveries bring reversal and recognition together.

## Apply and question
Map a play’s actions and their causal connections. Ask whether pity and fear arise from plot or spectacle. Then consider whose dramatic practices Aristotle’s model includes or leaves out.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define representation. 10–22: arrange a simple plot into beginning, middle and end. 22–32: identify reversal and recognition. 32–42: discuss translations of catharsis and hamartia. 42–50: apply one concept to a scene.

## Questions
Why does Aristotle prioritise plot? What is the difference between recognition and reversal? Why is catharsis debated?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:0.title: Horace · Ars Poetica — writing and poetic craft
course-27:0.text:
# Horace · Ars Poetica — writing and poetic craft
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Context
The Ars Poetica is a verse epistle by the Roman poet Horace, addressed to the Pisos. Its advice ranges across unity, genre, character, revision and the value of poetic skill. The syllabus prints “119–133” after the title, but does not identify the edition or say whether this refers to pages or verse lines. Check the course anthology before assuming its precise boundaries.

## Argument and examples
Horace begins with a grotesquely mismatched imagined figure to show the problem of parts that do not form a coherent whole. He asks writers to choose subjects suited to their powers and to make appropriate choices of style and genre. He discusses the challenge of handling inherited stories imaginatively and of introducing new ones.

In Latin lines 119–127 specifically, he advises writers either to follow tradition or invent a self-consistent character: famous figures such as Achilles carry inherited expectations, while a new character should remain coherent through the work. The surrounding passage discusses making familiar material one’s own. These line numbers are provided as one reference point, not a claim that they are the whole assigned extract.

Elsewhere the epistle values craft, revision and a combination of usefulness and pleasure. That broader formulation must not be treated as if it appears necessarily in the exact assigned passage.

## Critical application
Compare coherence with predictability: can a character change in a convincing way? Consider whether adherence to inherited expectations could also constrain imaginative reinterpretation.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish page numbers from verse numbers. 10–22: identify advice in the assigned passage. 22–32: discuss character consistency. 32–42: test a deliberate reinvention of a familiar character. 42–50: write one benefit and one limitation of Horace’s advice.

## Questions
Why does Horace value coherence? How might a writer transform inherited material? What must be checked about “119–133”?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:1.title: John Dryden · An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
course-27:1.text:
# John Dryden · An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Form and setting
Published in 1668, Dryden’s essay presents a conversation among four speakers on a barge against the background of an English–Dutch naval encounter. The dialogue allows competing claims to be tested rather than simply listing rules. Neander is often associated with Dryden’s views, but the speakers should not be flattened into identical positions.

## The debate
Crites praises ancient drama and its achievement, including discipline associated with the dramatic unities. Eugenius answers that modern writers inherit the ancients’ strengths and may improve on them. Lisideius argues for the order and regularity of French drama. Neander defends English drama’s variety, lively characterisation, subplots and mixing of tragic and comic elements.

The unities concern action, time and place, as understood in later classical criticism; do not attribute every later formulation equally to Aristotle. Lisideius praises disciplined structure, while Neander asks whether strict observance may sacrifice dramatic richness. In a final exchange about rhyme, Crites objects to it as unnatural for dramatic speech; Neander argues that rhyme can suit elevated serious drama when handled skilfully.

## Critical reading
Ask what each speaker means by representing nature and whether plausibility is the same as literal everyday speech. Examine how dialogue allows concessions as well as disagreement.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: map four speakers. 10–22: compare ancient and modern. 22–32: compare French and English practices. 32–42: debate rhyme and dramatic plausibility. 42–50: write one argument with its counterargument.

## Questions
Which speaker supports French drama? Why does Neander defend tragicomedy? Does a dialogue require one final answer?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:1.title: Matthew Arnold · The Study of Poetry
course-27:1.text:
# Matthew Arnold · The Study of Poetry
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## The importance of poetry
Arnold argues that poetry can help people interpret and sustain life and will become increasingly important as other inherited certainties are questioned. His influential account of poetry as a criticism of life places high value on poetic truth, beauty and seriousness. These are Arnold’s evaluative claims, not neutral measurements.

## Three estimates
The historic estimate can overvalue a work because of its place in literary development. The personal estimate can overvalue work because it appeals to a reader’s attachment, taste or local pride. Arnold proposes a real estimate: attentive judgment of the work’s poetic quality rather than either kind of overvaluation. He is not saying historical knowledge or personal pleasure has no use whatsoever.

## Touchstones
Arnold suggests keeping brief passages from recognised major poets in mind as touchstones for sensing excellence in other work. This is comparative judgment, not a mechanical test in which a new poem must imitate the passage. Ask how choices of canonical “great masters” reflect cultural power, and whether the method can give fair attention to different traditions and genres.

## Practice
Compare two short passages in the assigned edition. Separate an observation about their language from a preference, and explain the standards used to make a judgment.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: name a favourite work and a reason. 10–22: distinguish three estimates. 22–32: try comparative close reading. 32–42: question the choice of touchstones. 42–50: write an assessment with transparent criteria.

## Questions
What is a historic estimate? How does a touchstone work? Who gets to decide which poems serve as standards?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:1.title: William Wordsworth · Poetry and Poetic Diction
course-27:1.text:
# William Wordsworth · Poetry and Poetic Diction
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Context
The syllabus’s title points toward Wordsworth’s discussion of poetry and diction; confirm the exact prescribed extract. His Preface to Lyrical Ballads, introduced in 1800 and expanded in 1802, argues for renewed attention to common life and selected language associated with ordinary people, especially rural speakers.

## Main claims
Wordsworth opposes formulaic, ornamental poetic diction. The poet chooses and shapes language rather than merely transcribing every utterance. He describes the poet as a person speaking to people, distinguished by a greater capacity for feeling, observation and expression rather than belonging to a wholly different species.

His account of poetry joins powerful feeling with reflection: emotion is recollected in tranquillity, contemplated and reawakened in the process of composition. “Spontaneous” does not mean no thought, craft or revision. He argues that good prose and poetry can share language, while metre contributes to poetry’s distinctive effects.

## Evaluate
Consider how Wordsworth selects and idealises “rustic” experience. Compare his focus on feeling with Eliot’s later impersonal account without assuming either writer excludes craft or emotion entirely.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare ordinary and ornamental descriptions. 10–22: identify his argument about diction. 22–32: map experience, recollection and composition. 32–42: discuss selection and rural life. 42–50: rewrite a phrase and explain the effect.

## Questions
Why is selected everyday language important? How do feeling and reflection work together?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:1.title: T. S. Eliot · Tradition and the Individual Talent
course-27:1.text:
# T. S. Eliot · Tradition and the Individual Talent
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Argument
Eliot’s 1919 essay challenges the idea that a poet’s originality must mean complete separation from predecessors. Tradition is acquired through work. A historical sense involves seeing the past as present in relation to contemporary writing and locating a new work within an existing order. A significant new work can also alter how readers understand the relation among earlier works.

## Impersonality and the catalyst
Eliot argues that the poet’s mind transforms and combines feelings and experiences into artistic form rather than simply publishing a personal emotional history. His analogy compares the mind to a platinum catalyst involved in a reaction without being incorporated into the resulting product. It is a literary analogy, and the chemistry as Eliot states it has been criticised; do not learn it as a chemistry lesson.

When Eliot describes poetry as an escape from personality and emotion, he does not mean that poems are emotionless or that poets literally lack personalities. He asks readers to attend to emotion organised in the poem rather than treating biography as the final explanation.

## Compare
Wordsworth links poetic creation to feeling and reflection; Eliot stresses transformation, discipline and relation to tradition. Both positions are more complex than “emotion versus no emotion”. Ask whose works Eliot’s European-centred tradition privileges.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish inheritance from active tradition. 10–22: explain the historical sense. 22–32: sketch the catalyst analogy. 32–42: compare Wordsworth and Eliot. 42–50: write a claim about impersonality with a qualification.

## Questions
How can a new work change the order of tradition? What does the catalyst analogy explain and what are its limits?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:2.title: Viktor Shklovsky · Art as Technique
course-27:2.text:
# Viktor Shklovsky · Art as Technique
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Argument
In this foundational Russian Formalist essay, also translated as “Art as Device”, Shklovsky argues that habitual perception becomes automatic. We recognise familiar things quickly without attending closely to them. Artistic devices can interrupt that automatic recognition and prolong perception.

## Defamiliarisation
Defamiliarisation makes something habitual seem strange so that it can be experienced anew. It is not simply using obscure words or making a text randomly difficult. The question is what particular device changes perception and how it works in context.

Shklovsky discusses Tolstoy’s descriptions that withhold familiar labels. In the story Kholstomer a horse’s perspective makes human ideas of ownership look strange: what people call “mine” is not necessarily something they actually use or care for. An unfamiliar viewpoint exposes a familiar social practice to scrutiny.

## Apply and evaluate
Describe a classroom object without naming it, then compare the experience of reading the description with immediate recognition. Ask whether all art must produce estrangement, and whether attending to technique alone can overlook political or historical meanings.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: describe an object without naming it. 10–22: define habitual perception. 22–32: examine a Tolstoy example. 32–42: compare estrangement and mere obscurity. 42–50: identify one device and its effect in a passage.

## Questions
What is automatism? How does the horse’s point of view make ownership unfamiliar?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:2.title: Cleanth Brooks · The Language of Paradox
course-27:2.text:
# Cleanth Brooks · The Language of Paradox
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Argument
Brooks, associated with New Criticism, argues that paradox is central to poetic language. A paradox brings apparently conflicting ideas together in a way that can reveal a complex relation. It is not simply an accidental contradiction or a puzzle to be discarded once a message is found.

Words carry associations as well as dictionary meanings; their effects depend on the other words and patterns around them. Brooks therefore practises close reading: a poem’s meaning emerges from the interaction of its language and form, not from a bare prose summary alone.

## Examples
In Wordsworth’s Westminster Bridge sonnet, Brooks draws attention to the seemingly unlikely experience of finding natural majesty and calm in a great city. In Donne’s The Canonization, the lovers are imagined through the language of sainthood: religious and secular love produce tensions that structure the poem. The point is not that the poem has no literal sense, but that paraphrase alone cannot reproduce all its relations.

## Evaluate
A close reading can make detail visible; ask also what happens when history, readers or social context receive less attention. Not every poem must be forced into a single paradox.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish paradox from error. 10–22: read a short passage closely. 22–32: map sacred and secular language in Donne. 32–42: consider strengths and limits of textual focus. 42–50: write a claim grounded in two details.

## Questions
Why can paraphrase lose meaning? What tension does Brooks find in The Canonization?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:2.title: Roman Jakobson · Two Aspects of Language
course-27:2.text:
# Roman Jakobson · Two Aspects of Language
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Two operations
Jakobson analyses language through selection and combination. Selection chooses among alternatives that could occupy a position: “child”, “student” and “singer” might each fit a sentence in a particular context. Combination joins elements in an actual sequence: words are arranged to produce a sentence. Both operations work together.

He relates selection to similarity and metaphor, and combination to contiguity and metonymy. A metaphor makes meaning through resemblance, as in describing a brave person as a lion. Metonymy uses an association or adjacency, as when “the crown” refers to a monarchy. Real expressions can involve multiple relations; neither entire poems nor whole genres are exclusively one pole.

## Aphasia and careful reading
Jakobson examines different language difficulties associated with aphasia to explore disruptions to selection and combination. These are theoretical and historical models, not a diagnostic tool. Aphasia varies widely by person; it does not imply a lack of intelligence. Do not diagnose individuals from classroom exercises.

## Application
Compare a resemblance-based image with a part-for-whole or institution-based association, and explain why each relation makes sense in context.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: replace one word in a sentence. 10–22: distinguish choice from sequence. 22–32: compare metaphor and metonymy. 32–42: discuss the limits of aphasia models. 42–50: analyse one example of each.

## Questions
What changes when a word is substituted? How does metonymy differ from metaphor?

Teaching draft: compare the prescribed extract, translation and edition before class.

course-27:3.title: Jonathan Culler · The Linguistic Foundation
course-27:3.text:
# Jonathan Culler · The Linguistic Foundation
Literary Criticism I · Semester 5

## Structuralist question
In the chapter “The Linguistic Foundation” from Structuralist Poetics, Culler explores how linguistic models can help explain cultural meaning. Rather than treating a literary work as a self-explanatory object, structuralist poetics asks about the systems and conventions that make particular effects intelligible. Verify the assigned edition and selection.

## Concepts
Saussure distinguishes langue, the shared system of language, from parole, particular acts of speech or writing. Linguistic units gain value through relations and contrasts within a system. A sign joins a signifier, such as a sound-pattern, with a signified, a concept; their association is generally conventional rather than naturally required.

Culler considers relations, signs and the methods used to infer underlying systems from particular instances. Later parts of his book develop literary competence: the learned conventions that help readers recognise a genre or make sense of a text. This is related context, not necessarily content from the assigned chapter.

## Example
The opening of a detective story activates expectations about clues, suspicion and eventual explanation. These are conventions readers learn; a particular story may confirm or frustrate them. A structuralist asks what makes those expectations possible.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify a familiar genre convention. 10–22: explain system and instance. 22–32: compare signs and differences. 32–42: infer an interpretive convention from a passage. 42–50: distinguish chapter content from later related concepts.

## Questions
How does langue differ from parole? What is gained by asking about conventions rather than only a single interpretation?
